abstract: A novel unsupervised neural network for dimensionality reduction which seeks directions emphasizing multimodality is presented, and its connec(cid:173) tion to exploratory projection pursuit methods is discussed. This leads to a new statistical insight to the synaptic modification equations governing learning in Bienenstock, Cooper, and Munro (BCM) neurons (1982). The importance of a dimensionality reduction principle based solely on distinguishing features, is demonstrated using a linguistically motivated phoneme recognition experiment, and compared with feature extraction using back-propagation network.

paragraphs: This paper introduces an unsupervised neural network for reducing the dimensionality of speech-related data. Its selection principle is to seek directions that emphasize multimodality: representations in which the data show multiple distinct concentrations. The aim is to preserve distinguishing structure when converting a richer input into a smaller set of features.

The authors connect this approach to exploratory projection pursuit, framing the search for informative directions as a statistical problem. They also use the connection to provide a new statistical interpretation of the synaptic learning equations associated with Bienenstock, Cooper, and Munro neurons. The contribution therefore links a feature-extraction objective with a particular neural learning rule.

A linguistically motivated phoneme recognition experiment demonstrates the importance of building dimensionality reduction around distinguishing features. The study also compares the proposed feature extraction with extraction using a backpropagation network. The stated significance is the usefulness of this selection principle for speech recognition, together with the interpretation it supplies for BCM learning, rather than a numerical performance claim in the supplied abstract.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised network extracts distinguishing speech features by seeking multimodal projections and connects this objective to BCM learning.

title: Exploratory Feature Extraction in Speech Signals

paragraphs: This paper relates two ways to describe a network's capacity: VC dimension and statistical lower epsilon-capacity. VC dimension concerns the richness of a classifier family, while the statistical quantity concerns capacity under random sampling. The authors establish a relationship that gives an order-level lower bound on VC dimension from the statistical capacity.

The relationship is used to explain quantitatively how generalization occurs after memorization. It also connects consistency with the capacities of the best classifier in a fixed structural family and the Bayesian classifier. These connections place memorization and generalization within a shared analysis of what a network family can represent.

The paper then turns the relationship into a method for obtaining VC-dimension lower bounds for feed-forward networks. It applies that method to two hardware-relevant cases: a two-layer network with binary weights and specified threshold restrictions, and a single binary-weight neuron with zero threshold. The contribution combines a general capacity relationship with applications to architectures whose discrete parameters matter for hardware implementation.
summary.tldr: A relationship between statistical capacity and VC dimension yields lower bounds for hardware-oriented binary-weight networks.

title: The VC-Dimension versus the Statistical Capacity of Multilayer Networks
Learning in Computer Vision and Image Understanding

abstract: It has recently been shown that gradient descent learning algo(cid:173) rithms for recurrent neural networks can perform poorly on tasks that involve long-term dependencies. In this paper we explore this problem for a class of architectures called NARX networks, which have powerful representational capabilities. Previous work reported that gradient descent learning is more effective in NARX networks than in recurrent networks with "hidden states". We show that although NARX networks do not circumvent the prob(cid:173) lem of long-term dependencies, they can greatly improve perfor(cid:173) mance on such problems. We present some experimental 'results that show that NARX networks can often retain information for two to three times as long as conventional recurrent networks.

paragraphs: Tasks with long-term dependencies require a network to retain information that becomes useful much later. Gradient descent can struggle to train recurrent networks for such tasks. This paper examines whether choosing a NARX architecture makes that difficulty more manageable, building on earlier reports of more effective learning than in recurrent networks with hidden states.

The authors investigate NARX networks as a class with strong representational capabilities. Their central conclusion separates improvement from elimination of the problem: these networks still encounter long-term dependency difficulties, but their performance can be substantially better. Architecture therefore affects how severe the learning challenge becomes even when gradient-based training remains in use.

The reported experiments show that NARX networks can often retain information for two to three times as long as conventional recurrent networks. This is a comparative finding about the duration of useful memory in the studied tasks. It supports NARX networks as a way to extend that duration while preserving the paper's explicit conclusion that the underlying difficulty remains.
summary.tldr: NARX networks can retain information two to three times longer than conventional recurrent networks without eliminating long-term dependency difficulties.

title: Learning long-term dependencies is not as difficult with NARX networks

abstract: We introduce a new, non-parametric and principled, distance based clustering method. This method combines a pairwise based ap(cid:173) proach with a vector-quantization method which provide a mean(cid:173) ingful interpretation to the resulting clusters. The idea is based on turning the distance matrix into a Markov process and then examine the decay of mutual-information during the relaxation of this process. The clusters emerge as quasi-stable structures dur(cid:173) ing this relaxation, and then are extracted using the information bottleneck method. These clusters capture the information about the initial point of the relaxation in the most effective way. The method can cluster data with no geometric or other bias and makes no assumption about the underlying distribution.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a distance-based clustering method that combines pairwise relationships with vector quantization. Its starting point is a matrix of distances between data items. The method turns that matrix into a Markov process, making clustering a question about how information changes as a probabilistic process evolves.

During the process's relaxation, the method examines the decline in mutual information about the starting point. Clusters appear as structures that remain relatively stable while the overall process relaxes. This supplies an interpretation of a cluster: it is a grouping that persists in the dynamics and retains information about where those dynamics began.

The information bottleneck method then extracts these groupings to capture information about the initial point as effectively as possible. The authors describe the approach as nonparametric and requiring no assumption about the underlying distribution or imposed geometric bias. Its central contribution is the connection between distances, temporal persistence, and information preservation, which gives the resulting clusters a meaning tied to the constructed process.
summary.tldr: The method finds clusters as persistent structures in a distance-derived Markov process and extracts them through the information bottleneck.

title: Data Clustering by Markovian Relaxation and the Information Bottleneck Method

abstract: We present a new technique for achieving source separation when given only a single channel recording. The main idea is based on exploiting the inherent time structure of sound sources by learning a priori sets of basis ﬁlters in time domain that encode the sources in a statistically efﬁcient manner. We derive a learning algorithm using a maximum likelihood approach given the observed single channel data and sets of basis ﬁlters. For each time point we infer the source signals and their contribution factors. This inference is possible due to the prior knowledge of the basis ﬁlters and the associated coefﬁcient densities. A ﬂexible model for density estimation allows accurate modeling of the observation and our experimental results exhibit a high level of separation performance for mixtures of two music signals as well as the separation of two voice signals.

paragraphs: This paper addresses separating sound sources when only one recorded mixture is available. Its approach uses the temporal structure of sounds as prior information. Before separation, it learns sets of time-domain basis filters that represent sources statistically efficiently, providing a vocabulary of patterns with which to explain the mixed recording.

Given these filters and the observed recording, the authors derive a maximum-likelihood learning algorithm. At each time point, it infers the source signals and factors describing their contributions. The inference relies on both the previously learned filters and probability distributions for their coefficients. A flexible density model helps represent the observed data accurately.

Experiments report a high level of separation performance for mixtures of two music signals and for two voice signals. These results support using learned temporal structure to distinguish sources from a single channel. The role of prior information is central: the method's ability to infer separate signals depends on the basis filters and their associated coefficient distributions.
summary.tldr: Learned temporal filters and coefficient distributions enable probabilistic separation of two sound sources from a single recorded mixture.

title: A Probabilistic Approach to Single Channel Blind Signal Separation

abstract: We propose a mean-ﬁeld approximation that dramatically reduces the computational complexity of solving stochastic dynamic games. We pro- vide conditions that guarantee our method approximates an equilibrium as the number of agents grow. We then derive a performance bound to assess how well the approximation performs for any given number of agents. We apply our method to an important class of problems in ap- plied microeconomics. We show with numerical experiments that we are able to greatly expand the set of economic problems that can be analyzed computationally.
originalAbstract: We propose a mean-ﬁeld approximation that dramatically reduces the computational complexity of solving stochastic dynamic games. We pro- vide conditions that guarantee our method approximates an equilibrium as the number of agents grow. We then derive a performance bound to assess how well the approximation performs for any given number of agents. We apply our method to an important class of problems in ap- plied microeconomics. We show with numerical experiments that we are able to greatly expand the set of economic problems that can be analyzed computationally.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a mean-field approximation for stochastic dynamic games, where many agents make decisions in an evolving, uncertain setting. Its aim is to sharply reduce the computational work needed to solve these games. The approximation provides a more manageable route to analyzing interactions when the number of agents becomes large.

The authors give conditions under which their method approximates an equilibrium as the agent population grows. They also derive a performance bound for a specified finite number of agents. These are complementary contributions: one explains behavior in the large-population limit, while the other helps assess approximation quality at a particular population size.

The method is applied to an important class of problems in applied microeconomics. Numerical experiments show that it substantially expands the range of economic problems that can be studied computationally. The significance is the combination of computational savings and explicit approximation analysis, with the large-population equilibrium guarantee tied to the conditions established by the authors.
summary.tldr: A mean-field approximation makes large dynamic games more tractable, with conditional equilibrium guarantees and finite-population performance bounds.

title: Oblivious Equilibrium: A Mean Field Approximation for Large-Scale Dynamic Games

abstract: Survival in a non-stationary, potentially adversarial environment requires animals to detect sensory changes rapidly yet accurately, two oft competing desiderata. Neurons subserving such detections are faced with the corresponding challenge to discern "real" changes in inputs as quickly as possible, while ignoring noisy fluctuations. Mathematically, this is an example of a change-detection problem that is actively researched in the controlled stochastic processes community. In this paper, we utilize sophisticated tools developed in that community to formalize an instantiation of the problem faced by the nervous system, and characterize the Bayes-optimal decision policy under certain assumptions. We will derive from this optimal strategy an information accumulation and decision process that remarkably resembles the dynamics of a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron. This correspondence suggests that neurons are optimized for tracking input changes, and sheds new light on the computational import of intracellular properties such as resting membrane potential, voltage-dependent conductance, and post-spike reset voltage. We also explore the influence that factors such as timing, uncertainty, neuromodulation, and reward should and do have on neuronal dynamics and sensitivity, as the optimal decision strategy depends critically on these factors.

paragraphs: Detecting a real change in sensory input requires balancing speed against the risk of reacting to noise. This paper formalizes an instance of that problem using tools from controlled stochastic processes. Under certain assumptions, the authors characterize the Bayesian decision policy that optimally balances the competing demands.

From that policy, they derive a process for accumulating information and deciding when a change has occurred. Its dynamics closely resemble those of a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron. This correspondence supplies a computational interpretation of neuronal properties, including resting membrane potential, voltage-dependent conductance, and the voltage to which a neuron resets after a spike.

The authors also examine how timing, uncertainty, neuromodulation, and reward affect the optimal strategy and neuronal sensitivity. The resemblance between the derived decision process and a spiking neuron suggests that neurons may be optimized for tracking changes in their inputs. This is an interpretation supported by the modeled correspondence under the paper's assumptions, rather than a universal demonstration that every neuron implements an optimal detector.
summary.tldr: Under specified assumptions, optimal Bayesian change detection yields dynamics resembling a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron.

title: Optimal Change-Detection and Spiking Neurons

abstract: In this article, we propose fast subtree kernels on graphs. On graphs with n nodes and m edges and maximum degree d, these kernels comparing subtrees of height h can be computed in O(mh), whereas the classic subtree kernel by Ramon & G¨artner scales as O(n24dh). Key to this efﬁciency is the observation that the Weisfeiler-Lehman test of isomorphism from graph theory elegantly computes a subtree kernel as a byproduct. Our fast subtree kernels can deal with labeled graphs, scale up easily to large graphs and outperform state-of-the-art graph ker- nels on several classiﬁcation benchmark datasets in terms of accuracy and runtime.

paragraphs: This paper develops efficient ways to compare graphs using their subtree structure. A graph kernel supplies a similarity measure that a classifier can use, making the cost of computing that similarity important. The proposed kernels compare subtrees up to a chosen height while supporting graphs whose nodes carry labels.

The key observation links this learning problem to the Weisfeiler-Lehman graph isomorphism test. The authors show that the test produces the information needed for a subtree kernel as a byproduct. Reusing that computation gives a runtime of O(mh), where m is the number of edges and h is the subtree height, improving on the classic subtree kernel discussed in the paper.

This computational dependence makes comparisons practical on larger graphs and gives a clear account of how increasing structural depth affects cost. Experiments on several graph classification benchmarks report better accuracy and runtime than leading graph kernels. The contribution therefore combines an algorithmic efficiency result with empirical evidence that the faster structural comparison remains useful for prediction on the evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: Weisfeiler-Lehman computations yield subtree graph kernels with O(mh) runtime and strong benchmark classification performance.

title: Fast subtree kernels on graphs

abstract: The goal of decentralized optimization over a network is to optimize a global objective formed by a sum of local (possibly nonsmooth) convex functions using only local computation and communication. We develop and analyze distributed algorithms based on dual averaging of subgradients, and we provide sharp bounds on their convergence rates as a function of the network size and topology. Our analysis clearly separates the convergence of the optimization algorithm itself from the effects of communication constraints arising from the network structure. We show that the number of iterations required by our algorithm scales inversely in the spectral gap of the network. The sharpness of this prediction is confirmed both by theoretical lower bounds and simulations for various networks.

paragraphs: Decentralized optimization asks a network of participants to minimize a shared objective using only local computation and communication. Here, the shared objective is a sum of local convex functions, which may be nonsmooth. Each participant contributes part of the problem, while the network limits how information about those parts can travel.

The paper develops distributed algorithms based on dual averaging of subgradients and analyzes their convergence rates. A central feature of the analysis is that it separates progress attributable to the optimization method from the effects of restricted communication. This makes it possible to describe how network size and topology influence the time needed to reach a solution.

The required number of iterations scales inversely with the network's spectral gap, a quantity characterizing its communication structure. In this analysis, a smaller gap therefore implies more iterations. The authors support the sharpness of this dependence with theoretical lower bounds and simulations across different networks. The result ties computational progress to a concrete mathematical property of the network.
summary.tldr: Distributed dual averaging admits sharp convergence bounds that separate optimization progress from communication effects and depend inversely on the network's spectral gap.

title: Distributed Dual Averaging In Networks

abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) learns multiple related tasks simultaneously to improve generalization performance. Alternating structure optimization (ASO) is a popular MTL method that learns a shared low-dimensional predictive structure on hypothesis spaces from multiple related tasks. It has been applied successfully in many real world applications. As an alternative MTL approach, clustered multi-task learning (CMTL) assumes that multiple tasks follow a clustered structure, i.e., tasks are partitioned into a set of groups where tasks in the same group are similar to each other, and that such a clustered structure is unknown a priori. The objectives in ASO and CMTL differ in how multiple tasks are related. Interestingly, we show in this paper the equivalence relationship between ASO and CMTL, providing significant new insights into ASO and CMTL as well as their inherent relationship. The CMTL formulation is non-convex, and we adopt a convex relaxation to the CMTL formulation. We further establish the equivalence relationship between the proposed convex relaxation of CMTL and an existing convex relaxation of ASO, and show that the proposed convex CMTL formulation is significantly more efficient especially for high-dimensional data. In addition, we present three algorithms for solving the convex CMTL formulation. We report experimental results on benchmark datasets to demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper connects two approaches to learning related prediction tasks together. Alternating structure optimization learns a shared, low-dimensional predictive structure. Clustered multitask learning instead assumes that tasks belong to initially unknown groups, with similar tasks placed together. These descriptions suggest different ways for one task to benefit from information associated with others.

The authors establish an equivalence relationship between the two formulations. This gives a connection between learning shared predictive structure and discovering groups of related tasks. Because the clustered formulation is nonconvex, they also develop a convex relaxation, replacing the original optimization with a more tractable formulation. They then prove an equivalence between this relaxation and an existing convex relaxation of alternating structure optimization.

The connection has a computational payoff: the proposed convex clustered formulation is significantly more efficient, especially with high-dimensional data. The paper supplies three algorithms for solving it and reports benchmark experiments demonstrating their efficiency. Its contribution therefore combines a theoretical account of how task-sharing formulations relate with practical methods for solving the resulting optimization problems.
summary.tldr: The paper links shared-structure and clustered multitask learning, yielding an efficient convex formulation and three solution algorithms.

title: Clustered Multi-Task Learning Via Alternating Structure Optimization

abstract: Inferring key unobservable features of individuals is an important task in the applied sciences. In particular, an important source of data in fields such as marketing, social sciences and medicine is questionnaires: answers in such questionnaires are noisy measures of target unobserved features. While comprehensive surveys help to better estimate the latent variables of interest, aiming at a high number of questions comes at a price: refusal to participate in surveys can go up, as well as the rate of missing data; quality of answers can decline; costs associated with applying such questionnaires can also increase. In this paper, we cast the problem of refining existing models for questionnaire data as follows: solve a constrained optimization problem of preserving the maximum amount of information found in a latent variable model using only a subset of existing questions. The goal is to find an optimal subset of a given size. For that, we first define an information theoretical measure for quantifying the quality of a reduced questionnaire. Three different approximate inference methods are introduced to solve this problem. Comparisons against a simple but powerful heuristic are presented.

paragraphs: Questionnaires measure unobserved characteristics indirectly through noisy answers. More questions can help estimate those characteristics, but longer surveys can also increase refusal, missing responses, poor-quality answers, and administration costs. This paper studies how to shorten an existing questionnaire while retaining information about the latent variables it was designed to measure.

The authors formulate the task as constrained optimization: choose a subset of a specified size that preserves as much information as possible from an existing latent-variable model. They define an information-theoretic measure to assess the quality of a reduced questionnaire. This makes the selection criterion explicit rather than equating questionnaire quality with its length.

Three approximate inference methods are introduced to address the selection problem, and the paper compares them with a simple but strong heuristic. The optimization target is the best subset of the given size, while the proposed solution methods are approximate. The contribution is a model-based framework for deciding which existing questions retain the most information when survey length must be reduced.
summary.tldr: An information-theoretic optimization framework selects shorter questionnaires that preserve information about latent characteristics.

title: Thinning Measurement Models and Questionnaire Design

abstract: Time delay is pervasive in neural information processing. To achieve real-time tracking, it is critical to compensate the transmission and processing delays in a neural system. In the present study we show that dynamical synapses with short-term depression can enhance the mobility of a continuous attractor network to the extent that the system tracks time-varying stimuli in a timely manner. The state of the network can either track the instantaneous position of a moving stimulus perfectly (with zero-lag) or lead it with an effectively constant time, in agreement with experiments on the head-direction systems in rodents. The parameter regions for delayed, perfect and anticipative tracking correspond to network states that are static, ready-to-move and spontaneously moving, respectively, demonstrating the strong correlation between tracking performance and the intrinsic dynamics of the network. We also find that when the speed of the stimulus coincides with the natural speed of the network state, the delay becomes effectively independent of the stimulus amplitude.

paragraphs: Neural signals take time to transmit and process, creating a challenge for tracking moving stimuli as they change. This paper studies how the dynamics of synapses can help a continuous attractor network compensate for those delays. The relevant synaptic mechanism is short-term depression, a temporary reduction in synaptic effectiveness.

The authors show that this mechanism can make the network's activity state sufficiently mobile to track a stimulus without lag or even lead it by an effectively constant time. Different parameter regions support delayed, zero-lag, and anticipatory tracking. These correspond respectively to network states that are static, poised to move, or moving spontaneously, linking tracking behavior to the network's intrinsic dynamics.

The zero-lag and anticipatory behaviors agree with experiments on rodent head-direction systems. The authors also identify a specific condition under which delay becomes effectively independent of stimulus amplitude: the stimulus moves at the network state's natural speed. These findings explain how timely tracking can emerge from internal dynamics, with performance depending on the network's operating regime.
summary.tldr: Short-term synaptic depression can enable a neural network to track moving stimuli without lag or anticipate their position.

title: Delay Compensation with Dynamical Synapses

abstract: We study the problem of diverse feature selection in linear regression: selecting a small subset of diverse features that can predict a given objective. Diversity is useful for several reasons such as interpretability, robustness to noise, etc. We propose several spectral regularizers that capture a notion of diversity of features and show that these are all submodular set functions. These regularizers, when added to the objective function for linear regression, result in approximately submodular functions, which can then be maximized approximately by efficient greedy and local search algorithms, with provable guarantees. We compare our algorithms to traditional greedy and $\ell_1$-regularization schemes and show that we obtain a more diverse set of features that result in the regression problem being stable under perturbations.

paragraphs: Feature selection for linear regression usually seeks a small set of useful predictors. This paper also asks that the selected features be diverse, motivated by interpretability and robustness to noise. The aim is to make diversity an explicit part of the selection objective while retaining predictive usefulness.

The authors propose several spectral regularizers that express a notion of feature diversity and prove that these regularizers are submodular set functions. Adding them to the regression objective yields approximately submodular objectives. This structure allows efficient greedy and local-search algorithms to seek approximate solutions with provable guarantees.

Comparisons with traditional greedy selection and l1 regularization show that the proposed algorithms select more diverse features and produce regression problems that remain stable under perturbations. The empirical finding therefore links the diversity criterion to the motivating robustness concern. The theoretical contribution explains why the combined objective can be optimized approximately with guarantees, while the experiments show how the resulting selections behave relative to the evaluated alternatives.
summary.tldr: Spectral diversity penalties enable feature-selection algorithms with approximation guarantees and improved perturbation stability in experiments.

title: Selecting Diverse Features via Spectral Regularization

abstract: Inference in general Ising models is difficult, due to high treewidth making tree-based algorithms intractable. Moreover, when interactions are strong, Gibbs sampling may take exponential time to converge to the stationary distribution. We present an algorithm to project Ising model parameters onto a parameter set that is guaranteed to be fast mixing, under several divergences. We find that Gibbs sampling using the projected parameters is more accurate than with the original parameters when interaction strengths are strong and when limited time is available for sampling.

paragraphs: Inference in general Ising models faces two computational obstacles. High treewidth can make tree-based methods intractable, while strong interactions can cause Gibbs sampling to require exponential time to reach its stationary distribution. With a limited sampling budget, using the original model can therefore leave the sampler far from the behavior it is meant to represent.

The paper proposes projecting the model's parameters onto a set for which fast mixing is guaranteed. It develops this projection under several divergence measures, providing different ways to express the discrepancy between the original and modified models. The resulting parameters change the model while placing it in a regime where sampling converges quickly.

The authors find that Gibbs sampling with projected parameters is more accurate than sampling with the original parameters when interactions are strong and sampling time is limited. The finding highlights a practical tradeoff: altering parameters can improve finite-time inference when convergence is otherwise too slow. The reported advantage is tied to those interaction strengths and time constraints.
summary.tldr: Projecting Ising parameters into a fast-mixing set improves reported sampling accuracy under strong interactions and limited computation time.

title: Projecting Ising Model Parameters for Fast Mixing

abstract: The design of convex, calibrated surrogate losses, whose minimization entails consistency with respect to a desired target loss, is an important concept to have emerged in the theory of machine learning in recent years. We give an explicit construction of a convex least-squares type surrogate loss that can be designed to be calibrated for any multiclass learning problem for which the target loss matrix has a low-rank structure; the surrogate loss operates on a surrogate target space of dimension at most the rank of the target loss. We use this result to design convex calibrated surrogates for a variety of subset ranking problems, with target losses including the precision@q, expected rank utility, mean average precision, and pairwise disagreement.

paragraphs: A learning system may be judged by a target loss that is difficult to optimize directly. A surrogate loss provides an alternative training objective. The key theoretical question is whether optimizing that alternative is aligned with the original goal. This paper constructs convex surrogates that are calibrated, meaning their minimization supports consistency with respect to the desired target loss.

The construction applies to multiclass problems whose target loss matrix has low rank. That matrix records the costs associated with predictions and outcomes; its rank captures structure that can reduce the dimension needed for the surrogate. The proposed least-squares-style loss uses a target space with dimension no greater than the matrix rank.

The authors apply the construction to subset ranking, covering precision at a specified cutoff, expected rank utility, mean average precision, and pairwise disagreement. These applications show how one structural result can produce calibrated objectives for several distinct evaluation criteria. The contribution is an explicit design method connecting convex optimization, dimensionality, and the loss that ultimately matters.
summary.tldr: Low-rank loss matrices enable explicit convex, calibrated surrogates whose dimension is at most the target loss matrix's rank.

title: Convex Calibrated Surrogates for Low-Rank Loss Matrices with Applications to Subset Ranking Losses

abstract: We study the problem of estimating continuous quantities, such as prices, probabilities, and point spreads, using a crowdsourcing approach. A challenging aspect of combining the crowd's answers is that workers' reliabilities and biases are usually unknown and highly diverse. Control items with known answers can be used to evaluate workers' performance, and hence improve the combined results on the target items with unknown answers. This raises the problem of how many control items to use when the total number of items each workers can answer is limited: more control items evaluates the workers better, but leaves fewer resources for the target items that are of direct interest, and vice versa. We give theoretical results for this problem under different scenarios, and provide a simple rule of thumb for crowdsourcing practitioners. As a byproduct, we also provide theoretical analysis of the accuracy of different consensus methods.

Questions with known answers can help evaluate workers before their responses are combined on questions whose answers are unknown.

The difficulty is allocating a limited response budget. Giving each worker more control questions improves the information available about that worker, but leaves fewer answers for the target questions. Giving fewer controls preserves target responses while making worker assessment less informative. The paper treats this allocation as a theoretical problem rather than assuming that more evaluation is always beneficial.

The authors derive results for several scenarios and provide a simple rule of thumb for practitioners. Their analysis also yields theoretical results on the accuracy of different methods for forming consensus. The contribution connects worker evaluation to the ultimate quality of the combined estimate, accounting for the fact that assessment and target answering compete for the same limited resources.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes how to balance worker-scoring questions against target questions when crowdsourcing continuous estimates under a limited response budget.

title: Scoring Workers in Crowdsourcing: How Many Control Questions are Enough?

abstract: High-dimensional, simultaneous recordings of neural spiking activity are often explored, analyzed and visualized with the help of latent variable or factor models. Such models are however ill-equipped to extract structure beyond shared, distributed aspects of firing activity across multiple cells. Here, we extend unstructured factor models by proposing a model that discovers subpopulations or groups of cells from the pool of recorded neurons. The model combines aspects of mixture of factor analyzer models for capturing clustering structure, and aspects of latent dynamical system models for capturing temporal dependencies. In the resulting model, we infer the subpopulations and the latent factors from data using variational inference and model parameters are estimated by Expectation Maximization (EM). We also address the crucial problem of initializing parameters for EM by extending a sparse subspace clustering algorithm to integer-valued spike count observations. We illustrate the merits of the proposed model by applying it to calcium-imaging data from spinal cord neurons, and we show that it uncovers meaningful clustering structure in the data.

paragraphs: Factor models help summarize simultaneous recordings from many neurons by finding shared patterns of activity. However, unstructured models are poorly suited to discovering distinct groups of cells within those recordings. This paper extends factor modeling to infer neuronal subpopulations as well as the latent activity patterns associated with the data.

The proposed model combines clustering ideas from mixtures of factor analyzers with temporal modeling from latent dynamical systems. Variational inference estimates subpopulation assignments and latent factors, while expectation-maximization learns model parameters. The approach therefore represents both group structure across neurons and dependencies in activity over time within one model.

The authors also address parameter initialization, an important part of fitting the model with expectation-maximization. They adapt sparse subspace clustering to integer-valued spike counts to provide that starting point. An application to calcium-imaging data from spinal cord neurons reveals meaningful clustering structure. The example illustrates how explicitly modeling subpopulations can expose organization that a model focused only on shared, distributed activity is not equipped to extract.
summary.tldr: A clustered temporal factor model jointly discovers neuronal subpopulations and latent activity, revealing meaningful structure in spinal-cord imaging data.

title: Clustered factor analysis of multineuronal spike data

abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are powerful models that have achieved excellent performance on difficult learning tasks. Although DNNs work well whenever large labeled training sets are available, they cannot be used to map sequences to sequences. In this paper, we present a general end-to-end approach to sequence learning that makes minimal assumptions on the sequence structure. Our method uses a multilayered Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) to map the input sequence to a vector of a fixed dimensionality, and then another deep LSTM to decode the target sequence from the vector. Our main result is that on an English to French translation task from the WMT-14 dataset, the translations produced by the LSTM achieve a BLEU score of 34.8 on the entire test set, where the LSTM's BLEU score was penalized on out-of-vocabulary words. Additionally, the LSTM did not have difficulty on long sentences. For comparison, a phrase-based SMT system achieves a BLEU score of 33.3 on the same dataset. When we used the LSTM to rerank the 1000 hypotheses produced by the aforementioned SMT system, its BLEU score increases to 36.5, which is close to the previous state of the art. The LSTM also learned sensible phrase and sentence representations that are sensitive to word order and are relatively invariant to the active and the passive voice. Finally, we found that reversing the order of the words in all source sentences (but not target sentences) improved the LSTM's performance markedly, because doing so introduced many short term dependencies between the source and the target sentence which made the optimization problem easier.

Reversing source sentences, while leaving target sentences unchanged, markedly improves performance. The authors attribute this improvement to shorter dependencies between source and target, which make optimization easier. The findings show how both the encoder-decoder design and input ordering affect the reported translation results.
summary.tldr: An LSTM encoder-decoder learns sequence mappings and achieves strong translation results, with substantial improvement from reversing source-word order.

title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks

abstract: The $k$-support norm has successfully been applied to sparse vector prediction problems. We observe that it belongs to a wider class of norms, which we call the box-norms. Within this framework we derive an efficient algorithm to compute the proximity operator of the squared norm, improving upon the original method for the $k$-support norm. We extend the norms from the vector to the matrix setting and we introduce the spectral $k$-support norm. We study its properties and show that it is closely related to the multitask learning cluster norm. We apply the norms to real and synthetic matrix completion datasets. Our findings indicate that spectral $k$-support norm regularization gives state of the art performance, consistently improving over trace norm regularization and the matrix elastic net.

We extend the norms from the vector to the matrix setting and we introduce the spectral $k$-support norm. We study its properties and show that it is closely related to the multitask learning cluster norm. We apply the norms to real and synthetic matrix completion datasets. Our findings indicate that spectral $k$-support norm regularization gives state of the art performance, consistently improving over trace norm regularization and the matrix elastic net.

paragraphs: The k-support norm was developed for prediction problems involving sparse vectors. This paper places it within a larger family called box-norms. That broader perspective provides both a way to study related regularizers together and a route to improving the computation required to use them in optimization.

Within this framework, the authors derive an efficient proximity-operator algorithm for the squared norm, improving on the original k-support method. Such an operator handles the regularization part of an optimization update. They also move from vectors to matrices by introducing the spectral k-support norm and establish a close relationship with the multitask learning cluster norm.

The matrix norms are evaluated on real and synthetic matrix-completion datasets, where the task is to recover missing matrix entries. The reported findings indicate state-of-the-art performance for spectral k-support regularization, with consistent improvements over trace-norm regularization and the matrix elastic net in those experiments. The contribution thus combines a broader mathematical framework, improved optimization machinery, and empirical support for the matrix extension.
summary.tldr: The paper generalizes k-support regularization to matrices, improves a key optimization step, and reports strong matrix-completion performance.

title: Spectral k-Support Norm Regularization

abstract: To master a discipline such as algebra or physics, students must acquire a set of cognitive skills. Traditionally, educators and domain experts manually determine what these skills are and then select practice exercises to hone a particular skill. We propose a technique that uses student performance data to automatically discover the skills needed in a discipline. The technique assigns a latent skill to each exercise such that a student's expected accuracy on a sequence of same-skill exercises improves monotonically with practice. Rather than discarding the skills identified by experts, our technique incorporates a nonparametric prior over the exercise-skill assignments that is based on the expert-provided skills and a weighted Chinese restaurant process. We test our technique on datasets from five different intelligent tutoring systems designed for students ranging in age from middle school through college. We obtain two surprising results. First, in three of the five datasets, the skills inferred by our technique support significantly improved predictions of student performance over the expert-provided skills. Second, the expert-provided skills have little value: our technique predicts student performance nearly as well when it ignores the domain expertise as when it attempts to leverage it. We discuss explanations for these surprising results and also the relationship of our skill-discovery technique to alternative approaches.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether student performance can reveal the skills underlying practice exercises. Educators traditionally define these skills and assign exercises to them. The proposed method instead learns exercise-to-skill assignments from performance data, using improvement with practice as its organizing principle. Each exercise receives a latent skill, and expected accuracy on successive exercises involving that skill is constrained to improve monotonically.

Expert knowledge can still influence the assignments. The model includes a nonparametric prior based on expert-provided skills and a weighted Chinese restaurant process. This makes the experts' categorization an input to skill discovery rather than treating it as the final grouping. The inferred assignments are then assessed through their ability to predict student performance.

Tests cover five intelligent tutoring systems serving students from middle school through college. In three datasets, inferred skills significantly improve predictions over expert-defined skills. Predictions are also nearly as good when expert information is omitted as when it is incorporated. These findings concern the predictive usefulness of the skill groupings in those datasets, and suggest that performance patterns can provide substantial information about how exercises should be grouped.
summary.tldr: Learning skill assignments from student practice data improves performance prediction over expert assignments in three of five tutoring datasets.

title: Automatic Discovery of Cognitive Skills to Improve the Prediction of Student Learning

abstract: Hierarchical feed-forward networks have been successfully applied in object recognition. At each level of the hierarchy, features are extracted and encoded, followed by a pooling step. Within this processing pipeline, the common trend is to learn the feature coding templates, often referred as codebook entries, filters, or over-complete basis. Recently, an approach that apparently does not use templates has been shown to obtain very promising results. This is the second-order pooling (O2P). In this paper, we analyze O2P as a coding-pooling scheme. We find that at testing phase, O2P automatically adapts the feature coding templates to the input features, rather than using templates learned during the training phase. From this finding, we are able to bring common concepts of coding-pooling schemes to O2P, such as feature quantization. This allows for significant accuracy improvements of O2P in standard benchmarks of image classification, namely Caltech101 and VOC07.

paragraphs: Hierarchical recognition systems commonly extract features, encode them using templates, and pool the resulting codes. Those templates may be described as filters, codebook entries, or an overcomplete basis, and are often learned during training. Second-order pooling had produced promising results despite appearing to operate without such templates.

The paper reinterprets second-order pooling as a coding-and-pooling scheme. Its analysis finds that the method does use feature-coding templates, but adapts them automatically to the input features at test time. This explains the method through the same general language used for more familiar coding pipelines while identifying a distinctive source of adaptation.

That interpretation makes it possible to bring established coding-and-pooling concepts, including feature quantization, into second-order pooling. The resulting changes significantly improve accuracy on the Caltech101 and VOC07 image-classification benchmarks. The contribution therefore includes both an explanation of an existing method and a practical consequence of that explanation: understanding its implicit templates suggests ways to improve the representation it produces for recognition.
summary.tldr: Second-order pooling implicitly adapts coding templates at test time, an insight that enables accuracy improvements through concepts such as feature quantization.

title: Self-Adaptable Templates for Feature Coding

abstract: Kernel methods provide a principled way to perform non linear, nonparametric learning. They rely on solid functional analytic foundations and enjoy optimal statistical properties. However, at least in their basic form, they have limited applicability in large scale scenarios because of stringent computational requirements in terms of time and especially memory. In this paper, we take a substantial step in scaling up kernel methods, proposing FALKON, a novel algorithm that allows to efficiently process millions of points. FALKON is derived combining several algorithmic principles, namely stochastic subsampling, iterative solvers and preconditioning. Our theoretical analysis shows that optimal statistical accuracy is achieved requiring essentially $O(n)$ memory and $O(n\sqrt{n})$ time. An extensive experimental analysis on large scale datasets shows that, even with a single machine, FALKON outperforms previous state of the art solutions, which exploit parallel/distributed architectures.

paragraphs: Kernel methods offer a principled way to learn nonlinear relationships and have strong statistical foundations. Their basic implementations can nevertheless demand too much computation and memory for large datasets. FALKON addresses this gap between statistical appeal and practical scale with an algorithm designed to process millions of data points.

The method combines stochastic subsampling, iterative solvers, and preconditioning. Together, these algorithmic ingredients reduce the resources needed to carry out kernel learning. The theoretical analysis shows that optimal statistical accuracy can be achieved with essentially linear memory in the number of examples, n, and a running time proportional to n times the square root of n.

The significance is that computational savings are accompanied by an accuracy guarantee. The authors also evaluate FALKON extensively on large datasets and report that it outperforms previous state-of-the-art solutions using parallel or distributed architectures, even when FALKON runs on one machine. This supports its practicality in the tested settings alongside the theoretical scaling result.
summary.tldr: FALKON scales kernel learning to millions of examples while achieving optimal statistical accuracy with essentially linear memory.

title: FALKON: An Optimal Large Scale Kernel Method

abstract: We propose a deep learning-based approach to the problem of premise selection: selecting mathematical statements relevant for proving a given conjecture. We represent a higher-order logic formula as a graph that is invariant to variable renaming but still fully preserves syntactic and semantic information. We then embed the graph into a vector via a novel embedding method that preserves the information of edge ordering. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on the HolStep dataset, improving the classification accuracy from 83% to 90.3%.
originalAbstract: We propose a deep learning-based approach to the problem of premise selection: selecting mathematical statements relevant for proving a given conjecture. We represent a higher-order logic formula as a graph that is invariant to variable renaming but still fully preserves syntactic and semantic information. We then embed the graph into a vector via a novel embedding method that preserves the information of edge ordering. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on the HolStep dataset, improving the classification accuracy from 83% to 90.3%.

paragraphs: This paper uses deep learning to select mathematical statements that are relevant to proving a conjecture. Premise selection is a filtering problem: the system must recognize which available statements are useful for the proof under consideration. The authors focus on representing logical formulas in a way that exposes their structure to a learned model.

They encode higher-order logic formulas as graphs that remain unchanged under variable renaming while preserving syntactic and semantic information. This means that changing variable names does not change the representation of the formula’s content. A new graph embedding method then converts each graph into a vector while retaining information about the ordering of edges.

These representation choices let the model handle naming invariance without discarding structural distinctions carried by the formula. On the HolStep dataset, the approach raises classification accuracy from 83% to 90.3%, achieving state-of-the-art results. The reported finding concerns the premise-selection classification task and demonstrates the effectiveness of this structure-preserving graph representation in that evaluation.
summary.tldr: Structure-preserving graph embeddings improve premise-selection accuracy on HolStep from 83% to 90.3%.

title: Premise Selection for Theorem Proving by Deep Graph Embedding

abstract: We propose a Bayesian regression method that accounts for multi-way interactions of arbitrary orders among the predictor variables. Our model makes use of a factorization mechanism for representing the regression coefficients of interactions among the predictors, while the interaction selection is guided by a prior distribution on random hypergraphs, a construction which generalizes the Finite Feature Model. We present a posterior inference algorithm based on Gibbs sampling, and establish posterior consistency of our regression model. Our method is evaluated with extensive experiments on simulated data and demonstrated to be able to identify meaningful interactions in applications in genetics and retail demand forecasting.
originalAbstract: We propose a Bayesian regression method that accounts for multi-way interactions of arbitrary orders among the predictor variables. Our model makes use of a factorization mechanism for representing the regression coefficients of interactions among the predictors, while the interaction selection is guided by a prior distribution on random hypergraphs, a construction which generalizes the Finite Feature Model. We present a posterior inference algorithm based on Gibbs sampling, and establish posterior consistency of our regression model. Our method is evaluated with extensive experiments on simulated data and demonstrated to be able to identify meaningful interactions in applications in genetics and retail demand forecasting.

paragraphs: Predictors can influence an outcome through combinations involving several variables, rather than only through separate effects. This paper proposes a Bayesian regression model that accommodates interactions of arbitrary order. Its scope therefore includes relationships involving more than pairs of predictors, with interaction structure forming part of the modeling problem.

The model uses factorization to represent interaction coefficients and a prior over random hypergraphs to guide which interactions are selected. A hypergraph can represent groups containing multiple predictors, matching the multi-way nature of the relationships being considered. The prior construction generalizes the Finite Feature Model, while posterior inference is carried out with a Gibbs-sampling algorithm.

The authors establish posterior consistency, providing theoretical support for the model’s statistical behavior as evidence accumulates under the result’s conditions. Extensive simulated-data experiments evaluate the method, and applications in genetics and retail demand forecasting demonstrate its ability to identify meaningful interactions. The contribution brings interaction representation, selection, and Bayesian inference into a single regression approach.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian factorization model uses random-hypergraph priors to select multi-way predictor interactions and identifies meaningful relationships in reported applications.

title: Multi-way Interacting Regression via Factorization Machines

abstract: Motivated by applications in Optimization, Game Theory, and the training of Generative Adversarial Networks, the convergence properties of first order methods in min-max problems have received extensive study. It has been recognized that they may cycle, and there is no good understanding of their limit points when they do not. When they converge, do they converge to local min-max solutions? We characterize the limit points of two basic first order methods, namely Gradient Descent/Ascent (GDA) and Optimistic Gradient Descent Ascent (OGDA). We show that both dynamics avoid unstable critical points for almost all initializations. Moreover, for small step sizes and under mild assumptions, the set of OGDA-stable critical points is a superset of GDA-stable critical points, which is a superset of local min-max solutions (strict in some cases). The connecting thread is that the behavior of these dynamics can be studied from a dynamical systems perspective.
originalAbstract: Motivated by applications in Optimization, Game Theory, and the training of Generative Adversarial Networks, the convergence properties of first order methods in min-max problems have received extensive study. It has been recognized that they may cycle, and there is no good understanding of their limit points when they do not. When they converge, do they converge to local min-max solutions? We characterize the limit points of two basic first order methods, namely Gradient Descent/Ascent (GDA) and Optimistic Gradient Descent Ascent (OGDA). We show that both dynamics avoid unstable critical points for almost all initializations. Moreover, for small step sizes and under mild assumptions, the set of OGDA-stable critical points is a superset of GDA-stable critical points, which is a superset of local min-max solutions (strict in some cases). The connecting thread is that the behavior of these dynamics can be studied from a dynamical systems perspective.

paragraphs: In min-max optimization, one side minimizes an objective while another maximizes it. Gradient-based updates can cycle, but even convergence leaves an important question: does the limit represent a local min-max solution? This paper investigates that question for gradient descent/ascent and its optimistic variant using a dynamical-systems perspective.

The authors show that both dynamics avoid unstable critical points for almost all initializations. They then compare the sets of critical points that are stable under each method. With small step sizes and under mild assumptions, every GDA-stable critical point is OGDA-stable, and the GDA-stable set contains the local min-max solutions.

Some of these containments are strict, meaning the stable sets can include points beyond local min-max solutions. Consequently, stability or convergence of these dynamics does not by itself identify a local min-max solution. The analysis clarifies the relationship between an algorithm's stable behavior and the optimization target, while preserving the step-size and assumption conditions needed for the comparison.
summary.tldr: GDA and OGDA avoid unstable critical points for almost all initializations, but their stable points can extend beyond local min-max solutions.

title: The Limit Points of (Optimistic) Gradient Descent in Min-Max Optimization

abstract: In many structured prediction problems, complex relationships between variables are compactly defined using graphical structures. The most prevalent graphical prediction methods---probabilistic graphical models and large margin methods---have their own distinct strengths but also possess significant drawbacks. Conditional random fields (CRFs) are Fisher consistent, but they do not permit integration of customized loss metrics into their learning process. Large-margin models, such as structured support vector machines (SSVMs), have the flexibility to incorporate customized loss metrics, but lack Fisher consistency guarantees. We present adversarial graphical models (AGM), a distributionally robust approach for constructing a predictor that performs robustly for a class of data distributions defined using a graphical structure. Our approach enjoys both the flexibility of incorporating customized loss metrics into its design as well as the statistical guarantee of Fisher consistency. We present exact learning and prediction algorithms for AGM with time complexity similar to existing graphical models and show the practical benefits of our approach with experiments.

paragraphs: Structured prediction involves outputs whose parts are related, with graphs providing a compact description of those relationships. The paper identifies a trade-off between two established approaches. Conditional random fields provide Fisher consistency, a statistical alignment with the desired prediction problem, while structured support vector machines can directly incorporate customized measures of prediction error.

The authors introduce adversarial graphical models to bring these properties together. The predictor is constructed through distributionally robust optimization over a class of data distributions specified using graphical structure. Within this framework, the learning design can account for a task-specific loss while also retaining a Fisher consistency guarantee.

The paper supplies exact algorithms for learning and prediction with time complexity similar to existing graphical-model methods. Experiments demonstrate practical benefits of the approach. Its significance is that the choice of what counts as a costly prediction error can be integrated into a statistically principled graphical predictor. The robustness claim concerns the specified class of distributions, which defines the uncertainty the method addresses.
summary.tldr: Adversarial graphical models combine customized prediction losses with Fisher consistency through distributionally robust optimization.

title: Distributionally Robust Graphical Models

abstract: It is important to learn various types of classifiers given training data with noisy labels. Noisy labels, in the most popular noise model hitherto, are corrupted from ground-truth labels by an unknown noise transition matrix. Thus, by estimating this matrix, classifiers can escape from overfitting those noisy labels. However, such estimation is practically difficult, due to either the indirect nature of two-step approaches, or not big enough data to afford end-to-end approaches. In this paper, we propose a human-assisted approach called ''Masking'' that conveys human cognition of invalid class transitions and naturally speculates the structure of the noise transition matrix. To this end, we derive a structure-aware probabilistic model incorporating a structure prior, and solve the challenges from structure extraction and structure alignment. Thanks to Masking, we only estimate unmasked noise transition probabilities and the burden of estimation is tremendously reduced. We conduct extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with three noise structures as well as the industrial-level Clothing1M with agnostic noise structure, and the results show that Masking can improve the robustness of classifiers significantly.

paragraphs: A common model of label noise describes how true classes turn into incorrect observed labels through a transition matrix. Estimating that matrix can help classifiers avoid fitting corrupted labels, but the estimation itself is difficult. Indirect procedures complicate the process, while fully joint approaches can demand more data than are available.

Masking introduces human knowledge about class transitions considered invalid. This information constrains the possible structure of the noise matrix, leaving only unmasked transition probabilities to estimate. The authors develop a probabilistic model with a structural prior and address how to extract and align the relevant structure. Human input therefore reduces the estimation burden by narrowing which corruptions the model needs to consider.

Experiments cover CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 under three noise structures, plus Clothing1M with an unknown noise structure. The results show significant improvements in classifier robustness. The contribution is a way to incorporate knowledge about how labels can be confused into learning, with empirical evidence that this structural guidance helps handle noisy supervision.
summary.tldr: Masking uses human knowledge of invalid label transitions to simplify noise estimation and improve classifier robustness.

title: Masking: A New Perspective of Noisy Supervision

abstract: We study the problem of maximizing deep submodular functions (DSFs) subject to a matroid constraint. DSFs are an expressive class of submodular functions that include, as strict subfamilies, the facility location, weighted coverage, and sums of concave composed with modular functions. We use a strategy similar to the continuous greedy approach, but we show that the multilinear extension of any DSF has a natural and computationally attainable concave relaxation that we can optimize using gradient ascent. Our results show a guarantee of $\max_{0<\delta<1}(1-\epsilon-\delta-e^{-\delta^2\Omega(k)})$ with a running time of $O(\nicefrac{n^2}{\epsilon^2})$ plus time for pipage rounding to recover a discrete solution, where $k$ is the rank of the matroid constraint. This bound is often better than the standard $1-1/e$ guarantee of the continuous greedy algorithm, but runs much faster. Our bound also holds even for fully curved ($c=1$) functions where the guarantee of $1-c/e$ degenerates to $1-1/e$ where $c$ is the curvature of $f$. We perform computational experiments that support our theoretical results.

paragraphs: The paper studies maximizing deep submodular functions under a matroid constraint. This function class includes facility location, weighted coverage, and sums of concave functions applied to modular functions as strict subfamilies. Its breadth makes an efficient optimization method useful across several forms of structured subset selection.

The authors build on the continuous greedy perspective but identify a computationally accessible concave relaxation of the multilinear extension for any deep submodular function. They optimize that relaxation using gradient ascent, then use pipage rounding to recover a discrete solution. This separates an efficiently handled continuous optimization problem from the step that produces the selected subset.

The stated running time is O(n²/ε²), plus rounding time, and the method is reported to run much faster than continuous greedy. The bound also applies to fully curved functions, where a curvature-based guarantee returns to 1−1/e. Computational experiments support the theoretical results.
summary.tldr: A tractable concave relaxation enables fast gradient-based maximization of deep submodular functions with often stronger approximation guarantees.

title: Submodular Maximization via Gradient Ascent: The Case of Deep Submodular Functions

abstract: Image captioning models are becoming increasingly successful at describing the content of images in restricted domains. However, if these models are to function in the wild --- for example, as assistants for people with impaired vision --- a much larger number and variety of visual concepts must be understood. To address this problem, we teach image captioning models new visual concepts from labeled images and object detection datasets. Since image labels and object classes can be interpreted as partial captions, we formulate this problem as learning from partially-specified sequence data. We then propose a novel algorithm for training sequence models, such as recurrent neural networks, on partially-specified sequences which we represent using finite state automata. In the context of image captioning, our method lifts the restriction that previously required image captioning models to be trained on paired image-sentence corpora only, or otherwise required specialized model architectures to take advantage of alternative data modalities. Applying our approach to an existing neural captioning model, we achieve state of the art results on the novel object captioning task using the COCO dataset. We further show that we can train a captioning model to describe new visual concepts from the Open Images dataset while maintaining competitive COCO evaluation scores.

paragraphs: This paper helps image captioning models learn visual concepts beyond those covered by paired images and complete sentences. Labeled images and object detection datasets contain useful concept information, but usually do not provide full captions. The authors treat image labels and object classes as partial descriptions that can still supervise a captioning model.

They formulate the task as learning from partially specified sequences and represent those sequences using finite state automata. A new training algorithm allows sequence models, including recurrent neural networks, to use this form of supervision. It can be applied to an existing captioning model, expanding usable training data without requiring a specialized architecture for the alternative annotations.

On the COCO novel-object captioning task, the approach achieves the reported state of the art. The authors also teach a captioning model new concepts using Open Images while maintaining competitive COCO evaluation scores. These findings show that incomplete descriptive supervision can expand a model’s visual vocabulary while preserving competitive performance on the established captioning evaluation.
summary.tldr: Training on partially specified captions lets existing captioning models learn new visual concepts from labels and detection datasets.

title: Partially-Supervised Image Captioning

abstract: We investigate the problem of assigning trip requests to available vehicles in on-demand ridesourcing. Much of the literature has focused on maximizing the total value of served requests, achieving efficiency on the passengers’ side. However, such solutions may result in some drivers being assigned to insufficient or undesired trips, therefore losing fairness from the drivers’ perspective. In this paper, we focus on both the system efficiency and the fairness among drivers and quantitatively analyze the trade-offs between these two objectives. In particular, we give an explicit answer to the question of whether there always exists an assignment that achieves any target efficiency and fairness. We also propose a simple reassignment algorithm that can achieve any selected trade-off. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the algorithms through extensive experiments on real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Assigning ride requests to vehicles involves more than maximizing the total value of completed trips. An assignment that performs well by that measure can leave some drivers with too few trips or with trips they do not want. This paper studies allocation from both the system's efficiency perspective and the drivers' fairness perspective.

The authors quantitatively analyze the trade-offs between these objectives. They explicitly address whether an assignment can always satisfy a specified efficiency target together with a specified fairness target. That feasibility question matters because choosing two desirable targets does not itself establish that an assignment can meet both. The abstract states that the paper answers the question without specifying the answer's detailed form.

The paper also proposes a simple reassignment algorithm for achieving a selected trade-off and evaluates the algorithms extensively on real-world datasets. The contribution connects analysis of competing objectives with an operational way to revise assignments. It makes driver fairness an explicit part of allocation decisions alongside the value of served requests.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes efficiency–fairness trade-offs in ride assignment and proposes a reassignment algorithm for realizing a selected balance.

title: Balancing Efficiency and Fairness in On-Demand Ridesourcing

abstract: Image animation consists of generating a video sequence so that an object in a source image is animated according to the motion of a driving video. Our framework addresses this problem without using any annotation or prior information about the specific object to animate. Once trained on a set of videos depicting objects of the same category (e.g. faces, human bodies), our method can be applied to any object of this class. To achieve this, we decouple appearance and motion information using a self-supervised formulation. To support complex motions, we use a representation consisting of a set of learned keypoints along with their local affine transformations. A generator network models occlusions arising during target motions and combines the appearance extracted from the source image and the motion derived from the driving video. Our framework scores best on diverse benchmarks and on a variety of object categories.

paragraphs: Image animation transfers movement from a driving video to an object shown in a single source image. This paper learns that transfer without annotations or prior information about the particular object being animated. Training uses videos of objects from the same category, such as faces or human bodies; the trained method can then animate objects within that category.

The approach separates appearance from motion through self-supervision. Motion is represented by learned keypoints together with local affine transformations, which describe more than the movement of isolated points. This richer representation supports complex motion by describing how local regions transform. The source image supplies the appearance, while the driving video supplies the motion to apply.

A generator combines those two sources and models occlusions that arise as the object moves. Accounting for occlusions matters because target motions can change which regions are visible. The framework reports the best scores across diverse benchmarks and multiple object categories. Its results support learning reusable, category-specific motion representations without requiring manual labels for the objects or their movements.
summary.tldr: A self-supervised model animates a source image using learned keypoints, local transformations, and occlusion handling to transfer motion from a video.

title: First Order Motion Model for Image Animation

abstract: In off-policy deep reinforcement learning, it is usually hard to collect sufficient successful experiences with sparse rewards to learn from. Hindsight experience replay (HER) enables an agent to learn from failures by treating the achieved state of a failed experience as a pseudo goal. However, not all the failed experiences are equally useful to different learning stages, so it is not efficient to replay all of them or uniform samples of them. In this paper, we propose to 1) adaptively select the failed experiences for replay according to the proximity to the true goals and the curiosity of exploration over diverse pseudo goals, and 2) gradually change the proportion of the goal-proximity and the diversity-based curiosity in the selection criteria: we adopt a human-like learning strategy that enforces more curiosity in earlier stages and changes to larger goal-proximity later. This Goal-and-Curiosity-driven Curriculum Learning'' leads to Curriculum-guided HER (CHER)'', which adaptively and dynamically controls the exploration-exploitation trade-off during the learning process via hindsight experience selection. We show that CHER improves the state of the art in challenging robotics environments.

paragraphs: When rewards are sparse, a reinforcement learning agent may experience too few successes to learn effectively. Hindsight experience replay helps by treating a state reached during a failed attempt as an alternative goal. The attempt then becomes useful evidence about accomplishing that alternative, even though it did not achieve the original objective.

This paper argues that the usefulness of these relabeled experiences changes as learning progresses. Its method, Curriculum-guided Hindsight Experience Replay, selects failed experiences using two considerations: how close their achieved states are to the true goals, and how much diversity they offer among alternative goals. The balance changes over training, emphasizing curiosity early and proximity to the intended goals later.

The resulting curriculum adjusts exploration and exploitation through the choice of experiences replayed, rather than treating all failures as equally valuable. The authors report improvements over the state of the art in challenging robotics environments. Those findings support adapting hindsight selection to the agent's learning stage.
summary.tldr: CHER improves hindsight replay by gradually shifting experience selection from diverse alternative goals toward states closer to the true goals.

title: Curriculum-guided Hindsight Experience Replay

abstract: We study the problem of top-k selection over a large domain universe subject to user-level differential privacy. Typically, the exponential mechanism or report noisy max are the algorithms used to solve this problem. However, these algorithms require querying the database for the count of each domain element. We focus on the setting where the data domain is unknown, which is different than the setting of frequent itemsets where an apriori type algorithm can help prune the space of domain elements to query. We design algorithms that ensures (approximate) differential privacy and only needs access to the true top-k' elements from the data for any chosen k' ≥ k. This is a highly desirable feature for making differential privacy practical, since the algorithms require no knowledge of the domain. We consider both the setting where a user's data can modify an arbitrary number of counts by at most 1, i.e. unrestricted sensitivity, and the setting where a user's data can modify at most some small, fixed number of counts by at most 1, i.e. restricted sensitivity. Additionally, we provide a pay-what-you-get privacy composition bound for our algorithms. That is, our algorithms might return fewer than k elements when the top-k elements are queried, but the overall privacy budget only decreases by the size of the outcome set.
