paragraphs: Privately selecting the most frequent items becomes difficult when the universe of possible items is large or unknown. Common methods require counts for every domain element. This paper develops user-level differentially private top-k selection algorithms that need access only to the actual top-k-prime items, where k-prime can be any chosen value at least as large as k.

The algorithms provide approximate differential privacy without requiring knowledge of the full domain. The authors consider two contribution settings: a user can change arbitrarily many counts by at most one each, or can change only a small fixed number of counts by at most one. This makes the treatment cover both unrestricted and restricted sensitivity.

The paper also introduces a pay-what-you-get composition bound. An algorithm may return fewer than the requested k items, but privacy accounting decreases the available budget according to the number actually returned. This connects the privacy cost to the delivered output. Together, limited access requirements and output-sensitive accounting address practical obstacles to private selection over an unknown domain.
summary.tldr: Private top-k algorithms work without knowing the full item domain and account for privacy cost according to how many items they return.

title: Practical Differentially Private Top-k Selection with Pay-what-you-get Composition

abstract: When we take photos through glass windows or doors, the transmitted background scene is often blended with undesirable reflection. Separating two layers apart to enhance the image quality is of vital importance for both human and machine perception. In this paper, we propose to exploit physical constraints from a pair of unpolarized and polarized images to separate reflection and transmission layers. Due to the simplified capturing setup, the system becomes more underdetermined compared with existing polarization based solutions that take three or more images as input. We propose to solve semireflector orientation estimation first to make the physical image formation well-posed and then learn to reliably separate two layers using a refinement network with gradient loss. Quantitative and qualitative experimental results show our approach performs favorably over existing polarization and single image based solutions.

paragraphs: Photographs taken through glass often combine the scene behind the glass with a reflected scene. This paper tries to separate those two layers using just two captures: one unpolarized and one polarized image. The pair provides physical information about image formation while keeping the capture setup relatively simple.

Using fewer images creates a tradeoff. Compared with polarization methods requiring three or more captures, the separation problem has more unresolved ambiguity. The authors first estimate the orientation of the partially reflecting surface, which makes the physical image-formation problem well-posed. This estimation supplies structure needed to use the limited observations.

A refinement network then learns to separate the transmission and reflection layers, trained with a gradient loss. The approach thus combines physical constraints with learned refinement, addressing the ambiguity before refining the reconstructed layers. Quantitative and qualitative experiments show favorable performance against existing polarization-based and single-image solutions. The reported results support using this two-image setup to simplify acquisition while still obtaining effective reflection separation.
summary.tldr: Surface-orientation estimation and learned refinement separate reflections from transmitted scenes using one polarized and one unpolarized image.

title: Reflection Separation using a Pair of Unpolarized and Polarized Images

abstract: We study finite sample expressivity, i.e., memorization power of ReLU networks. Recent results require $N$ hidden nodes to memorize/interpolate arbitrary $N$ data points. In contrast, by exploiting depth, we show that 3-layer ReLU networks with $\Omega(\sqrt{N})$ hidden nodes can perfectly memorize most datasets with $N$ points. We also prove that width $\Theta(\sqrt{N})$ is necessary and sufficient for memorizing $N$ data points, proving tight bounds on memorization capacity. The sufficiency result can be extended to deeper networks; we show that an $L$-layer network with $W$ parameters in the hidden layers can memorize $N$ data points if $W = \Omega(N)$. Combined with a recent upper bound $O(WL\log W)$ on VC dimension, our construction is nearly tight for any fixed $L$. Subsequently, we analyze memorization capacity of residual networks under a general position assumption; we prove results that substantially reduce the known requirement of $N$ hidden nodes. Finally, we study the dynamics of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), and show that when initialized near a memorizing global minimum of the empirical risk, SGD quickly finds a nearby point with much smaller empirical risk.

paragraphs: This paper studies finite-sample expressivity: how large a ReLU network must be to fit a collection of data points perfectly. It shows how depth can reduce the number of hidden nodes needed for memorization. For three-layer networks, the authors construct networks with square-root-in-N hidden-node scaling that memorize most datasets containing N points.

The analysis gives matching necessary and sufficient width scaling of order sqrt(N) for its memorization result. It also extends the construction to deeper networks, where a number of hidden-layer parameters scaling at least linearly with N is sufficient. Combined with an existing VC-dimension upper bound, the construction is nearly tight when depth is fixed.

The authors separately study residual networks under a general-position assumption, substantially reducing earlier hidden-node requirements. They also analyze SGD near a memorizing global minimum, showing that such an initialization quickly leads to a nearby point with much lower empirical risk. This optimization result is local: its stated starting condition is proximity to a memorizing minimum.
summary.tldr: Depth enables compact ReLU networks to memorize many samples, with tight width bounds and a local SGD result near memorizing minima.

title: Small ReLU networks are powerful memorizers: a tight analysis of memorization capacity

abstract: Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD), a popular sampling algorithm, is often described as the kernelized gradient flow for the Kullback-Leibler divergence in the geometry of optimal transport. We introduce a new perspective on SVGD that instead views SVGD as the kernelized gradient flow of the chi-squared divergence. Motivated by this perspective, we provide a convergence analysis of the chi-squared gradient flow. We also show that our new perspective provides better guidelines for choosing effective kernels for SVGD.

We introduce a new perspective on SVGD that instead views SVGD as the kernelized gradient flow of the chi-squared divergence. Motivated by this perspective, we provide a convergence analysis of the chi-squared gradient flow. We also show that our new perspective provides better guidelines for choosing effective kernels for SVGD.

paragraphs: Stein variational gradient descent is a sampling algorithm whose behavior can be understood through the evolution of probability distributions. A common explanation views it as a kernelized gradient flow that reduces Kullback-Leibler divergence in optimal-transport geometry. This paper offers a different mathematical perspective, centered on the chi-squared divergence.

The new interpretation views SVGD as a kernelized Wasserstein gradient flow of that alternative discrepancy measure. In plain terms, it changes the lens used to describe how a distribution moves toward its target. This matters because the mathematical description can guide both the analysis of convergence and the design choices that shape the algorithm’s behavior.

Motivated by this perspective, the authors analyze convergence of the chi-squared gradient flow. They also show that the interpretation supplies better guidance for choosing effective SVGD kernels. The contribution is therefore a theoretical reframing with a practical design consequence: the choice of divergence helps explain which kernels are useful, connecting the underlying distributional dynamics to a central component of the sampling method.
summary.tldr: Viewing SVGD through chi-squared gradient flow yields convergence analysis and improved guidance for kernel selection.

title: SVGD as a kernelized Wasserstein gradient flow of the chi-squared divergence

abstract: The sampling of probability distributions specified up to a normalization constant is an important problem in both machine learning and statistical mechanics. While classical stochastic sampling methods such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) or Langevin Dynamics (LD) can suffer from slow mixing times there is a growing interest in using normalizing flows in order to learn the transformation of a simple prior distribution to the given target distribution. Here we propose a generalized and combined approach to sample target densities: Stochastic Normalizing Flows (SNF) – an arbitrary sequence of deterministic invertible functions and stochastic sampling blocks. We show that stochasticity overcomes expressivity limitations of normalizing flows resulting from the invertibility constraint, whereas trainable transformations between sampling steps improve efficiency of pure MCMC/LD along the flow. By invoking ideas from non-equilibrium statistical mechanics we derive an efficient training procedure by which both the sampler's and the flow's parameters can be optimized end-to-end, and by which we can compute exact importance weights without having to marginalize out the randomness of the stochastic blocks. We illustrate the representational power, sampling efficiency and asymptotic correctness of SNFs on several benchmarks including applications to sampling molecular systems in equilibrium.
originalAbstract: The sampling of probability distributions specified up to a normalization constant is an important problem in both machine learning and statistical mechanics. While classical stochastic sampling methods such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) or Langevin Dynamics (LD) can suffer from slow mixing times there is a growing interest in using normalizing flows in order to learn the transformation of a simple prior distribution to the given target distribution. Here we propose a generalized and combined approach to sample target densities: Stochastic Normalizing Flows (SNF) – an arbitrary sequence of deterministic invertible functions and stochastic sampling blocks. We show that stochasticity overcomes expressivity limitations of normalizing flows resulting from the invertibility constraint, whereas trainable transformations between sampling steps improve efficiency of pure MCMC/LD along the flow. By invoking ideas from non-equilibrium statistical mechanics we derive an efficient training procedure by which both the sampler's and the flow's parameters can be optimized end-to-end, and by which we can compute exact importance weights without having to marginalize out the randomness of the stochastic blocks. We illustrate the representational power, sampling efficiency and asymptotic correctness of SNFs on several benchmarks including applications to sampling molecular systems in equilibrium.

paragraphs: Sampling from a distribution can be difficult when its density is known only up to a normalization constant. Classical stochastic samplers may move slowly through that distribution, while normalizing flows learn invertible transformations from a simpler one. This paper combines the two approaches in Stochastic Normalizing Flows, or SNFs.

An SNF can interleave deterministic invertible transformations with stochastic sampling blocks in an arbitrary sequence. The stochastic steps overcome expressive restrictions imposed by invertibility, while learned transformations between them improve the efficiency of otherwise purely stochastic sampling. The construction gives both components a role in moving samples toward the target distribution.

Using ideas from non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, the authors derive an efficient procedure that trains sampler and flow parameters together. They also compute exact importance weights without integrating out the stochastic blocks' randomness. Benchmarks, including equilibrium molecular sampling, illustrate expressive power, sampling efficiency, and asymptotic correctness. The exact weighting result and the asymptotic claim have distinct roles: the former concerns computable sample weights, while the latter concerns correctness in the limiting sampling regime.
summary.tldr: Stochastic Normalizing Flows interleave learned invertible transformations and stochastic sampling to improve expressivity and efficiency while retaining exact importance weights.

title: Stochastic Normalizing Flows

abstract: Exploration is one of the core challenges in reinforcement learning. A common formulation of curiosity-driven exploration uses the difference between the real future and the future predicted by a learned model. However, predicting the future is an inherently difficult task which can be ill-posed in the face of stochasticity. In this paper, we introduce an alternative form of curiosity that rewards novel associations between different senses. Our approach exploits multiple modalities to provide a stronger signal for more efficient exploration. Our method is inspired by the fact that, for humans, both sight and sound play a critical role in exploration. We present results on several Atari environments and Habitat (a photorealistic navigation simulator), showing the benefits of using an audio-visual association model for intrinsically guiding learning agents in the absence of external rewards. For videos and code, see https://vdean.github.io/audio-curiosity.html.

paragraphs: A learning agent needs a reason to explore when an environment supplies no external reward. One common curiosity signal measures how poorly a model predicts future observations. The paper points out that this can be problematic when the future is inherently stochastic, because prediction itself may be difficult or ill-posed.

The proposed alternative rewards novel associations between sensory modalities, specifically sight and sound. An audio-visual association model supplies an intrinsic signal based on the relationship between what the agent sees and hears. The approach draws on the role of multiple senses in human exploration and uses their combination to guide the agent's learning.

Experiments in several Atari environments and the photorealistic Habitat navigation simulator show benefits from this association-based curiosity without external rewards. The findings support cross-sensory novelty as a useful source of exploration guidance. The contribution is a different target for curiosity: discovering relationships between sensory inputs, with empirical evidence that this can help agents explore more efficiently.
summary.tldr: Rewarding novel sight–sound associations provides an intrinsic exploration signal that helps agents learn without external rewards.

title: See, Hear, Explore: Curiosity via Audio-Visual Association

abstract: This work addresses efficient inference and learning in switching Gaussian linear dynamical systems using a Rao-Blackwellised particle filter and a corresponding Monte Carlo objective. To improve the forecasting capabilities, we extend this classical model by conditionally linear state-to-switch dynamics, while leaving the partial tractability of the conditional Gaussian linear part intact. Furthermore, we use an auxiliary variable approach with a decoder-type neural network that allows for more complex non-linear emission models and multivariate observations. We propose a Monte Carlo objective that leverages the conditional linearity by computing the corresponding conditional expectations in closed-form and a suitable proposal distribution that is factorised similarly to the optimal proposal distribution. We evaluate our approach on several popular time series forecasting datasets as well as image streams of simulated physical systems. Our results show improved forecasting performance compared to other deep state-space model approaches.

paragraphs: This paper improves time-series forecasting with models whose hidden dynamics can switch between different linear Gaussian regimes. Such models retain useful mathematical structure, but richer forecasting behavior calls for additional flexibility. The authors extend the relationship between the hidden state and regime switches while preserving the part of the model that remains tractable when conditioned on other variables.

Inference uses a Rao-Blackwellised particle filter, and learning uses a corresponding Monte Carlo objective. The objective takes advantage of conditional linearity by calculating relevant conditional expectations exactly. A specially structured proposal distribution supports the sampling procedure. An auxiliary-variable construction with a neural decoder adds nonlinear observation models and accommodates observations containing multiple variables.

The resulting design combines richer dynamics and observations with calculations that still exploit the original model’s structure. Evaluations cover established forecasting datasets and image sequences from simulated physical systems. The authors report better forecasting performance than other deep state-space approaches in these experiments, supporting the value of preserving tractable components while expanding the model’s expressive capabilities.
summary.tldr: A neural extension of switching dynamical models improves forecasting while retaining exact calculations for conditionally tractable components.

title: Deep Rao-Blackwellised Particle Filters for Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Given a combinatorial optimization problem taking an input, can we learn a strategy to solve it from the examples of input-solution pairs without knowing its objective function? In this paper, we consider such a setting and study the misinformation prevention problem. Given the examples of attacker-protector pairs, our goal is to learn a strategy to compute protectors against future attackers, without the need of knowing the underlying diffusion model. To this end, we design a structured prediction framework, where the main idea is to parameterize the scoring function using random features constructed through distance functions on randomly sampled subgraphs, which leads to a kernelized scoring function with weights learnable via the large margin method. Evidenced by experiments, our method can produce near-optimal protectors without using any information about the diffusion model, and it outperforms other possible graph-based and learning-based methods by an evident margin.

paragraphs: StratLearner asks whether a strategy for a combinatorial problem can be learned from input-solution examples without knowing the objective function. Its application is misinformation prevention: given examples pairing attackers with protectors, the method learns to choose protectors against future attackers without access to the underlying diffusion model.

The proposed structured-prediction framework learns a scoring function for these decisions. It constructs random features from distance functions on randomly sampled subgraphs, producing a kernelized score whose weights are learned through a large-margin method. This uses graph structure and example solutions to guide future choices without explicitly modeling how misinformation spreads.

Experiments show that the method can produce near-optimal protectors without diffusion-model information and outperforms the compared graph-based and learning-based alternatives by a clear margin. Those findings support learning a prevention strategy directly from examples in the evaluated settings. More broadly, the paper demonstrates an instance of learning optimization behavior when successful input-solution pairs are available but the objective governing them is unknown.
summary.tldr: StratLearner learns misinformation-protection strategies from attacker-protector examples using graph features, without knowing the diffusion model.

title: StratLearner: Learning a Strategy for Misinformation Prevention in Social Networks

abstract: Despite strong performance in numerous applications, the fragility of deep learning to input perturbations has raised serious questions about its use in safety-critical domains. While adversarial training can mitigate this issue in practice, state-of-the-art methods are increasingly application-dependent, heuristic in nature, and suffer from fundamental trade-offs between nominal performance and robustness. Moreover, the problem of finding worst-case perturbations is non-convex and underparameterized, both of which engender a non-favorable optimization landscape. Thus, there is a gap between the theory and practice of robust learning, particularly with respect to when and why adversarial training works. In this paper, we take a constrained learning approach to address these questions and to provide a theoretical foundation for robust learning. In particular, we leverage semi-infinite optimization and non-convex duality theory to show that adversarial training is equivalent to a statistical problem over perturbation distributions. Notably, we show that a myriad of previous robust training techniques can be recovered for particular, sub-optimal choices of these distributions. Using these insights, we then propose a hybrid Langevin Markov Chain Monte Carlo approach for which several common algorithms (e.g., PGD) are special cases. Finally, we show that our approach can mitigate the trade-off between nominal and robust performance, yielding state-of-the-art results on MNIST and CIFAR-10. Our code is available at: https://github.com/arobey1/advbench.

paragraphs: Adversarial training aims to make models withstand input perturbations, but finding damaging perturbations is itself a difficult optimization problem. Existing methods also face a trade-off between ordinary predictive performance and robustness. This paper develops a constrained learning perspective to explain how robust training methods relate and to guide the design of an alternative.

Using semi-infinite optimization and nonconvex duality, the authors establish an equivalence between adversarial training and a statistical problem involving distributions over perturbations. This changes the focus from a single worst-case perturbation to the distribution used in the equivalent formulation. Several earlier robust training methods emerge as particular, suboptimal choices of these distributions.

The resulting algorithm uses a hybrid Langevin Markov chain Monte Carlo approach, with common methods such as projected gradient descent included as special cases. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 report state-of-the-art results and show that the approach can reduce the nominal-performance versus robustness trade-off. The contribution combines a unifying theoretical account with an empirically effective training method; it does not claim the trade-off disappears.
summary.tldr: A distribution-based formulation of adversarial training motivates a sampling method that can improve the trade-off between ordinary accuracy and robustness.

title: Adversarial Robustness with Semi-Infinite Constrained Learning

abstract: Almost every single image restoration problem has a closely related parameter, such as the scale factor in super-resolution, the noise level in image denoising, and the quality factor in JPEG deblocking. Although recent studies on image restoration problems have achieved great success due to the development of deep neural networks, they handle the parameter involved in an unsophisticated way. Most previous researchers either treat problems with different parameter levels as independent tasks, and train a specific model for each parameter level; or simply ignore the parameter, and train a single model for all parameter levels. The two popular approaches have their own shortcomings. The former is inefficient in computing and the latter is ineffective in performance. In this work, we propose a novel system called functional neural network (FuncNet) to solve a parametric image restoration problem with a single model. Unlike a plain neural network, the smallest conceptual element of our FuncNet is no longer a floating-point variable, but a function of the parameter of the problem. This feature makes it both efficient and effective for a parametric problem. We apply FuncNet to super-resolution, image denoising, and JPEG deblocking. The experimental results show the superiority of our FuncNet on all three parametric image restoration tasks over the state of the arts.

paragraphs: Image restoration often depends on a parameter describing the problem, such as enlargement scale, noise level, or JPEG quality. Training a separate network for every setting duplicates computation, while using one network that ignores the parameter can sacrifice performance. This paper proposes a single model that explicitly changes its computations with the restoration parameter.

The functional neural network, or FuncNet, replaces its smallest scalar building blocks with functions of that parameter. Instead of treating parameter settings as disconnected tasks, the network incorporates their relationship into its own representation. This makes parameter dependence part of the model’s structure and provides a way to serve multiple restoration settings through one network.

The authors apply FuncNet to super-resolution, denoising, and JPEG deblocking. They report improvements over state-of-the-art approaches on all three tasks. The findings support the idea that a shared restoration model can benefit from expressing how its internal quantities should vary with the problem parameter, addressing both efficiency and restoration quality.
summary.tldr: FuncNet makes network components functions of the restoration parameter, allowing one model to handle multiple image-restoration settings.

title: Functional Neural Networks for Parametric Image Restoration Problems

abstract: We consider the problem of stochastic optimization with delayed gradients in which, at each time step $t$, the algorithm makes an update using a stale stochastic gradient from step $t - d_t$ for some arbitrary delay $d_t$. This setting abstracts asynchronous distributed optimization where a central server receives gradient updates computed by worker machines. These machines can experience computation and communication loads that might vary significantly over time. In the general non-convex smooth optimization setting, we give a simple and efficient algorithm that requires $O( \sigma^2/\epsilon^4 + \tau/\epsilon^2 )$ steps for finding an $\epsilon$-stationary point $x$. Here, $\tau$ is the \emph{average} delay $\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T d_t$ and $\sigma^2$ is the variance of the stochastic gradients. This improves over previous work, which showed that stochastic gradient decent achieves the same rate but with respect to the \emph{maximal} delay $\max_{t} d_t$, that can be significantly larger than the average delay especially in heterogeneous distributed systems. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy and robustness of our algorithm in cases where the delay distribution is skewed or heavy-tailed.

paragraphs: In distributed optimization, workers can return gradients computed from old parameter values. Delays may vary widely because of changing computation and communication loads. This paper studies stochastic optimization with arbitrary gradient delays and seeks guarantees that are not dominated by one unusually slow update.

For smooth nonconvex objectives, the authors give an algorithm requiring O(sigma²/epsilon⁴ + tau/epsilon²) steps to find an epsilon-stationary point, where sigma² is gradient variance and tau is average delay. Earlier comparable guarantees depended on the maximum delay instead.

Experiments show effectiveness and robustness when delay distributions are skewed or heavy-tailed, settings in which the mean can be much smaller than the maximum. The theoretical target is stationarity, not global optimality. The abstract provides no numerical speedups, but the improved delay dependence directly addresses heterogeneous distributed systems where a few slow workers should not dictate the entire bound.
summary.tldr: An asynchronous optimizer’s convergence depends on average gradient delay rather than the worst delay.

title: Asynchronous Stochastic Optimization Robust to Arbitrary Delays

abstract: We study differentially private stochastic optimization in convex and non-convex settings. For the convex case, we focus on the family of non-smooth generalized linear losses (GLLs). Our algorithm for the $\ell_2$ setting achieves optimal excess population risk in near-linear time, while the best known differentially private algorithms for general convex losses run in super-linear time. Our algorithm for the $\ell_1$ setting has nearly-optimal excess population risk $\tilde{O}\big(\sqrt{\frac{\log{d}}{n}}\big)$, and circumvents the dimension dependent lower bound of \cite{Asi:2021} for general non-smooth convex losses. In the differentially private non-convex setting, we provide several new algorithms for approximating stationary points of the population risk. For the $\ell_1$-case with smooth losses and polyhedral constraint, we provide the first nearly dimension independent rate, $\tilde O\big(\frac{\log^{2/3}{d}}{{n^{1/3}}}\big)$ in linear time. For the constrained $\ell_2$-case, with smooth losses, we obtain a linear-time algorithm with rate $\tilde O\big(\frac{1}{n^{3/10}d^{1/10}}+\big(\frac{d}{n^2}\big)^{1/5}\big)$. Finally, for the $\ell_2$-case we provide the first method for {\em non-smooth weakly convex} stochastic optimization with rate $\tilde O\big(\frac{1}{n^{1/4}}+\big(\frac{d}{n^2}\big)^{1/6}\big)$ which matches the best existing non-private algorithm when $d= O(\sqrt{n})$. We also extend all our results above for the non-convex $\ell_2$ setting to the $\ell_p$ setting, where $1 < p \leq 2$, with only polylogarithmic (in the dimension) overhead in the rates.

paragraphs: This paper develops differentially private stochastic optimization algorithms for several convex and non-convex settings. For convex problems, it focuses on non-smooth generalized linear losses. Exploiting this particular family allows stronger efficiency and accuracy results than those available for general non-smooth convex losses.

In the Euclidean setting, the convex algorithm achieves optimal excess population risk in near-linear time. In the l1 setting, it achieves nearly optimal risk with logarithmic dependence on dimension, avoiding a dimension-dependent lower bound that applies to the broader loss family. For non-convex problems, the goal is instead to approximate stationary points. The authors give linear-time algorithms for smooth constrained problems, including a nearly dimension-independent rate under l1 geometry and polyhedral constraints.

They also introduce a method for non-smooth weakly convex optimization in Euclidean geometry. Its rate matches the best existing non-private algorithm when dimension is at most on the order of the square root of sample size. The non-convex Euclidean results extend to lp geometries for 1 < p ≤ 2 with only polylogarithmic dimension overhead.
summary.tldr: New private optimization algorithms improve computational and statistical guarantees under specified loss, constraint, and geometry assumptions.

title: Differentially Private Stochastic Optimization: New Results in Convex and Non-Convex Settings

abstract: In collaborative machine learning(CML), multiple agents pool their resources(e.g., data) together for a common learning task. In realistic CML settings where the agents are self-interested and not altruistic, they may be unwilling to share data or model information without adequate rewards. Furthermore, as the data/model information shared by the agents may differ in quality, designing rewards which are fair to them is important so that they would not feel exploited nor discouraged from sharing. In this paper, we adopt federated learning as the CML paradigm, propose a novel cosine gradient Shapley value(CGSV) to fairly evaluate the expected marginal contribution of each agent’s uploaded model parameter update/gradient without needing an auxiliary validation dataset, and based on the CGSV, design a novel training-time gradient reward mechanism with a fairness guarantee by sparsifying the aggregated parameter update/gradient downloaded from the server as reward to each agent such that its resulting quality is commensurate to that of the agent’s uploaded parameter update/gradient. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of our fair gradient reward mechanism on multiple benchmark datasets in terms of fairness, predictive performance, and time overhead.

paragraphs: Collaborative learning depends on participants contributing resources, but self-interested participants may need rewards that reflect the quality of what they share. This paper studies that issue in federated learning, where participants upload model updates or gradients. Fairness here concerns matching the learning benefit returned to each participant with the value of its contribution.

The authors introduce a cosine gradient Shapley value to evaluate a participant's expected marginal contribution. This evaluation does not require an auxiliary validation dataset. They then use the resulting contribution assessment to determine the gradient reward sent back during training. The server sparsifies the aggregated update separately for each participant so that the returned update's quality is commensurate with the uploaded contribution.

The proposed reward mechanism comes with a fairness guarantee, connecting contribution assessment to the training information participants receive. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets examine fairness, predictive performance, and time overhead, and report the mechanism's effectiveness. The approach makes model-update quality the basis of both valuation and reward, directly integrating contribution-sensitive incentives into the federated training process.
summary.tldr: A gradient-based contribution measure allocates participant-specific federated learning updates with a fairness guarantee and no auxiliary validation dataset.

title: Gradient Driven Rewards to Guarantee Fairness in Collaborative Machine Learning

abstract: Many differentially private algorithms for answering database queries involve astep that reconstructs a discrete data distribution from noisy measurements. Thisprovides consistent query answers and reduces error, but often requires space thatgrows exponentially with dimension. PRIVATE-PGM is a recent approach that usesgraphical models to represent the data distribution, with complexity proportional tothat of exact marginal inference in a graphical model with structure determined bythe co-occurrence of variables in the noisy measurements. PRIVATE-PGM is highlyscalable for sparse measurements, but may fail to run in high dimensions with densemeasurements. We overcome the main scalability limitation of PRIVATE-PGMthrough a principled approach that relaxes consistency constraints in the estimationobjective. Our new approach works with many existing private query answeringalgorithms and improves scalability or accuracy with no privacy cost.

paragraphs: Many private query-answering methods reconstruct a discrete data distribution from noisy measurements. This reconstruction can make answers mutually consistent and reduce error, but representing the distribution may require space that grows exponentially with the number of variables. The paper addresses this computational obstacle within the PRIVATE-PGM approach.

PRIVATE-PGM represents the distribution through a graphical model whose structure depends on which variables occur together in the measurements. Its computational demands follow the difficulty of exact marginal inference in that graph. Sparse measurements can therefore be handled efficiently, while dense measurements in high dimensions can make the method unable to run.

The proposed solution relaxes consistency constraints in the estimation objective. This changes the reconstruction problem so that the main scalability barrier can be reduced. The approach is compatible with many existing private query-answering algorithms and provides improvements in scalability or accuracy without additional privacy cost. Its significance is that the reconstruction stage can be made more practical while retaining the underlying privacy budget.
summary.tldr: Relaxing reconstruction consistency constraints improves the scalability or accuracy of private query answering without additional privacy cost.

title: Relaxed Marginal Consistency for Differentially Private Query Answering

abstract: Visual environments are structured, consisting of distinct objects or entities. These entities have properties---visible or latent---that determine the manner in which they interact with one another. To partition images into entities, deep-learning researchers have proposed structural inductive biases such as slot-based architectures. To model interactions among entities, equivariant graph neural nets (GNNs) are used, but these are not particularly well suited to the task for two reasons. First, GNNs do not predispose interactions to be sparse, as relationships among independent entities are likely to be. Second, GNNs do not factorize knowledge about interactions in an entity-conditional manner. As an alternative, we take inspiration from cognitive science and resurrect a classic approach, production systems, which consist of a set of rule templates that are applied by binding placeholder variables in the rules to specific entities. Rules are scored on their match to entities, and the best fitting rules are applied to update entity properties. In a series of experiments, we demonstrate that this architecture achieves a flexible, dynamic flow of control and serves to factorize entity-specific and rule-based information. This disentangling of knowledge achieves robust future-state prediction in rich visual environments, outperforming state-of-the-art methods using GNNs, and allows for the extrapolation from simple (few object) environments to more complex environments.

paragraphs: Visual scenes contain distinct entities whose properties determine how they interact. The paper argues that modeling these interactions benefits from sparse relationships and a separation between knowledge about particular entities and knowledge about interaction rules. It identifies these as weaknesses of the graph neural networks commonly used for the task.

Neural Production Systems adapt the classical idea of rule templates with placeholders that can be bound to specific entities. The architecture scores how well rules match the available entities, selects the best-fitting rules, and applies them to update entity properties. This creates a flexible flow of computation in which the rules used depend on the current entities.

Experiments show that the architecture separates entity-specific information from rule-based information and supports dynamic control. It achieves robust future-state prediction in rich visual environments, outperforming state-of-the-art graph neural network methods in the reported comparisons. It also supports extrapolation from environments with few objects to more complex ones. These findings connect reusable interaction rules with the ability to predict behavior beyond the simpler environments used for learning.
summary.tldr: Neural Production Systems learn entity-conditioned interaction rules that improve visual future-state prediction and support extrapolation to more complex environments.

title: Neural Production Systems

abstract: Can Transformer perform $2\mathrm{D}$ object- and region-level recognition from a pure sequence-to-sequence perspective with minimal knowledge about the $2\mathrm{D}$ spatial structure? To answer this question, we present You Only Look at One Sequence (YOLOS), a series of object detection models based on the vanilla Vision Transformer with the fewest possible modifications, region priors, as well as inductive biases of the target task. We find that YOLOS pre-trained on the mid-sized ImageNet-$1k$ dataset only can already achieve quite competitive performance on the challenging COCO object detection benchmark, e.g., YOLOS-Base directly adopted from BERT-Base architecture can obtain $42.0$ box AP on COCO val. We also discuss the impacts as well as limitations of current pre-train schemes and model scaling strategies for Transformer in vision through YOLOS. Code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/hustvl/YOLOS.

paragraphs: Object detection requires recognizing objects and locating regions in a two-dimensional image. This paper asks how far a Transformer can go when it treats that task primarily as sequence-to-sequence processing, with minimal built-in knowledge of spatial structure. YOLOS is designed to investigate that question through a deliberately minimally modified Vision Transformer.

The model family limits task-specific architectural changes, region priors, and inductive biases. This makes detection a test of how much the general Transformer architecture can accomplish after pretraining. The authors report that pretraining only on ImageNet-1k already yields competitive results on the COCO detection benchmark.

One reported example is YOLOS-Base, directly adapted from the BERT-Base architecture, which achieves 42.0 box AP on COCO validation data. The paper also uses YOLOS to examine the effects and limitations of existing pretraining and model-scaling strategies for vision Transformers. The findings show that competitive detection is possible with relatively little task-specific structural machinery, while leaving the broader role of pretraining and scaling central to the investigation.
summary.tldr: YOLOS achieves competitive object detection with a minimally modified Vision Transformer and limited task-specific spatial assumptions.

title: You Only Look at One Sequence: Rethinking Transformer in Vision through Object Detection

abstract: Estimating personalized treatment effects from high-dimensional observational data is essential in situations where experimental designs are infeasible, unethical, or expensive. Existing approaches rely on fitting deep models on outcomes observed for treated and control populations. However, when measuring individual outcomes is costly, as is the case of a tumor biopsy, a sample-efficient strategy for acquiring each result is required. Deep Bayesian active learning provides a framework for efficient data acquisition by selecting points with high uncertainty. However, existing methods bias training data acquisition towards regions of non-overlapping support between the treated and control populations. These are not sample-efficient because the treatment effect is not identifiable in such regions. We introduce causal, Bayesian acquisition functions grounded in information theory that bias data acquisition towards regions with overlapping support to maximize sample efficiency for learning personalized treatment effects. We demonstrate the performance of the proposed acquisition strategies on synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets IHDP and CMNIST and their extensions, which aim to simulate common dataset biases and pathologies.

paragraphs: Learning personalized treatment effects from observational data requires outcomes from treated and untreated populations. Measuring those outcomes can be expensive, so choosing which ones to acquire matters. This paper examines how to make that choice efficiently when deep models work with high-dimensional observations.

Ordinary Bayesian active learning often selects examples where a model is uncertain. The authors identify a problem with applying this strategy directly: it can favor regions where treated and control populations do not overlap. Treatment effects are not identifiable in those regions, so high uncertainty alone does not make an outcome measurement useful for the intended causal comparison.

Causal-BALD introduces information-theoretic Bayesian acquisition functions that favor regions with overlapping support. These functions aim to direct measurement effort toward examples that inform personalized treatment effects. The authors evaluate the strategies on synthetic and semi-synthetic IHDP and CMNIST datasets and extensions designed to represent common biases and pathologies. The work connects active data acquisition to the conditions needed for meaningful treatment-effect estimation.
summary.tldr: Causal-BALD selects costly outcome measurements with attention to treated-control overlap, aiming to make personalized treatment-effect learning more sample-efficient.

title: Causal-BALD: Deep Bayesian Active Learning of Outcomes to Infer Treatment-Effects from Observational Data

abstract: There is a tendency across different subfields in AI to see value in a small collection of influential benchmarks, which we term 'general' benchmarks. These benchmarks operate as stand-ins or abstractions for a range of anointed common problems that are frequently framed as foundational milestones on the path towards flexible and generalizable AI systems. State-of-the-art performance on these benchmarks is widely understood as indicative of progress towards these long-term goals. In this position paper, we explore how such benchmarks are designed, constructed and used in order to reveal key limitations of their framing as the functionally 'general' broad measures of progress they are set up to be.

paragraphs: This position paper examines how a small set of influential benchmarks comes to represent progress across AI. The authors call these general benchmarks because researchers treat them as proxies for a broader collection of problems. Success on them is often interpreted as movement toward flexible systems that generalize well.

The paper focuses on the relationship between the tasks a benchmark contains and the larger ambitions attached to its results. A benchmark offers an abstraction of selected problems, while the goals of general and flexible AI extend beyond that selection. The authors investigate how benchmark design, construction, and use contribute to framing particular evaluations as broad measures of progress.

Its contribution is a critique of that framing rather than a new benchmark or learning algorithm. By examining the role these evaluations play across AI subfields, the paper aims to expose limitations in treating their scores as functionally general evidence. The central question is how much a result on an influential evaluation can support claims about AI's longer-term goals.
summary.tldr: This position paper questions how influential AI benchmarks become broad proxies for progress toward flexible, generalizable intelligence.

title: AI and the Everything in the Whole Wide World Benchmark

abstract: Few-shot segmentation~(FSS) aims at performing semantic segmentation on novel classes given a few annotated support samples. With a rethink of recent advances, we find that the current FSS framework has deviated far from the supervised segmentation framework: Given the deep features, FSS methods typically use an intricate decoder to perform sophisticated pixel-wise matching, while the supervised segmentation methods use a simple linear classification head. Due to the intricacy of the decoder and its matching pipeline, it is not easy to follow such an FSS framework. This paper revives the straightforward framework of ``feature extractor $+$ linear classification head'' and proposes a novel Feature-Proxy Transformer (FPTrans) method, in which the ``proxy'' is the vector representing a semantic class in the linear classification head. FPTrans has two keypoints for learning discriminative features and representative proxies: 1) To better utilize the limited support samples, the feature extractor makes the query interact with the support features from bottom to top layers using a novel prompting strategy. 2) FPTrans uses multiple local background proxies (instead of a single one) because the background is not homogeneous and may contain some novel foreground regions. These two keypoints are easily integrated into the vision transformer backbone with the prompting mechanism in the transformer. Given the learned features and proxies, FPTrans directly compares their cosine similarity for segmentation. Although the framework is straightforward, we show that FPTrans achieves competitive FSS accuracy on par with state-of-the-art decoder-based methods.

paragraphs: Few-shot segmentation identifies pixels belonging to a new class using only a few annotated examples. Many methods accomplish this through elaborate decoders that match pixels between support and query images. FPTrans returns to a simpler arrangement: a feature extractor followed by a linear classification head whose class-representing vectors are called proxies.

To make that simple head effective, FPTrans allows query features to interact with support features throughout the feature extractor using transformer prompts. It also represents the background through multiple local proxies. This matters because background regions need not form one coherent category and may contain objects that would be foreground for another novel class.

Both mechanisms fit into a vision transformer through prompting. Once the model has learned features and proxies, segmentation uses their cosine similarity directly. The reported accuracy is competitive with state-of-the-art methods that use complex decoders. The finding supports investing in informative features and representative class vectors as a way to obtain strong few-shot segmentation within a straightforward prediction framework.
summary.tldr: FPTrans combines support-aware transformer features with class proxies to achieve competitive few-shot segmentation using a simple prediction head.

title: Feature-Proxy Transformer for Few-Shot Segmentation

abstract: A wide range of models have been proposed for Graph Generative Models, necessitating effective methods to evaluate their quality. So far, most techniques use either traditional metrics based on subgraph counting, or the representations of randomly initialized Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). We propose using representations from constrastively trained GNNs, rather than random GNNs, and show this gives more reliable evaluation metrics. Neither traditional approaches nor GNN-based approaches dominate the other, however: we give examples of graphs that each approach is unable to distinguish. We demonstrate that Graph Substructure Networks (GSNs), which in a way combine both approaches, are better at distinguishing the distances between graph datasets.

Neither traditional approaches nor GNN-based approaches dominate the other, however: we give examples of graphs that each approach is unable to distinguish. paragraphs: Evaluating a graph generator requires a meaningful way to compare collections of graphs. Existing techniques described in this paper either count graph substructures or use representations produced by randomly initialized graph neural networks. The authors investigate whether learning those representations can make the resulting evaluation metrics more reliable.

Their proposed approach uses features from graph neural networks trained with a contrastive objective. They find that these learned features provide more reliable metrics than features from random networks. However, the comparison with traditional subgraph-counting approaches reveals an important qualification: neither family dominates the other. The paper gives examples of graphs that each approach fails to distinguish.

The authors then examine Graph Substructure Networks, which combine aspects of substructure-based and neural approaches. These networks better distinguish distances between graph datasets in the reported study. The overall finding favors learned representations while also showing why representation choice matters: a metric can miss structural differences that another metric detects. Combining complementary sources of structural information offers a stronger basis for the evaluated comparisons.
summary.tldr: Contrastively learned graph features improve generator evaluation, while combining neural and substructure information helps address complementary blind spots.

title: Evaluating Graph Generative Models with Contrastively Learned Features

abstract: For Generative Adversarial Networks which map a latent distribution to the target distribution, in this paper, we study how the sampling in latent space can affect the generation performance, especially for images. We observe that, as the neural generator is a continuous function, two close samples in latent space would be mapped into two nearby images, while their quality can differ much as the quality generally does not exhibit a continuous nature in pixel space. From such a continuous mapping function perspective, it is also possible that two distant latent samples can be mapped into two close images (if not exactly the same). In particular, if the latent samples are mapped in aggregation into a single mode, mode collapse occurs. Accordingly, we propose adding an implicit latent transform before the mapping function to improve latent $z$ from its initial distribution, e.g., Gaussian. This is achieved using well-developed adversarial sample mining techniques, e.g. iterative fast gradient sign method (I-FGSM). We further propose new GAN training pipelines to obtain better generative mappings w.r.t quality and diversity by introducing targeted latent transforms into the bi-level optimization of GAN. Experimental results on visual data show that our method can effectively achieve improvement in both quality and diversity.

paragraphs: This paper studies how the latent samples supplied to a GAN affect the quality and diversity of its generated images. The authors observe that nearby latent samples produce nearby images through a continuous generator, yet those images can differ greatly in quality. Conversely, distant latent samples can produce similar or even identical images.

That second possibility connects latent sampling to mode collapse, where samples collectively map into a single mode. The proposed response is to insert an implicit transformation of the latent sample before it reaches the generator. Adversarial sample-mining techniques, including iterative fast gradient sign methods, construct these transformations from an initial latent distribution such as a Gaussian.

The authors also introduce GAN training pipelines that incorporate targeted latent transformations into the model's bilevel optimization. The intended benefit is to improve the learned mapping in both output quality and diversity. Experiments on visual data report improvements in both respects, supporting latent-space transformation as a useful intervention in the generation and training process.
summary.tldr: Adversarially constructed latent transformations improve reported GAN image quality and diversity by changing the samples used for generation and training.

title: Improving Generative Adversarial Networks via Adversarial Learning in Latent Space

abstract: We present LogiGAN, an unsupervised adversarial pre-training framework for improving logical reasoning abilities of language models. Upon automatic identification of logical reasoning phenomena in massive text corpus via detection heuristics, we train language models to predict the masked-out logical statements. Inspired by the facilitation effect of reflective thinking in human learning, we analogically simulate the learning-thinking process with an adversarial Generator-Verifier architecture to assist logic learning. LogiGAN implements a novel sequential GAN approach that (a) circumvents the non-differentiable challenge of the sequential GAN by leveraging the Generator as a sentence-level generative likelihood scorer with a learning objective of reaching scoring consensus with the Verifier; (b) is computationally feasible for large-scale pre-training with arbitrary target length. Both base and large size language models pre-trained with LogiGAN demonstrate obvious performance improvement on 12 datasets requiring general reasoning abilities, revealing the fundamental role of logic in broad reasoning, as well as the effectiveness of LogiGAN. Ablation studies on LogiGAN components reveal the relative orthogonality between linguistic and logic abilities and suggest that reflective thinking's facilitation effect might also generalize to machine learning.

paragraphs: LogiGAN aims to strengthen a language model’s logical reasoning through unsupervised pre-training. It uses heuristics to find reasoning-related statements in a large text collection, masks selected statements, and trains models to predict them. This creates a learning task centered on logical content found automatically in existing text.

The framework pairs a Generator with a Verifier in an adversarial architecture inspired by reflective learning. To handle the difficulty of differentiating through generated text sequences, the Generator also serves as a sentence-level likelihood scorer and learns to bring its scores into agreement with the Verifier. The resulting sequential GAN approach is designed to remain computationally feasible for large-scale pre-training with arbitrary target lengths.

Both base-sized and large models improve across twelve datasets requiring general reasoning. Component ablations suggest that linguistic ability and logical ability are relatively distinct, and that the reflective-learning analogy may extend to machine learning. These findings support the usefulness of the training framework while keeping the broader interpretation about reflective thinking tentative.
summary.tldr: LogiGAN uses adversarial Generator–Verifier pre-training on automatically identified logical statements to improve language-model reasoning.

title: LogiGAN: Learning Logical Reasoning via Adversarial Pre-training

abstract: We show that Contrastive Learning (CL) under a broad family of loss functions (including InfoNCE) has a unified formulation of coordinate-wise optimization on the network parameter $\vtheta$ and pairwise importance $\alpha$, where the \emph{max player} $\vtheta$ learns representation for contrastiveness, and the \emph{min player} $\alpha$ puts more weights on pairs of distinct samples that share similar representations. The resulting formulation, called \boldmethod{}, unifies not only various existing contrastive losses, which differ by how sample-pair importance $\alpha$ is constructed, but also is able to extrapolate to give novel contrastive losses beyond popular ones, opening a new avenue of contrastive loss design. These novel losses yield comparable (or better) performance on CIFAR10, STL-10 and CIFAR-100 than classic InfoNCE. Furthermore, we also analyze the max player in detail: we prove that with fixed $\alpha$, max player is equivalent to Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for deep linear network, and almost all local minima are global and rank-1, recovering optimal PCA solutions. Finally, we extend our analysis on max player to 2-layer ReLU networks, showing that its fixed points can have higher ranks. Codes are available in https://github.com/facebookresearch/luckmatters/tree/main/ssl/real-dataset.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning can be understood as jointly choosing a representation and deciding which sample pairs deserve attention. This paper formalizes that view for a broad family of losses, including InfoNCE. One optimization player updates network parameters for contrastiveness, while another assigns greater importance to distinct samples whose representations remain similar.

This coordinate-wise formulation unifies existing losses through their different ways of constructing pairwise importance weights. It also suggests new losses beyond the commonly used choices. On CIFAR-10, STL-10, and CIFAR-100, those new losses achieve performance comparable to or better than classic InfoNCE, supporting the formulation as a tool for loss design.

The authors further analyze the representation-learning player with pairwise weights held fixed. For deep linear networks, it is equivalent to principal component analysis, and almost all local minima are global, rank-one solutions recovering the optimal PCA result. Extending the analysis to two-layer ReLU networks reveals that fixed points can have higher rank. The distinction clarifies how nonlinear networks can behave differently within the same optimization framework.
summary.tldr: A two-player optimization view unifies contrastive losses, suggests new objectives, and connects fixed-weight deep linear learning to PCA.

title: Understanding Deep Contrastive Learning via Coordinate-wise Optimization

abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a popular method for efficiently inferring optima of an expensive black-box function via a sequence of queries. Existing information-theoretic BO procedures aim to make queries that most reduce the uncertainty about optima, where the uncertainty is captured by Shannon entropy. However, an optimal measure of uncertainty would, ideally, factor in how we intend to use the inferred quantity in some downstream procedure. In this paper, we instead consider a generalization of Shannon entropy from work in statistical decision theory (DeGroot 1962, Rao 1984), which contains a broad class of uncertainty measures parameterized by a problem-specific loss function corresponding to a downstream task. We first show that special cases of this entropy lead to popular acquisition functions used in BO procedures such as knowledge gradient, expected improvement, and entropy search. We then show how alternative choices for the loss yield a flexible family of acquisition functions that can be customized for use in novel optimization settings. Additionally, we develop gradient-based methods to efficiently optimize our proposed family of acquisition functions, and demonstrate strong empirical performance on a diverse set of sequential decision making tasks, including variants of top-$k$ optimization, multi-level set estimation, and sequence search.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization chooses which evaluations of an expensive black-box function to request. Information-based approaches often select queries that reduce uncertainty about the optimum, measured with Shannon entropy. This paper asks how query selection should change when the useful information depends on a particular downstream decision.

The authors adopt a decision-theoretic generalization of entropy parameterized by a task-specific loss function. That loss describes how inferred information will be used, allowing the uncertainty measure to reflect the eventual objective. They show that special cases recover familiar acquisition functions, including knowledge gradient, expected improvement, and entropy search.

Changing the loss produces a flexible family of acquisition functions for other optimization settings. The paper also develops gradient-based methods to optimize these functions efficiently. Experiments report strong performance across sequential decision tasks involving variants of top-k optimization, multi-level set estimation, and sequence search. The contribution thus combines a common interpretation of existing methods with a mechanism for designing query policies around different downstream goals.
summary.tldr: Task-specific decision losses generalize entropy-based Bayesian optimization and yield customizable query-selection rules.

title: Generalizing Bayesian Optimization with Decision-theoretic Entropies

abstract: We consider the classic facility location problem in fully dynamic data streams, where elements can be both inserted and deleted. In this problem, one is interested in maintaining a stable and high quality solution throughout the data stream while using only little time per update (insertion or deletion). We study the problem and provide the first algorithm that at the same time maintains a constant approximation and incurs polylogarithmic amortized recourse per update. We complement our theoretical results with an experimental analysis showing the practical efficiency of our method.
originalAbstract: We consider the classic facility location problem in fully dynamic data streams, where elements can be both inserted and deleted. In this problem, one is interested in maintaining a stable and high quality solution throughout the data stream while using only little time per update (insertion or deletion). We study the problem and provide the first algorithm that at the same time maintains a constant approximation and incurs polylogarithmic amortized recourse per update. We complement our theoretical results with an experimental analysis showing the practical efficiency of our method.

paragraphs: The paper considers facility location when the input changes continuously through both insertions and deletions. In this setting, maintaining a good solution is only part of the challenge. The solution should also remain stable as updates arrive, and processing those updates should be efficient enough to support an ongoing data stream.

The authors give an algorithm that combines a constant-factor approximation with polylogarithmic amortised recourse per update. The approximation guarantee controls solution quality relative to the optimum. Recourse measures changes to the maintained solution, so the second guarantee concerns stability. Because it is amortised, it controls the average amount of change over a sequence of updates rather than stating that every individual update has the same small cost.

The paper identifies this simultaneous combination of approximation quality and recourse as its first-of-its-kind contribution for the problem. An experimental analysis also supports the method's practical efficiency. Together, these results address the need to keep a changing solution useful without requiring excessive rearrangement whenever the underlying data changes.
summary.tldr: A dynamic facility location algorithm combines constant-factor solution quality with polylogarithmic amortised changes per update.

title: Efficient and Stable Fully Dynamic Facility Location

abstract: In this paper, we study the episodic reinforcement learning (RL) problem modeled by finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with constraint on the number of batches. The multi-batch reinforcement learning framework, where the agent is required to provide a time schedule to update policy before everything, which is particularly suitable for the scenarios where the agent suffers extensively from changing the policy adaptively. Given a finite-horizon MDP with $S$ states, $A$ actions and planning horizon $H$, we design a computational efficient algorithm to achieve near-optimal regret of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{SAH^3K\ln(1/\delta)})$\footnote{$\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ hides logarithmic terms of $(S,A,H,K)$} in $K$ episodes using $O\left(H+\log_2\log_2(K) \right)$ batches with confidence parameter $\delta$. To our best of knowledge, it is the first $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{SAH^3K})$ regret bound with $O(H+\log_2\log_2(K))$ batch complexity. Meanwhile, we show that to achieve $\tilde{O}(\mathrm{poly}(S,A,H)\sqrt{K})$ regret, the number of batches is at least $\Omega\left(H/\log_A(K)+ \log_2\log_2(K) \right)$, which matches our upper bound up to logarithmic terms.Our technical contribution are two-fold: 1) a near-optimal design scheme to explore over the unlearned states; 2) an computational efficient algorithm to explore certain directions with an approximated transition model.ion model.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we study the episodic reinforcement learning (RL) problem modeled by finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with constraint on the number of batches. The multi-batch reinforcement learning framework, where the agent is required to provide a time schedule to update policy before everything, which is particularly suitable for the scenarios where the agent suffers extensively from changing the policy adaptively. Given a finite-horizon MDP with $S$ states, $A$ actions and planning horizon $H$, we design a computational efficient algorithm to achieve near-optimal regret of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{SAH^3K\ln(1/\delta)})$\footnote{$\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ hides logarithmic terms of $(S,A,H,K)$} in $K$ episodes using $O\left(H+\log_2\log_2(K) \right)$ batches with confidence parameter $\delta$. To our best of knowledge, it is the first $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{SAH^3K})$ regret bound with $O(H+\log_2\log_2(K))$ batch complexity. Meanwhile, we show that to achieve $\tilde{O}(\mathrm{poly}(S,A,H)\sqrt{K})$ regret, the number of batches is at least $\Omega\left(H/\log_A(K)+ \log_2\log_2(K) \right)$, which matches our upper bound up to logarithmic terms.Our technical contribution are two-fold: 1) a near-optimal design scheme to explore over the unlearned states; 2) an computational efficient algorithm to explore certain directions with an approximated transition model.ion model.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when an agent must commit in advance to a schedule of policy updates. That restriction matters when changing a policy adaptively is costly. The setting uses finite-horizon Markov decision processes, and the goal is to learn effectively while keeping the number of update batches small.

For S states, A actions, horizon H, and K episodes, the authors give a computationally efficient algorithm with near-optimal regret scaling as the square root of SAH³K, apart from logarithmic and confidence factors. It needs only O(H + log₂ log₂ K) batches. Its technical ingredients are an exploration design for states that remain insufficiently learned and an efficient way to explore selected directions using an approximate transition model.

The paper also establishes a lower bound on the batches required to obtain square-root-in-K regret with polynomial dependence on the other problem sizes. That bound matches the algorithm's batch requirement up to logarithmic terms. Together, the results characterize how infrequently policies can be updated while retaining the targeted learning performance.
summary.tldr: An efficient reinforcement-learning algorithm achieves near-optimal regret with a small, predetermined number of policy-update batches.

title: Near-Optimal Regret Bounds for Multi-batch Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Using Unbiased Learning to Rank (ULTR) to train the ranking model with biased click logs has attracted increased research interest. The key idea is to explicitly model the user's observation behavior when building the ranker with a large number of click logs. Considering the simplicity, recent efforts are mainly based on the position bias hypothesis, in which the observation only depends on the position. However, this hypothesis does not hold in many scenarios due to the neglect of the distinct characteristics of individuals in the same position. On the other hand, directly modeling observation bias for each individual is quite challenging, since the effects of each individual's features on relevance and observation are entangled. It is difficult to ravel out this coupled effect and thus obtain a correct relevance model from click data. To address this issue, we first present the concept of coupling effect for individual-level ULTR. Then, we develop the novel Lipschitz and Bernoulli Decoupling (LBD) model to decouple the effects on relevance and observation at the individual level. We prove theoretically that our proposed method could recover the correct relevance order for the ranking objective. Empirical results on two LTR benchmark datasets show that the proposed model outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines and verify its effectiveness in debiasing data.

paragraphs: Click logs can help train ranking systems, but a click reflects both relevance and whether a user observed an item. Many approaches simplify the observation process by assuming it depends only on ranking position. This paper addresses cases where that assumption fails because individuals at the same position have different characteristics.

A more detailed observation model introduces another difficulty: individual features can affect both relevance and observation. Their contributions become entangled, making it hard to learn the correct relevance ranking from clicks. The authors formalize this coupling and introduce Lipschitz and Bernoulli Decoupling, or LBD, to separate the two effects at the individual level.

The paper provides a theoretical result showing that the method could recover the correct relevance ordering for the ranking objective. Experiments on two learning-to-rank benchmarks report improvements over the compared state-of-the-art methods and support its ability to reduce bias. The contribution is a way to model observation beyond position alone while directly addressing the ambiguity between being relevant and being seen.
summary.tldr: LBD separates individual-level influences on relevance and observation to learn less biased rankings from click logs.

title: LBD: Decouple Relevance and Observation for Individual-Level Unbiased Learning to Rank

abstract: In this paper we explore the recent topic of point cloud completion, guided by an auxiliary image. We show how it is possible to effectively combine the information from the two modalities in a localized latent space, thus avoiding the need for complex point cloud reconstruction methods from single views used by the state-of-the-art. We also investigate a novel self-supervised setting where the auxiliary image provides a supervisory signal to the training process by using a differentiable renderer on the completed point cloud to measure fidelity in the image space. Experiments show significant improvements over state-of-the-art supervised methods for both unimodal and multimodal completion. We also show the effectiveness of the self-supervised approach which outperforms a number of supervised methods and is competitive with the latest supervised models only exploiting point cloud information.

We also investigate a novel self-supervised setting where the auxiliary image provides a supervisory signal to the training process by using a differentiable renderer on the completed point cloud to measure fidelity in the image space. paragraphs: Point cloud completion fills in missing parts of a shape represented by a collection of three-dimensional points. This paper studies how an additional image can guide that process. The image and partial point cloud supply different information, creating an opportunity to improve completion by combining their representations.

The proposed approach joins the two modalities in a localized latent space. This lets image information contribute to completion without requiring the complex reconstruction of a point cloud from a single image used by existing approaches. The paper also explores self-supervised training, in which the auxiliary image itself supplies a training signal.

For that setting, a differentiable renderer converts the completed point cloud into an image-space representation, allowing image fidelity to guide learning. Experiments report significant improvements over state-of-the-art supervised methods for both unimodal and multimodal completion. The self-supervised approach also exceeds several supervised methods and is competitive with recent supervised models using only point clouds. Together, the results show two useful roles for images: informing the completion representation and supervising the completed shape.
summary.tldr: Combining images and point clouds in a localized representation improves shape completion and enables image-based self-supervision.

title: Cross-modal Learning for Image-Guided Point Cloud Shape Completion

abstract: Deep classifiers are known to rely on spurious features — patterns which are correlated with the target on the training data but not inherently relevant to the learning problem, such as the image backgrounds when classifying the foregrounds. In this paper we evaluate the amount of information about the core (non-spurious) features that can be decoded from the representations learned by standard empirical risk minimization (ERM) and specialized group robustness training. Following recent work on Deep Feature Reweighting (DFR), we evaluate the feature representations by re-training the last layer of the model on a held-out set where the spurious correlation is broken. On multiple vision and NLP problems, we show that the features learned by simple ERM are highly competitive with the features learned by specialized group robustness methods targeted at reducing the effect of spurious correlations. Moreover, we show that the quality of learned feature representations is greatly affected by the design decisions beyond the training method, such as the model architecture and pre-training strategy. On the other hand, we find that strong regularization is not necessary for learning high-quality feature representations.Finally, using insights from our analysis, we significantly improve upon the best results reported in the literature on the popular Waterbirds, CelebA hair color prediction and WILDS-FMOW problems, achieving 97\%, 92\% and 50\% worst-group accuracies, respectively.
