paragraphs: A classifier may exploit misleading training correlations, such as backgrounds associated with particular objects. This paper asks how much useful information about the actual target remains in its learned representation. That question separates the quality of the learned features from the way the final prediction layer uses them.

The authors evaluate representations by retraining only the last layer on held-out data where the spurious correlation is broken, following Deep Feature Reweighting. Across several vision and language problems, ordinary empirical risk minimization learns features highly competitive with those from specialized group-robustness training. Architecture and pretraining choices strongly affect feature quality, while strong regularization is not necessary for learning high-quality representations.

Using these insights, the authors report improved worst-group accuracies of 97% on Waterbirds, 92% on CelebA hair-color prediction, and 50% on WILDS-FMOW. The results indicate that models trained conventionally can retain useful core information even when spurious correlations influence their predictions. They also highlight the importance of representation design and the held-out data used to reweight those features.
summary.tldr: Standard training can learn core features competitive with specialized robustness methods, and retraining the final layer helps reveal their quality.

title: On Feature Learning in the Presence of Spurious Correlations

abstract: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for creating trustworthy machine learning models. Recent years have seen a steep rise in UQ methods that can flag suspicious examples, however, it is often unclear what exactly these methods identify. In this work, we propose a framework for categorizing uncertain examples flagged by UQ methods. We introduce the confusion density matrix---a kernel-based approximation of the misclassification density---and use this to categorize suspicious examples identified by a given uncertainty method into three classes: out-of-distribution (OOD) examples, boundary (Bnd) examples, and examples in regions of high in-distribution misclassification (IDM). Through extensive experiments, we show that our framework provides a new and distinct perspective for assessing differences between uncertainty quantification methods, thereby forming a valuable assessment benchmark.

paragraphs: Uncertainty methods can flag suspicious examples without making clear what kinds of difficulty those examples represent. This paper proposes a framework for interpreting the examples an uncertainty method selects. The goal is to understand differences between methods through the nature of their warnings, beyond the fact that they produce warnings.

The central tool is a confusion density matrix, a kernel-based approximation of misclassification density. The framework uses it to organize flagged examples into three categories: out-of-distribution inputs, boundary examples, and inputs in regions with high in-distribution misclassification. These categories distinguish different situations that can all appear under the broad label of uncertainty.

Extensive experiments show that this categorization offers a distinct perspective for comparing uncertainty quantification methods. Two methods can be assessed according to which types of suspicious examples they identify, making their differences more interpretable. The contribution is an assessment framework and benchmark for understanding what uncertainty methods flag. It adds structure to the evaluation of their outputs rather than treating all flagged examples as a single undifferentiated group.
summary.tldr: A confusion density matrix categorizes uncertainty warnings into out-of-distribution, boundary, and high-error in-distribution examples to clarify differences between methods.

title: What is Flagged in Uncertainty Quantification? Latent Density Models for Uncertainty Categorization

abstract: Subgame solving is an essential technique in addressing large imperfect information games, with various approaches developed to enhance the performance of refined strategies in the abstraction of the target subgame. However, directly applying existing subgame solving techniques may be difficult, due to the intricate nature and substantial size of many real-world games. To overcome this issue, recent subgame solving methods allow for subgame solving on limited knowledge order subgames, increasing their applicability in large games; yet this may still face obstacles due to extensive information set sizes. To address this challenge, we propose a generative subgame solving (GS2) framework, which utilizes a generation function to identify a subset of the earliest-reached nodes, reducing the size of the subgame. Our method is supported by a theoretical analysis and employs a diversity-based generation function to enhance safety. Experiments conducted on medium-sized games as well as the challenging large game of GuanDan demonstrate a significant improvement over the blueprint.

paragraphs: Subgame solving improves a strategy by concentrating computation on a relevant part of a larger game. In imperfect-information games, however, the player’s uncertainty can leave that part extremely large. The paper addresses a remaining obstacle in approaches that already restrict the knowledge considered: information sets can still contain too many possibilities for convenient refinement.

The proposed generative subgame solving framework, GS2, uses a generation function to select a subset of the earliest-reached nodes. Restricting those starting possibilities reduces the size of the subgame to be solved. The authors support the framework with theoretical analysis and introduce a generation function based on diversity to improve safety.

Experiments cover medium-sized games and the much larger game GuanDan. The resulting strategies significantly improve on the blueprint, the strategy being refined. The contribution is therefore a way to make local strategy improvement more manageable in large games while considering the quality of the selected subset. The stated results support improvement over the blueprint without claiming that every possible selection is safe or optimal.
summary.tldr: GS2 reduces subgame size by generating a subset of starting nodes and improves on blueprint strategies in the evaluated games.

title: Efficient Subgame Refinement for Extensive-form Games

abstract: Recently, Meta-Black-Box Optimization with Reinforcement Learning (MetaBBO-RL) has showcased the power of leveraging RL at the meta-level to mitigate manual fine-tuning of low-level black-box optimizers. However, this field is hindered by the lack of a unified benchmark. To fill this gap, we introduce MetaBox, the first benchmark platform expressly tailored for developing and evaluating MetaBBO-RL methods. MetaBox offers a flexible algorithmic template that allows users to effortlessly implement their unique designs within the platform. Moreover, it provides a broad spectrum of over 300 problem instances, collected from synthetic to realistic scenarios, and an extensive library of 19 baseline methods, including both traditional black-box optimizers and recent MetaBBO-RL methods. Besides, MetaBox introduces three standardized performance metrics, enabling a more thorough assessment of the methods. In a bid to illustrate the utility of MetaBox for facilitating rigorous evaluation and in-depth analysis, we carry out a wide-ranging benchmarking study on existing MetaBBO-RL methods. Our MetaBox is open-source and accessible at: https://github.com/GMC-DRL/MetaBox.

paragraphs: Meta-black-box optimization with reinforcement learning uses a learned higher-level process to reduce manual tuning of underlying optimizers. Comparing approaches is difficult without a common evaluation setting. MetaBox addresses that gap with a benchmark platform specifically designed for developing and assessing methods in this area.

The platform provides a flexible algorithmic template for implementing different designs. Its evaluation collection contains more than 300 problem instances spanning synthetic and realistic scenarios. It also includes 19 baseline methods covering traditional black-box optimization and more recent reinforcement-learning-based meta-optimization approaches. Three standardized performance metrics provide a shared basis for assessing methods from multiple perspectives.

The authors demonstrate the platform through a broad benchmarking study of existing methods. The stated contribution is the infrastructure for rigorous comparison and deeper analysis, rather than a claim that one new optimizer dominates the others. By bringing implementations, problem instances, comparison methods, and measurements into one open-source platform, MetaBox supports a more consistent development and evaluation process for the field.
summary.tldr: MetaBox provides shared problems, baselines, metrics, and implementation support for evaluating reinforcement-learning-based meta-black-box optimization.

title: MetaBox: A Benchmark Platform for Meta-Black-Box Optimization with Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Diffusion MRI (dMRI) is a widely used imaging modality, but requires long scanning times to acquire high resolution datasets. By leveraging the unique geometry present within this domain, we present a novel approach to dMRI angular super-resolution that extends upon the parametric continuous convolution (PCConv) framework. We introduce several additions to the operation including a Fourier feature mapping, 'global' co-ordinates, and domain specific context. Using this framework, we build a fully parametric continuous convolution network (PCCNN) and compare against existing models. We demonstrate the PCCNN performs competitively while using significantly fewer parameters. Moreover, we show that this formulation generalises well to clinically relevant downstream analyses such as fixel-based analysis, and neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging.

paragraphs: Acquiring high-resolution diffusion MRI data requires long scanning times. This paper addresses angular super-resolution by designing a neural operation around the geometry of diffusion MRI. The objective is to improve angular detail through a model that makes explicit use of the structure of this imaging domain.

The authors extend parametric continuous convolution with Fourier feature mapping, global coordinates, and domain-specific context. These additions form the basis of a fully parametric continuous convolution network, PCCNN. The design brings information about spatial and angular organization into the convolution framework used to process the measurements.

Compared with existing models, PCCNN achieves competitive performance while using significantly fewer parameters. The authors also examine whether the formulation remains useful for downstream analyses, reporting good generalization to fixel-based analysis and neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging. Those evaluations matter because a reconstruction method must support subsequent analysis as well as the super-resolution task itself. The findings therefore connect parameter efficiency with utility in the clinically relevant analyses named in the abstract.
summary.tldr: A geometry-aware continuous convolution network performs diffusion MRI angular super-resolution competitively with fewer parameters and supports relevant downstream analyses.

title: Spatio-Angular Convolutions for Super-resolution in Diffusion MRI

abstract: Data over non-Euclidean manifolds, often discretized as surface meshes, naturally arise in computer graphics and biological and physical systems. In particular, solutions to partial differential equations (PDEs) over manifolds depend critically on the underlying geometry. While graph neural networks have been successfully applied to PDEs, they do not incorporate surface geometry and do not consider local gauge symmetries of the manifold. Alternatively, recent works on gauge equivariant convolutional and attentional architectures on meshes leverage the underlying geometry but underperform in modeling surface PDEs with complex nonlinear dynamics. To address these issues, we introduce a new gauge equivariant architecture using nonlinear message passing. Our novel architecture achieves higher performance than either convolutional or attentional networks on domains with highly complex and nonlinear dynamics. However, similar to the non-mesh case, design trade-offs favor convolutional, attentional, or message passing networks for different tasks; we investigate in which circumstances our message passing method provides the most benefit.

paragraphs: Predicting dynamics on a curved surface requires accounting for its geometry. Such surfaces are often represented by meshes, and the partial differential equations defined over them can depend strongly on that geometry. This paper targets a gap between graph networks that overlook surface geometry and geometry-aware architectures that struggle with complex nonlinear dynamics.

The authors introduce a gauge-equivariant architecture based on nonlinear message passing. Gauge equivariance makes the computation consistent with changes in local coordinate conventions on the surface. Combining that geometric property with nonlinear exchanges of information between mesh locations gives the model a way to represent complex dynamics while respecting the structure of the underlying surface.

The architecture achieves better performance than convolutional and attentional alternatives on domains with highly complex nonlinear dynamics. The paper also investigates when message passing provides the greatest benefit. Its conclusion remains task-dependent: design trade-offs can favor convolution, attention, or message passing in different circumstances. The contribution is therefore both a new architecture and an examination of where its particular combination of geometry and nonlinear computation is most useful.
summary.tldr: Gauge-equivariant nonlinear message passing improves modeling of complex surface dynamics, with benefits that depend on the task.

title: Modeling Dynamics over Meshes with Gauge Equivariant Nonlinear Message Passing

abstract: Continual table semantic parsing aims to train a parser on a sequence of tasks, where each task requires the parser to translate natural language into SQL based on task-specific tables but only offers limited training examples. Conventional methods tend to suffer from overfitting with limited supervision, as well as catastrophic forgetting due to parameter updates.Despite recent advancements that partially alleviate these issues through semi-supervised data augmentation and retention of a few past examples, the performance is still limited by the volume of unsupervised data and stored examples.To overcome these challenges, this paper introduces a novel method integrating parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and in-context tuning (ICT) for training a continual table semantic parser. Initially, we present a task-adaptive PEFT framework capable of fully circumventing catastrophic forgetting, which is achieved by freezing the pre-trained model backbone and fine-tuning small-scale prompts. Building on this, we propose a teacher-student framework-based solution. The teacher addresses the few-shot problem using ICT, which procures contextual information by demonstrating a few training examples. In turn, the student leverages the proposed PEFT framework to learn from the teacher's output distribution, and subsequently compresses and saves the contextual information to the prompts, eliminating the need to store any training examples.Experimental evaluations on two benchmarks affirm the superiority of our method over prevalent few-shot and continual learning baselines across various metrics.

paragraphs: Continual table semantic parsing trains a model across a sequence of tasks that translate natural language into SQL for different tables. Each task provides few examples, creating risks of overfitting and forgetting earlier tasks. Existing approaches also depend on the amount of additional unlabeled data or retained past examples.

The proposed method combines parameter-efficient finetuning with in-context tuning. Its task-adaptive framework freezes the pretrained backbone and trains small prompts; the authors state that this setup fully avoids catastrophic forgetting. A teacher model uses a few demonstrated examples to obtain contextual information and address the limited-supervision problem.

A student then learns from the teacher's output distribution using the prompt-based framework. This transfers contextual information into the prompts, allowing it to be saved without retaining training examples. Experiments on two benchmarks show improvements over the evaluated few-shot and continual-learning baselines across multiple metrics. The key idea is to preserve the usefulness of example-based context by encoding it into a small trainable representation.
summary.tldr: A teacher-student method compresses example-based context into small prompts for continual text-to-SQL learning without storing training examples.

title: Parameterizing Context: Unleashing the Power of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning and In-Context Tuning for Continual Table Semantic Parsing

abstract: Neuro-symbolic systems combine the abilities of neural perception and logical reasoning. However, end-to-end learning of neuro-symbolic systems is still an unsolved challenge. This paper proposes a natural framework that fuses neural network training, symbol grounding, and logical constraint synthesis into a coherent and efficient end-to-end learning process. The capability of this framework comes from the improved interactions between the neural and the symbolic parts of the system in both the training and inference stages. Technically, to bridge the gap between the continuous neural network and the discrete logical constraint, we introduce a difference-of-convex programming technique to relax the logical constraints while maintaining their precision. We also employ cardinality constraints as the language for logical constraint learning and incorporate a trust region method to avoid the degeneracy of logical constraint in learning. Both theoretical analyses and empirical evaluations substantiate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

paragraphs: Neuro-symbolic systems combine neural perception with logical reasoning, but learning the two components together remains challenging. Neural networks operate with continuous quantities, while logical constraints make discrete distinctions. This paper proposes a unified training process that learns neural parameters, connects observations to symbols, and synthesizes logical constraints.

The framework uses difference-of-convex programming to relax logical constraints while preserving their precision. It represents learnable rules through cardinality constraints, which express restrictions on how many conditions hold. A trust-region method helps prevent the logical constraints from degenerating during learning. Together, these techniques address both the continuous–discrete mismatch and the stability of the learned logical component.

The authors attribute the framework's capability to improved interaction between neural and symbolic components during both training and inference. Theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation support its effectiveness. The contribution is a coherent mechanism for learning perception and constraints jointly, so the symbolic component participates in the learning process alongside the neural network and remains relevant when the system makes predictions.
summary.tldr: A unified neuro-symbolic framework jointly learns neural representations, symbol grounding, and logical constraints through continuous optimization.

title: Neuro-symbolic Learning Yielding Logical Constraints

abstract: The discovery of neural architectures from simple building blocks is a long-standing goal of Neural Architecture Search (NAS). Hierarchical search spaces are a promising step towards this goal but lack a unifying search space design framework and typically only search over some limited aspect of architectures. In this work, we introduce a unifying search space design framework based on context-free grammars that can naturally and compactly generate expressive hierarchical search spaces that are 100s of orders of magnitude larger than common spaces from the literature. By enhancing and using their properties, we effectively enable search over the complete architecture and can foster regularity. Further, we propose an efficient hierarchical kernel design for a Bayesian Optimization search strategy to efficiently search over such huge spaces. We demonstrate the versatility of our search space design framework and show that our search strategy can be superior to existing NAS approaches. originalAbstract: The discovery of neural architectures from simple building blocks is a long-standing goal of Neural Architecture Search (NAS). Hierarchical search spaces are a promising step towards this goal but lack a unifying search space design framework and typically only search over some limited aspect of architectures. In this work, we introduce a unifying search space design framework based on context-free grammars that can naturally and compactly generate expressive hierarchical search spaces that are 100s of orders of magnitude larger than common spaces from the literature. By enhancing and using their properties, we effectively enable search over the complete architecture and can foster regularity. Further, we propose an efficient hierarchical kernel design for a Bayesian Optimization search strategy to efficiently search over such huge spaces. We demonstrate the versatility of our search space design framework and show that our search strategy can be superior to existing NAS approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/automl/hierarchical_nas_construction.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search seeks useful networks by exploring combinations of building blocks. Hierarchical search spaces can express structures at multiple levels, but their design has lacked a common framework and often exposes only limited architectural choices. This paper proposes context-free grammars as a unified way to describe and generate these spaces.

The grammar provides compact construction rules for expressive hierarchical architectures. The resulting spaces are hundreds of orders of magnitude larger than common spaces discussed in the literature. By extending and exploiting grammatical properties, the approach enables search over complete architectures and can encourage regularity. This makes the specification of the search space a central part of the method.

To navigate these enormous spaces, the authors introduce a hierarchical kernel for Bayesian optimization. This supplies the search strategy with a way to account for architectural hierarchy while choosing candidates. Their demonstrations show versatility in defining spaces and indicate that the search strategy can outperform existing NAS approaches. The stated advantage is a demonstrated possibility, rather than a guarantee that every larger grammar-defined space yields a better architecture.
summary.tldr: Context-free grammars define expansive hierarchical architecture spaces, paired with a Bayesian optimization strategy designed to search them efficiently.

title: Construction of Hierarchical Neural Architecture Search Spaces based on Context-free Grammars

abstract: We study the performance of empirical risk minimization on the $p$-norm linear regression problem for $p \in (1, \infty)$. We show that, in the realizable case, under no moment assumptions, and up to a distribution-dependent constant, $O(d)$ samples are enough to exactly recover the target. Otherwise, for $p \in [2, \infty)$, and under weak moment assumptions on the target and the covariates, we prove a high probability excess risk bound on the empirical risk minimizer whose leading term matches, up to a constant that depends only on $p$, the asymptotically exact rate. We extend this result to the case $p \in (1, 2)$ under mild assumptions that guarantee the existence of the Hessian of the risk at its minimizer.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes linear regression fitted by empirical risk minimization, using a family of losses indexed by p greater than one. It asks how much data is sufficient and how closely the fitted model approaches the best achievable population risk. The results distinguish an exactly representable target from the more general case.

When the target is realizable, the authors show that a sample count proportional to dimension suffices for exact recovery, up to a distribution-dependent constant. This result requires no moment assumptions. In the general case with p at least two, weak moment assumptions on the target and input variables yield a high-probability bound on excess risk.

The leading term of that bound matches the asymptotically exact rate up to a constant depending only on p. The authors extend the result to p between one and two under mild assumptions ensuring that the risk has a Hessian at its minimizer. The contribution gives sharply characterized statistical guarantees while making clear which assumptions support each regime.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes exact-recovery and sharp excess-risk guarantees for empirical p-norm linear regression under regime-specific assumptions.

title: Optimal Excess Risk Bounds for Empirical Risk Minimization on $p$-Norm Linear Regression

abstract: We introduce OpenIllumination, a real-world dataset containing over 108K images of 64 objects with diverse materials, captured under 72 camera views and a large number of different illuminations. For each image in the dataset, we provide accurate camera parameters, illumination ground truth, and foreground segmentation masks. Our dataset enables the quantitative evaluation of most inverse rendering and material decomposition methods for real objects. We examine several state-of-the-art inverse rendering methods on our dataset and compare their performances. The dataset and code can be found on the project page: https://oppo-us-research.github.io/OpenIllumination.

paragraphs: OpenIllumination is a dataset for evaluating methods that infer scene properties from images, including inverse rendering and material decomposition. It contains more than 108,000 images of 64 real objects with varied materials. The objects are captured from 72 camera views under many different lighting conditions.

Each image comes with accurate camera parameters, ground-truth illumination, and a foreground segmentation mask. These annotations supply information about how the image was captured and which pixels belong to the object. The combination of viewpoint variation, lighting variation, and accompanying annotations provides a basis for quantitative evaluation on real objects.

The authors use the dataset to examine several state-of-the-art inverse rendering methods and compare their performance. Its main contribution is the evaluation resource: varied real-object observations paired with known capture information allow methods to be assessed in a shared setting. The dataset is intended to support most inverse rendering and material decomposition approaches, and the authors make both the dataset and code available.
summary.tldr: OpenIllumination provides over 108,000 annotated images of real objects under varied views and lighting for evaluating inverse rendering.

title: OpenIllumination: A Multi-Illumination Dataset for Inverse Rendering Evaluation on Real Objects

abstract: Visual stylization has been a very popular research area in recent times. While image stylization has seen a rapid advancement in the recent past, video stylization, while being more challenging, is relatively less explored. The immediate method of stylizing videos by stylizing each frame independently has been tried with some success. To the best of our knowledge, we present the first approach to video stylization using 3D CNN directly, building upon insights from 2D image stylization. Stylizing video is highly challenging, as the appearance and video motion, which includes both camera and subject motions, are inherently entangled in the representations learnt by a 3D CNN. Hence, a naive extension of 2D CNN stylization methods to 3D CNN does not work. To perform stylization with 3D CNN, we propose to explicitly disentangle motion and appearance, stylize the appearance part, and then add back the motion component and decode the final stylized video. In addition, we propose a dataset, curated from existing datasets, to train video stylization networks. We also provide an independently collected test set to study the generalization of video stylization methods. We provide results on this test dataset comparing the proposed method with 2D stylization methods applied frame by frame. We show successful stylization with 3D CNN for the first time, and obtain better stylization in terms of texture cf.\ the existing 2D methods.

paragraphs: Video stylization changes a video’s visual appearance while dealing with motion across frames. Applying an image stylization method independently to each frame is one approach. This paper instead investigates direct stylization with a 3D convolutional network, whose learned representations combine appearance with motion from both the camera and the subjects.

That entanglement makes a straightforward extension of 2D stylization methods ineffective in the setting studied. ViSt3D explicitly separates appearance and motion, applies stylization to the appearance component, then restores the motion component before decoding the final video. The design gives appearance transformation a distinct place in a representation that also contains temporal information.

The authors assemble a training dataset from existing datasets and independently collect a test set for examining generalization. On that test set, they compare their approach with 2D methods applied frame by frame and report better texture stylization. They present the work as, to their knowledge, the first direct use of a 3D CNN for video stylization. The results support disentangling appearance and motion as a route to successful stylization with such networks.
summary.tldr: ViSt3D separates appearance from motion in a 3D CNN and reports better texture stylization than frame-by-frame 2D methods.

title: ViSt3D: Video Stylization with 3D CNN

abstract: Adaptive optimizers, such as Adam, have achieved remarkable success in deep learning. A key component of these optimizers is the so-called preconditioning matrix, providing enhanced gradient information and regulating the step size of each gradient direction. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to designing the preconditioning matrix by utilizing the gradient difference between two successive steps as the diagonal elements. These diagonal elements are closely related to the Hessian and can be perceived as an approximation of the inner product between the Hessian row vectors and difference of the adjacent parameter vectors. Additionally, we introduce an auto-switching function that enables the preconditioning matrix to switch dynamically between Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) and the adaptive optimizer. Based on these two techniques, we develop a new optimizer named AGD that enhances the generalization performance. We evaluate AGD on public datasets of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Computer Vision (CV), and Recommendation Systems (RecSys). Our experimental results demonstrate that AGD outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) optimizers, achieving highly competitive or significantly better predictive performance. Furthermore, we analyze how AGD is able to switch automatically between SGD and the adaptive optimizer and its actual effects on various scenarios. The code is available at https://github.com/intelligent-machine-learning/dlrover/tree/master/atorch/atorch/optimizers.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers adjust how strongly training moves in different parameter directions. Their preconditioning matrix controls this adjustment, making its construction central to the optimizer’s behavior. This paper proposes AGD, which builds that adjustment around the difference between gradients at two consecutive training steps.

The gradient difference supplies the diagonal entries of the proposed preconditioning matrix. The authors relate these entries to the Hessian, which describes how gradients change as parameters move. More specifically, they interpret the entries as approximations to products between Hessian rows and the change in parameters. This connects the update rule to local changes in the loss surface.

AGD also includes a function that dynamically switches the preconditioning behavior between stochastic gradient descent and an adaptive optimizer. Evaluations span natural language processing, computer vision, and recommendation tasks, with predictive performance reported as highly competitive or significantly better than leading optimizers. The paper also examines when switching occurs and its effects, linking the proposed mechanism to observed generalization performance.
summary.tldr: AGD uses consecutive gradient differences and automatic switching between SGD and adaptive updates to improve predictive performance.

title: AGD: an Auto-switchable Optimizer using Stepwise Gradient Difference for Preconditioning Matrix

abstract: DNN pruning is a popular way to reduce the size of a model, improve the inferencelatency, and minimize the power consumption on DNN accelerators. However,existing approaches might be too complex, expensive or ineffective to apply toa variety of vision/language tasks, DNN architectures and to honor structuredpruning constraints. In this paper, we propose an efficient yet effective train-timepruning scheme, Parameter-free Differentiable Pruning (PDP), which offers state-of-the-art qualities in model size, accuracy, and training cost. PDP uses a dynamicfunction of weights during training to generate soft pruning masks for the weightsin a parameter-free manner for a given pruning target. While differentiable, thesimplicity and efficiency of PDP make it universal enough to deliver state-of-the-artrandom/structured/channel pruning results on various vision and natural languagetasks. For example, for MobileNet-v1, PDP can achieve 68.2% top-1 ImageNet1kaccuracy at 86.6% sparsity, which is 1.7% higher accuracy than those from thestate-of-the-art algorithms. Also, PDP yields over 83.1% accuracy on Multi-GenreNatural Language Inference with 90% sparsity for BERT, while the next best fromthe existing techniques shows 81.5% accuracy. In addition, PDP can be applied tostructured pruning, such as N:M pruning and channel pruning. For 1:4 structuredpruning of ResNet18, PDP improved the top-1 ImageNet1k accuracy by over 3.6%over the state-of-the-art. For channel pruning of ResNet50, PDP reduced the top-1ImageNet1k accuracy by 0.6% from the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Pruning removes parts of a neural network to reduce its size and potentially improve inference latency and power use. PDP performs pruning during training using soft masks computed dynamically from the model’s weights. For a specified pruning target, mask generation introduces no additional parameters and remains differentiable.

This simple mechanism supports multiple pruning patterns, including random, structured, and channel pruning, across vision and language tasks. The reported examples include MobileNet-v1 reaching 68.2% ImageNet1k top-1 accuracy at 86.6% sparsity, and BERT exceeding 83.1% accuracy on Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference at 90% sparsity. The latter compares with 81.5% for the next-best existing technique.

The results also show that improvements vary by setting. PDP reports an accuracy gain of over 3.6% for 1:4 structured pruning of ResNet18, but a 0.6% accuracy reduction relative to the state of the art for ResNet50 channel pruning. The contribution is an efficient, broadly applicable training-time mechanism with strong reported size, accuracy, and training-cost results across the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: PDP computes differentiable pruning masks directly from weights, delivering strong compression results across several pruning patterns and tasks.

title: PDP: Parameter-free Differentiable Pruning is All You Need

abstract: We introduce a relevant yet challenging problem named Personalized Dictionary Learning (PerDL), where the goal is to learn sparse linear representations from heterogeneous datasets that share some commonality. In PerDL, we model each dataset's shared and unique features as global and local dictionaries. Challenges for PerDL not only are inherited from classical dictionary learning(DL), but also arise due to the unknown nature of the shared and unique features. In this paper, we rigorously formulate this problem and provide conditions under which the global and local dictionaries can be provably disentangled. Under these conditions, we provide a meta-algorithm called Personalized Matching and Averaging (PerMA) that can recover both global and local dictionaries from heterogeneous datasets. PerMA is highly efficient; it converges to the ground truth at a linear rate under suitable conditions. Moreover, it automatically borrows strength from strong learners to improve the prediction of weak learners. As a general framework for extracting global and local dictionaries, we show the application of PerDL in different learning tasks, such as training with imbalanced datasets and video surveillance.

paragraphs: Related datasets may share useful features while also containing patterns specific to each dataset. Personalized Dictionary Learning, or PerDL, formalizes the problem of learning sparse linear representations that preserve both kinds of information. It represents common features with a global dictionary and dataset-specific features with local dictionaries, while treating their separation as something to learn.

The challenge extends beyond ordinary dictionary learning because the shared and unique components are initially unknown. The authors establish conditions under which the global and local dictionaries can be provably disentangled. They then introduce Personalized Matching and Averaging, or PerMA, a meta-algorithm that recovers both dictionary types under these conditions. Its convergence to the ground truth is linear under suitable assumptions.

PerMA also lets stronger learners improve the predictions of weaker learners by sharing useful information. The paper illustrates PerDL in tasks including training with imbalanced datasets and video surveillance. The framework’s significance is its explicit handling of commonality and individuality, backed by conditional recovery guarantees rather than an assumption that every heterogeneous collection can automatically be separated correctly.
summary.tldr: PerDL separates shared and dataset-specific sparse representations, with a recovery algorithm that converges linearly under suitable conditions.

title: Personalized Dictionary Learning for Heterogeneous Datasets

abstract: The contrastive vision-language pre-training, known as CLIP, demonstrates remarkable potential in perceiving open-world visual concepts, enabling effective zero-shot image recognition. Nevertheless, few-shot learning methods based on CLIP typically require offline fine-tuning of the parameters on few-shot samples, resulting in longer inference time and the risk of overfitting in certain domains. To tackle these challenges, we propose the Meta-Adapter, a lightweight residual-style adapter, to refine the CLIP features guided by the few-shot samples in an online manner. With a few training samples, our method can enable effective few-shot learning capabilities and generalize to unseen data or tasks without additional fine-tuning, achieving competitive performance and high efficiency. Without bells and whistles, our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art online few-shot learning method by an average of 3.6\% on eight image classification datasets with higher inference speed. Furthermore, our model is simple and flexible, serving as a plug-and-play module directly applicable to downstream tasks. Without further fine-tuning, Meta-Adapter obtains notable performance improvements in open-vocabulary object detection and segmentation tasks.

paragraphs: CLIP can recognize visual concepts without task-specific examples, but adapting it to a few labeled examples often involves offline parameter fine-tuning. That process can increase inference time and risk overfitting in some domains. Meta-Adapter instead introduces a lightweight residual-style component that refines CLIP features online using the available examples as guidance.

The adapter is designed to support few-shot recognition and transfer to unseen data or tasks without additional fine-tuning. Its role is to adjust the features used for recognition through a small, reusable module. This makes the method relevant when new examples need to inform predictions efficiently, without carrying out another parameter-tuning process for the new setting.

Across eight image classification datasets, the authors report an average 3.6% improvement over the state-of-the-art online few-shot method, together with faster inference. They also apply the module to open-vocabulary object detection and segmentation and report improvements without further fine-tuning. These findings support both the efficiency of the adaptation mechanism and its usefulness beyond image classification.
summary.tldr: Meta-Adapter refines CLIP features online from a few examples, improving recognition speed and performance while transferring without further fine-tuning.

title: Meta-Adapter: An Online Few-shot Learner for Vision-Language Model

abstract: The zero-shot open-vocabulary setting poses challenges for image classification.Fortunately, utilizing a vision-language model like CLIP, pre-trained on image-textpairs, allows for classifying images by comparing embeddings. Leveraging largelanguage models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT can further enhance CLIP’s accuracyby incorporating class-specific knowledge in descriptions. However, CLIP stillexhibits a bias towards certain classes and generates similar descriptions for similarclasses, disregarding their differences. To address this problem, we present anovel image classification framework via hierarchical comparisons. By recursivelycomparing and grouping classes with LLMs, we construct a class hierarchy. Withsuch a hierarchy, we can classify an image by descending from the top to the bottomof the hierarchy, comparing image and text embeddings at each level. Throughextensive experiments and analyses, we demonstrate that our proposed approach isintuitive, effective, and explainable. Code will be released upon publication.

paragraphs: In zero-shot, open-vocabulary image classification, a model must choose among text-described categories without task-specific training examples for those categories. CLIP enables this by comparing image and text representations. Language models can enrich the descriptions with category knowledge, but the paper identifies two problems: preferences for particular classes and descriptions that fail to distinguish similar classes.

The proposed framework uses a language model to compare categories recursively and organize them into a hierarchy. Classification then proceeds from the top of that hierarchy toward a final category. At each level, the system compares the image representation with the relevant text representations, turning classification into a sequence of progressively narrower comparisons.

This organization makes differences between related categories part of the decision process. It also provides an interpretable path through the hierarchy, rather than only a final category choice. The authors' experiments and analyses support the approach's effectiveness and explainability. The stated result is a useful classification framework, without a claim that hierarchical comparison eliminates all category bias.
summary.tldr: Language-model-generated class hierarchies guide CLIP through progressively finer comparisons, improving open-vocabulary image classification in the reported experiments.

title: ChatGPT-Powered Hierarchical Comparisons for Image Classification

abstract: Image restoration involves recovering a high-quality clean image from its degraded version. Deep learning-based methods have significantly improved image restoration performance, however, they have limited generalization ability to different degradation types and levels. This restricts their real-world application since it requires training individual models for each specific degradation and knowing the input degradation type to apply the relevant model. We present a prompt-based learning approach, PromptIR, for All-In-One image restoration that can effectively restore images from various types and levels of degradation. In particular, our method uses prompts to encode degradation-specific information, which is then used to dynamically guide the restoration network. This allows our method to generalize to different degradation types and levels, while still achieving state-of-the-art results on image denoising, deraining, and dehazing. Overall, PromptIR offers a generic and efficient plugin module with few lightweight prompts that can be used to restore images of various types and levels of degradation with no prior information on the corruptions present in the image. Our code and pre-trained models are available here: https://github.com/va1shn9v/PromptIR

paragraphs: PromptIR addresses image restoration when the corruption type and severity are not known in advance. Many restoration methods generalize poorly across different degradations, creating a need for separate models and a way to choose among them. The paper aims to restore varied degraded images within an all-in-one approach.

Its method uses a small set of lightweight prompts to encode information specific to the degradation. These prompts dynamically guide the restoration network, allowing its behavior to respond to the corruption present in the image. The prompt mechanism is presented as a generic, efficient plugin module, making this conditioning mechanism the central architectural contribution.

The authors report state-of-the-art results for denoising, deraining, and dehazing, alongside the ability to handle different degradation types and levels without prior corruption information. The practical significance is that restoration can be guided by degradation-specific information inside the model rather than requiring the user to identify the corruption first. The reported tasks demonstrate how that approach supports several distinct forms of image cleanup.
summary.tldr: PromptIR uses lightweight degradation-aware prompts to guide one restoration approach across noise, rain, and haze without prior corruption information.

title: PromptIR: Prompting for All-in-One Image Restoration

abstract: Inspired by the insights in cognitive science with respect to human memory and reasoning mechanism, a novel evolvable LLM-based (Large Language Model) agent framework is proposed as Rememberer. By equipping the LLM with a long-term experience memory, Rememberer is capable of exploiting the experiences from the past episodes even for different task goals, which excels an LLM-based agent with fixed exemplars or equipped with a transient working memory. We further introduce **R**einforcement **L**earning with **E**xperience **M**emory (**RLEM**) to update the memory. Thus, the whole system can learn from the experiences of both success and failure, and evolve its capability without fine-tuning the parameters of the LLM. In this way, the proposed Rememberer constitutes a semi-parametric RL agent. Extensive experiments are conducted on two RL task sets to evaluate the proposed framework. The average results with different initialization and training sets exceed the prior SOTA by 4% and 2% for the success rate on two task sets and demonstrate the superiority and robustness of Rememberer.

By equipping the LLM with a long-term experience memory, Rememberer is capable of exploiting the experiences from the past episodes even for different task goals, which excels an LLM-based agent with fixed exemplars or equipped with a transient working memory. We further introduce **R**einforcement **L**earning with **E**xperience **M**emory (**RLEM**) to update the memory. Thus, the whole system can learn from the experiences of both success and failure, and evolve its capability without fine-tuning the parameters of the LLM. In this way, the proposed Rememberer constitutes a semi-parametric RL agent. Extensive experiments are conducted on two RL task sets to evaluate the proposed framework. The average results with different initialization and training sets exceed the prior SOTA by 4% and 2% for the success rate on two task sets and demonstrate the superiority and robustness of Rememberer.

paragraphs: Rememberer is an agent framework that lets a large language model improve through a long-term memory of experience. Its motivation comes from human memory and reasoning: past episodes can remain useful even when the current task has a different goal. The framework extends what an agent can draw on beyond fixed examples or a temporary working memory.

The authors introduce Reinforcement Learning with Experience Memory to update this memory using both successful and failed experiences. Learning therefore changes the experience store without fine-tuning the language model's parameters. This combination of a parameterized language model and an evolving external memory is what makes the system a semi-parametric reinforcement-learning agent.

Experiments evaluate Rememberer on two reinforcement-learning task sets using different initializations and training sets. Average success rates exceed the previous state of the art by 4% and 2% on the respective sets. The authors interpret the results as evidence of stronger and more robust performance, supporting persistent experience memory as a useful learning mechanism for the evaluated agents.
summary.tldr: Rememberer improves an LLM agent by updating long-term experience memory without fine-tuning the model's parameters.

title: Large Language Models Are Semi-Parametric Reinforcement Learning Agents

abstract: In this paper, we introduce DeAR (_Decompose-Analyze-Rethink_), a framework that iteratively builds a reasoning tree to tackle intricate problems within a single large language model (LLM). Unlike approaches that extend or search for rationales, DeAR is featured by 1) adopting a tree-based question decomposition manner to plan the organization of rationales, which mimics the logical planning inherentin human cognition; 2) globally updating the rationales at each reasoning step through natural language feedback. Specifically, the _Decompose_ stage decomposes the question into simpler sub-questions, storing them as new nodes; the _Analyze_ stage generates and self-checks rationales for sub-questions at each node evel; and the _Rethink_ stage updates parent-node rationales based on feedback from their child nodes. By generating and updating the reasoning process from a more global perspective, DeAR constructs more adaptive and accurate logical structures for complex problems, facilitating timely error correction compared to rationale-extension and search-based approaches such as Tree-of-Thoughts (ToT) and Graph-of-Thoughts (GoT). We conduct extensive experiments on three reasoning benchmarks, including ScienceQA, StrategyQA, and GSM8K, which cover a variety of reasoning tasks, demonstrating that our approach significantly reduces logical errors and enhances performance across various LLMs. Furthermore, we validate that DeAR is an efficient method that achieves a superior trade-off between accuracy and reasoning time compared to ToT and GoT.

paragraphs: DeAR organizes a language model’s reasoning around a tree of questions and subquestions. Its central idea is that solving a complex problem involves both planning smaller tasks and revising the larger explanation as those tasks are resolved. The framework performs this iterative process within a single language model.

The Decompose stage breaks a question into simpler questions and adds them as tree nodes. Analyze generates and checks explanations at each node. Rethink then uses feedback from child nodes to revise their parents’ explanations. This creates a route for local findings to change the broader reasoning structure, rather than only extending a previously generated path or searching among completed alternatives.

Experiments on ScienceQA, StrategyQA, and GSM8K show significantly fewer logical errors and improved performance across multiple language models. The authors also report a better balance between accuracy and reasoning time than Tree-of-Thoughts and Graph-of-Thoughts. These results support the value of revisiting earlier explanations as new subproblem information becomes available, with error correction built into the organization of the reasoning process.
summary.tldr: DeAR improves complex reasoning by decomposing questions and repeatedly revising parent explanations using feedback from subquestions.

title: Decompose, Analyze and Rethink: Solving Intricate Problems with Human-like Reasoning Cycle

abstract: We introduce VASA, a framework for generating lifelike talking faces with appealing visual affective skills (VAS) given a single static image and a speech audio clip. Our premiere model, VASA-1, is capable of not only generating lip movements that are exquisitely synchronized with the audio, but also producing a large spectrum of facial nuances and natural head motions that contribute to the perception of authenticity and liveliness. The core innovations include a diffusion-based holistic facial dynamics and head movement generation model that works in a face latent space, and the development of such an expressive and disentangled face latent space using videos.Through extensive experiments including evaluation on a set of new metrics, we show that our method significantly outperforms previous methods along various dimensions comprehensively. Our method delivers high video quality with realistic facial and head dynamics and also supports the online generation of 512$\times$512 videos at up to 40 FPS with negligible starting latency.It paves the way for real-time engagements with lifelike avatars that emulate human conversational behaviors.

paragraphs: VASA-1 generates a talking-face video from one still image and a speech recording. Its goal extends beyond matching mouth movements to sound: it also produces facial expressions and head motion that make the resulting face appear more natural and lively. These behaviors are generated together as part of the facial dynamics.

The system uses a diffusion model operating in a learned face latent space, a representation of facial information. The authors develop this space from videos so that it is expressive and disentangled, supporting the modeling of facial movement and head motion. This representation and the holistic movement-generation model are the central technical contributions.

Experiments, including newly introduced evaluation metrics, report substantial improvements over prior methods across several dimensions. The model supports online generation of 512-by-512 video at up to 40 frames per second with negligible starting latency. These findings combine visual quality with responsiveness, supporting the possibility of real-time avatar interactions that reproduce aspects of human conversational facial behavior.
summary.tldr: VASA-1 turns a still face and speech audio into expressive talking video, supporting 512-by-512 generation at up to 40 frames per second.

title: VASA-1: Lifelike Audio-Driven Talking Faces Generated in Real Time

abstract: This paper presents UltraEdit, a large-scale (~ 4M editing samples), automatically generated dataset for instruction-based image editing. Our key idea is to address the drawbacks in existing image editing datasets like InstructPix2Pix and MagicBrush, and provide a *systematic* approach to producing massive and high-quality image editing samples: 1) UltraEdit includes more diverse editing instructions by combining LLM creativity and in-context editing examples by human raters; 2) UltraEdit is anchored on real images (photographs or artworks), which offers more diversity and less biases than those purely synthesized by text-to-image models; 3) UltraEdit supports region-based editing with high-quality, automatically produced region annotations. Our experiments show that canonical diffusion-based editing baselines trained on UltraEdit set new records on challenging MagicBrush and Emu-Edit benchmarks, respectively. Our analysis further confirms the crucial role of real image anchors and region-based editing data. The dataset, code, and models will be made public.

paragraphs: UltraEdit is an automatically generated dataset containing approximately four million examples of editing images from written instructions. The paper focuses on how to produce editing data at scale while improving instruction diversity, image diversity, and support for changes to particular regions. Its contribution is a systematic data-generation approach as well as the resulting dataset.

Instruction generation combines language-model creativity with editing examples provided by human raters. The source images are real photographs or artworks, which the authors report offer greater diversity and less bias than images produced entirely by text-to-image models. Automatically generated region annotations additionally support edits directed at specific parts of an image.

Diffusion-based editing baselines trained on UltraEdit achieve new records on the MagicBrush and Emu-Edit benchmarks. Further analysis confirms the important roles of real image anchors and region-based editing data. These findings indicate that the composition of editing examples, including their source imagery and localized guidance, contributes to the reported performance alongside the dataset's scale.
summary.tldr: UltraEdit supplies roughly four million instruction-based image edits, using real image anchors and region annotations to improve benchmark performance.

title: UltraEdit: Instruction-based Fine-Grained Image Editing at Scale

abstract: We introduce a new benchmark designed to advance the development of general-purpose, large-scale vision-language models for remote sensing images. Although several vision-language datasets in remote sensing have been proposed to pursue this goal, existing datasets are typically tailored to single tasks, lack detailed object information, or suffer from inadequate quality control. Exploring these improvement opportunities, we present a Versatile vision-language Benchmark for Remote Sensing image understanding, termed VRSBench. This benchmark comprises 29,614 images, with 29,614 human-verified detailed captions, 52,472 object references, and 123,221 question-answer pairs. It facilitates the training and evaluation of vision-language models across a broad spectrum of remote sensing image understanding tasks. We further evaluated state-of-the-art models on this benchmark for three vision-language tasks: image captioning, visual grounding, and visual question answering. Our work aims to significantly contribute to the development of advanced vision-language models in the field of remote sensing. The data and code can be accessed at https://vrsbench.github.io.

paragraphs: VRSBench is a dataset for training and evaluating vision-language models on remote sensing imagery. The authors identify three shortcomings in existing datasets: narrow focus on individual tasks, insufficient object detail, and inadequate quality control. Their benchmark brings several forms of language supervision together to support broader image understanding.

The dataset contains 29,614 images and an equal number of detailed, human-verified captions. It also includes 52,472 object references and 123,221 question-answer pairs. These annotation types support complementary capabilities: describing an image, locating an object referred to in language, and answering questions about image content.

The authors evaluate leading models on image captioning, visual grounding, and visual question answering using the benchmark. These evaluations provide a common setting for examining multiple capabilities relevant to general-purpose remote sensing models. The main contribution is the combination of detailed captions, object references, and questions within one resource, allowing development and assessment to extend beyond a single narrowly defined task.
summary.tldr: VRSBench combines captions, object references, and question-answer pairs to evaluate multiple vision-language capabilities on remote sensing images.

title: VRSBench: A Versatile Vision-Language Benchmark Dataset for Remote Sensing Image Understanding

abstract: Tree ensembles are one of the most widely used model classes. However, these models are susceptible to adversarial examples, i.e., slightly perturbed examples that elicit a misprediction. There has been significant research on designing approaches to construct such examples for tree ensembles. But this is a computationally challenging problem that often must be solved a large number of times (e.g., for all examples in a training set). This is compounded by the fact that current approaches attempt to find such examples from scratch. In contrast, we exploit the fact that multiple similar problems are being solved. Specifically, our approach exploits the insight that adversarial examples for tree ensembles tend to perturb a consistent but relatively small set of features. We show that we can quickly identify this set of features and use this knowledge to speedup constructing adversarial examples.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the computational cost of repeatedly constructing adversarial examples for tree ensembles. These examples make small changes to inputs that cause a model to predict incorrectly. Finding such changes is challenging, and the expense becomes especially important when the procedure must be repeated across many inputs, such as an entire training set.

The authors exploit a pattern shared across these searches: adversarial examples for tree ensembles tend to modify a relatively small and consistent subset of features. Instead of treating every input as an unrelated search problem, the approach identifies that subset and uses the resulting knowledge to help construct further adversarial examples.

The stated finding is that the relevant feature set can be identified quickly and used to speed up construction. The contribution therefore concerns reuse across repeated evasion problems, with the observed consistency providing the opportunity for savings. This matters when the total workload contains many similar searches, because information obtained about influential features can remain useful beyond the individual input that first revealed it.
summary.tldr: The method speeds repeated attacks on tree ensembles by identifying and reusing a small set of commonly perturbed features.

title: Faster Repeated Evasion Attacks in Tree Ensembles

abstract: Given a relational database (RDB), how can we predict missing column values in some target table of interest? Although RDBs store vast amounts of rich, informative data spread across interconnected tables, the progress of predictive machine learning models as applied to such tasks arguably falls well behind advances in other domains such as computer vision or natural language processing. This deficit stems, at least in part, from the lack of established/public RDB benchmarks as needed for training and evaluation purposes. As a result, related model development thus far often defaults to tabular approaches trained on ubiquitous single-table benchmarks, or on the relational side, graph-based alternatives such as GNNs applied to a completely different set of graph datasets devoid of tabular characteristics. To more precisely target RDBs lying at the nexus of these two complementary regimes, we explore a broad class of baseline models predicated on: (i) converting multi-table datasets into graphs using various strategies equipped with efficient subsampling, while preserving tabular characteristics; and (ii) trainable models with well-matched inductive biases that output predictions based on these input subgraphs. Then, to address the dearth of suitable public benchmarks and reduce siloed comparisons, we assemble a diverse collection of (i) large-scale RDB datasets and (ii) coincident predictive tasks. From a delivery standpoint, we operationalize the above four dimensions (4D) of exploration within a unified, scalable open-source toolbox called 4DBInfer; please see https://github.com/awslabs/multi-table-benchmark .

paragraphs: Predicting a missing value in a database can require information scattered across several connected tables. Yet many machine-learning benchmarks either treat data as a single table or study graphs without the attributes typical of databases. This paper addresses the gap between those settings, where both table contents and relationships can matter.

The authors explore ways to convert multi-table databases into graphs while preserving their tabular information. They pair these conversions with efficient subsampling and models designed to make predictions from the resulting subgraphs. This creates a framework for examining how the representation of a database interacts with the model trained on it.

The paper also assembles large relational datasets and corresponding prediction tasks. These resources, graph-construction choices, and predictive models come together in the open-source 4DBInfer toolbox. Its main contribution is a shared setting for developing and comparing database prediction methods, helping research move beyond comparisons conducted on disconnected collections of tables or graphs.
summary.tldr: 4DBInfer combines relational datasets, prediction tasks, graph construction, and models in a shared toolbox for learning across connected database tables.

title: 4DBInfer: A 4D Benchmarking Toolbox for Graph-Centric Predictive Modeling on RDBs

abstract: Diffusion models learn to denoise data and the trained denoiser is then used to generate new samples from the data distribution. In this paper, we revisit the diffusion sampling process and identify a fundamental cause of sample quality degradation: the denoiser is poorly estimated in regions that are far Outside Of the training Distribution (OOD), and the sampling process inevitably evaluates in these OOD regions.This can become problematic for all sampling methods, especially when we move to parallel sampling which requires us to initialize and update the entire sample trajectory of dynamics in parallel, leading to many OOD evaluations. To address this problem, we introduce a new self-supervised training objective that differentiates the levels of noise added to a sample, leading to improved OOD denoising performance. The approach is based on our observation that diffusion models implicitly define a log-likelihood ratio that distinguishes distributions with different amounts of noise, and this expression depends on denoiser performance outside the standard training distribution.We show by diverse experiments that the proposed contrastive diffusion training is effective for both sequential and parallel settings, and it improves the performance and speed of parallel samplers significantly. Code for our paper can be found at https://github.com/yunshuwu/ContrastiveDiffusionLoss

In this paper, we revisit the diffusion sampling process and identify a fundamental cause of sample quality degradation: the denoiser is poorly estimated in regions that are far Outside Of the training Distribution (OOD), and the sampling process inevitably evaluates in these OOD regions.This can become problematic for all sampling methods, especially when we move to parallel sampling which requires us to initialize and update the entire sample trajectory of dynamics in parallel, leading to many OOD evaluations. Code for our paper can be found at https://github.com/yunshuwu/ContrastiveDiffusionLoss

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate samples using a learned denoiser, but sampling can visit regions far outside the denoiser's training distribution. The paper identifies inaccurate denoising in those regions as a fundamental source of degraded sample quality. The issue is especially pronounced in parallel sampling, where an entire trajectory is initialized and updated together.

The authors observe that a diffusion model implicitly defines a log-likelihood ratio for distinguishing distributions with different amounts of added noise. That expression depends on denoiser behavior beyond its standard training distribution. They turn this observation into a self-supervised contrastive objective that teaches the model to distinguish noise levels.

The extra objective improves denoising outside the usual training distribution. Experiments show benefits for both sequential and parallel sampling, with significant improvements in the performance and speed of parallel samplers. The contribution connects a classification interpretation of diffusion models to a training change aimed at the states encountered during generation, especially when sampling procedures make many out-of-distribution evaluations.
summary.tldr: Contrastive training that distinguishes noise levels improves out-of-distribution denoising and boosts sequential and parallel diffusion sampling.

title: Your Diffusion Model is Secretly a Noise Classifier and Benefits from Contrastive Training

abstract: We study the problem of learning latent community structure from multiple correlated networks, focusing on edge-correlated stochastic block models with two balanced communities. Recent work of Gaudio, Rácz, and Sridhar (COLT 2022) determined the precise information-theoretic threshold for exact community recovery using two correlated graphs; in particular, this showcased the subtle interplay between community recovery and graph matching. Here we study the natural setting of more than two graphs. The main challenge lies in understanding how to aggregate information across several graphs when none of the pairwise latent vertex correspondences can be exactly recovered. Our main result derives the precise information-theoretic threshold for exact community recovery using any constant number of correlated graphs, answering a question of Gaudio, Rácz, and Sridhar (COLT 2022). In particular, for every $K \geq 3$ we uncover and characterize a region of the parameter space where exact community recovery is possible using $K$ correlated graphs, even though (1) this is information-theoretically impossible using any $K-1$ of them and (2) none of the latent matchings can be exactly recovered.

paragraphs: Several networks can provide different, correlated views of the same hidden community structure. Combining them is difficult when the correspondence between vertices across networks is unknown. This paper studies that problem in edge-correlated stochastic block models with two communities of equal size, extending the analysis beyond two graphs.

The central result gives the precise information-theoretic threshold for exact community recovery using any fixed number of correlated graphs. Such a threshold identifies when the available information permits complete recovery of community memberships. The challenge is to characterize this boundary even when none of the pairwise vertex correspondences can themselves be recovered exactly.

For every number of graphs K of at least three, the authors identify a parameter region where all K graphs together permit exact community recovery, but every selection of K minus one graphs fails to do so. Exact latent matching also remains impossible there. The result shows that recovering communities can require less correspondence information than recovering complete graph alignments, and that an additional graph can cross a genuine recoverability boundary.
summary.tldr: Multiple correlated graphs can permit exact community recovery even when fewer graphs and exact vertex matching are insufficient.

title: Harnessing Multiple Correlated Networks for Exact Community Recovery

abstract: Recent advancements in text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis show that large-scale models trained with extensive web data produce highly natural-sounding output. However, such data is scarce for Indian languages due to the lack of high-quality, manually subtitled data on platforms like LibriVox or YouTube. To address this gap, we enhance existing large-scale ASR datasets containing natural conversations collected in low-quality environments to generate high-quality TTS training data. Our pipeline leverages the cross-lingual generalization of denoising and speech enhancement models trained on English and applied to Indian languages. This results in IndicVoices-R (IV-R), the largest multilingual Indian TTS dataset derived from an ASR dataset, with 1,704 hours of high-quality speech from 10,496 speakers across 22 Indian languages. IV-R matches the quality of gold-standard TTS datasets like LJSpeech, LibriTTS, and IndicTTS. We also introduce the IV-R Benchmark, the first to assess zero-shot, few-shot, and many-shot speaker generalization capabilities of TTS models on Indian voices, ensuring diversity in age, gender, and style. We demonstrate that fine-tuning an English pre-trained model on a combined dataset of high-quality IndicTTS and our IV-R dataset results in better zero-shot speaker generalization compared to fine-tuning on the IndicTTS dataset alone. Further, our evaluation reveals limited zero-shot generalization for Indian voices in TTS models trained on prior datasets, which we improve by fine-tuning the model on our data containing diverse set of speakers across language families. We open-source code and data for all 22 official Indian languages.

paragraphs: Training natural-sounding speech synthesis requires substantial high-quality audio, which is scarce for many Indian languages. This work repurposes conversational recordings originally collected for speech recognition in lower-quality environments. Its pipeline applies denoising and speech enhancement models trained on English to Indian languages, using their ability to generalize across languages to improve the recordings.

The resulting IndicVoices-R dataset contains 1,704 hours of speech from 10,496 speakers across 22 Indian languages. The authors report quality matching established speech synthesis datasets. They also introduce a benchmark for evaluating how synthesis models generalize to speakers under zero-shot, few-shot, and many-shot conditions, with diversity in age, gender, and speaking style.

The evaluation also finds limited zero-shot generalization to Indian voices in models trained on earlier datasets. These results support expanding speaker and language-family diversity through restored recognition data, alongside releasing the dataset and code for all 22 official Indian languages.
summary.tldr: IndicVoices-R restores conversational speech into a large Indian-language synthesis dataset and improves zero-shot speaker generalization in the reported fine-tuning comparison.

title: IndicVoices-R: Unlocking a Massive Multilingual Multi-speaker Speech Corpus for Scaling Indian TTS

abstract: Recent years have witnessed the rapid development of Neuro-Symbolic (NeSy) AI systems, which integrate symbolic reasoning into deep neural networks.However, most of the existing benchmarks for NeSy AI fail to provide long-horizon reasoning tasks with complex multi-agent interactions.Furthermore, they are usually constrained by fixed and simplistic logical rules over limited entities, making them far from real-world complexities.To address these crucial gaps, we introduce LogiCity, the first simulator based on customizable first-order logic (FOL) for an urban-like environment with multiple dynamic agents.LogiCity models diverse urban elements using semantic and spatial concepts, such as $\texttt{IsAmbulance}(\texttt{X})$ and $\texttt{IsClose}(\texttt{X}, \texttt{Y})$. These concepts are used to define FOL rules that govern the behavior of various agents. Since the concepts and rules are abstractions, they can be universally applied to cities with any agent compositions, facilitating the instantiation of diverse scenarios.Besides, a key feature of LogiCity is its support for user-configurable abstractions, enabling customizable simulation complexities for logical reasoning.To explore various aspects of NeSy AI, LogiCity introduces two tasks, one features long-horizon sequential decision-making, and the other focuses on one-step visual reasoning, varying in difficulty and agent behaviors.Our extensive evaluation reveals the advantage of NeSy frameworks in abstract reasoning. Moreover, we highlight the significant challenges of handling more complex abstractions in long-horizon multi-agent scenarios or under high-dimensional, imbalanced data.With its flexible design, various features, and newly raised challenges, we believe LogiCity represents a pivotal step forward in advancing the next generation of NeSy AI.All the code and data are open-sourced at our website.
