paragraphs: Observed routes reveal decisions, but the costs that produced those decisions may be unknown. Learning a representation of such routes also requires respecting structural constraints when reconstructing them. The proposed Inverse Optimization Latent Variable Model addresses both issues by learning a latent distribution of cost functions and using an optimization solver to produce feasible outputs.

The solver remains inside the reconstruction process, so generated solutions satisfy the constrained optimization problem. Because the deterministic solver is not differentiable, the method uses estimated gradients of a Fenchel–Young loss to shape the latent space. Learning a distribution of costs allows the representation to capture varied solution behaviors, including variation associated with agents or conditions unavailable during training.

The authors evaluate the approach on ship routes, taxi routes, and paths through synthetic graphs. They demonstrate reconstruction of paths and cycles, prediction of their distributions, and interpretable latent representations. The central result is a connection between flexible representation learning and constraint-respecting optimization: diversity is represented through costs, while a solver supplies valid structured solutions.
summary.tldr: IO-LVM learns a distribution of hidden route costs and reconstructs feasible solutions through an optimization solver.

title: Inverse Optimization Latent Variable Models for Learning Costs Applied to Route Problems

abstract: Dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) effectively extends the high-speed rendering capabilities of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to represent volumetric videos. However, the large number of Gaussians, substantial temporal redundancies, and especially the absence of an entropy-aware compression framework result in large storage requirements. Consequently, this poses significant challenges for practical deployment, efficient edge-device processing, and data transmission. In this paper, we introduce a novel end-to-end RD-optimized compression framework tailored for 4DGS, aiming to enable flexible, high-fidelity rendering across varied computational platforms. Leveraging Fully Explicit Dynamic Gaussian Splatting (Ex4DGS), one of the state-of-the-art 4DGS methods, as our baseline, we start from the existing 3DGS compression methods for compatibility while effectively addressing additional challenges introduced by the temporal axis. In particular, instead of storing motion trajectories independently per point, we employ a wavelet transform to reflect the real-world smoothness prior, significantly enhancing storage efficiency. This approach yields significantly improved compression ratios and provides a user-controlled balance between compression efficiency and rendering quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, achieving up to 91$\times$ compression compared to the original Ex4DGS model while maintaining high visual fidelity. These results highlight the applicability of our framework for real-time dynamic scene rendering in diverse scenarios, from resource-constrained edge devices to high-performance environments. The source code is available at https://github.com/HyeongminLEE/RD4DGS.

title: Temporal Smoothness-Aware Rate-Distortion Optimized 4D Gaussian Splatting

abstract: We propose a new method for the problem of controlling linear dynamical systems under partial observation and adversarial disturbances. Our new algorithm, Double Spectral Control (DSC), matches the best known regret guarantees while exponentially improving runtime complexity over previous approaches in its dependence on the system's stability margin. Our key innovation is a two-level spectral approximation strategy, leveraging double convolution with a universal basis of spectral filters, enabling efficient and accurate learning of the best linear dynamical controllers.
originalAbstract: We propose a new method for the problem of controlling linear dynamical systems under partial observation and adversarial disturbances. Our new algorithm, Double Spectral Control (DSC), matches the best known regret guarantees while exponentially improving runtime complexity over previous approaches in its dependence on the system's stability margin. Our key innovation is a two-level spectral approximation strategy, leveraging double convolution with a universal basis of spectral filters, enabling efficient and accurate learning of the best linear dynamical controllers.

paragraphs: The paper considers controlling a linear dynamical system when the controller sees only part of its state and disturbances may be adversarial. A controller must choose actions from incomplete observations while coping with unfavorable external influences. The proposed algorithm, Double Spectral Control, targets efficient learning of the best linear dynamical controllers in this setting.

Its central mechanism is a two-level spectral approximation. The method applies a double convolution using a universal basis of spectral filters, providing a structured way to approximate the dynamics involved in control. The two approximation levels are the key innovation behind the algorithm’s combination of computational efficiency and accurate controller learning.

Double Spectral Control matches the best known regret guarantees while improving runtime dependence on the system’s stability margin by an exponential factor. Regret measures performance relative to the comparison controllers over time. Thus, the stated advance preserves the existing quality of that guarantee while making a particular source of computational difficulty substantially less costly; the exponential improvement specifically concerns stability-margin dependence.
summary.tldr: Double Spectral Control matches leading regret guarantees while exponentially improving runtime dependence on the stability margin for partially observed linear systems.

title: Efficient Spectral Control of Partially Observed Linear Dynamical Systems

abstract: Evaluating the step-by-step reliability of large language model (LLM) reasoning, such as Chain-of-Thought, remains challenging due to the difficulty and cost of obtaining high-quality step-level supervision. In this paper, we introduce Self-Play Critic (SPC), a novel approach where a critic model evolves its ability to assess reasoning steps through adversarial self-play games, eliminating the need for manual step-level annotation. SPC involves fine-tuning two copies of a base model to play two roles, namely a "sneaky generator" that deliberately produces erroneous steps designed to be difficult to detect, and a "critic" that analyzes the correctness of reasoning steps. These two models engage in an adversarial game in which the generator aims to fool the critic, while the critic model seeks to identify the generator's errors. Using reinforcement learning based on the game outcomes, the models iteratively improve; the winner of each confrontation receives a positive reward and the loser receives a negative reward, driving continuous self-evolution. Experiments on three reasoning process benchmarks (ProcessBench, PRM800K, DeltaBench) demonstrate that our SPC progressively enhances its error detection capabilities (e.g., accuracy increases from 70.8% to 77.7% on ProcessBench) and surpasses strong baselines, including distilled R1 model. Furthermore, SPC can guide the test-time search of diverse LLMs and significantly improve their mathematical reasoning performance on MATH500 and AIME2024, surpassing those guided by state-of-the-art process reward models.

title: SPC: Evolving Self-Play Critic via Adversarial Games for LLM Reasoning

abstract: Monocular 3D tracking aims to capture the long-term motion of pixels in 3D space from a single monocular video and has witnessed rapid progress in recent years. However, we argue that the existing monocular 3D tracking methods still fall short in separating the camera motion from foreground dynamic motion and cannot densely track newly emerging dynamic subjects in the videos. To address these two limitations, we propose TrackingWorld, a novel pipeline for dense 3D tracking of almost all pixels within a world-centric 3D coordinate system. First, we introduce a tracking upsampler that efficiently lifts the arbitrary sparse 2D tracks into dense 2D tracks. Then, to generalize the current tracking methods to newly emerging objects, we apply the upsampler to all frames and reduce the redundancy of 2D tracks by eliminating the tracks in overlapped regions. Finally, we present an efficient optimization-based framework to back-project dense 2D tracks into world-centric 3D trajectories by estimating the camera poses and the 3D coordinates of these 2D tracks. Extensive evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our system achieves accurate and dense 3D tracking in a world-centric coordinate frame.

To address these two limitations, we propose TrackingWorld, a novel pipeline for dense 3D tracking of almost all pixels within a world-centric 3D coordinate system. Extensive evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our system achieves accurate and dense 3D tracking in a world-centric coordinate frame.

paragraphs: Tracking three-dimensional motion from a single video requires separating movement of the camera from movement of objects. The authors identify another weakness in existing methods: they cannot densely track dynamic subjects that appear later in the video. TrackingWorld addresses both problems with a pipeline that represents trajectories in a world-centered coordinate system.

The pipeline first turns sparse two-dimensional tracks into dense tracks using a tracking upsampler. Applying this upsampler to every frame lets the system include newly emerging objects. Tracks from overlapping regions are then removed to reduce redundancy. Finally, an optimization framework estimates camera poses and three-dimensional coordinates, converting the dense image-space tracks into trajectories expressed in a shared world coordinate frame.

This organization combines broad pixel coverage with an explicit treatment of camera motion. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate accurate, dense three-dimensional tracking. The claim is tracking almost all pixels, with particular attention to subjects entering after the initial frames, rather than restricting the tracked set to objects already visible at the beginning.
summary.tldr: TrackingWorld converts dense video tracks into world-centered 3D trajectories while accounting for camera motion and newly appearing objects.

title: TrackingWorld: World-centric Monocular 3D Tracking of Almost All Pixels

abstract: A full understanding of the behavior of a large language model (LLM) requires our grasp of its input token space. If this space differs from our assumptions, our comprehension of and conclusions about the LLM will likely be flawed. We elucidate the structure of the token embeddings both empirically and theoretically. We present a novel statistical test assuming that the neighborhood around each token has a relatively flat and smooth structure as the null hypothesis. Failing to reject the null is uninformative, but rejecting it at a specific token $\psi$ implies an irregularity in the token subspace in a $\psi$-neighborhood, $B(\psi)$. The structure assumed in the null is a generalization of a manifold with boundary called a \emph{smooth fiber bundle} (which can be split into two spatial regimes -- small and large radius), so we denote our new hypothesis test as the ``fiber bundle hypothesis.'' By running our test over several open-source LLMs, each with unique token embeddings, we find that the null is frequently rejected, and so the evidence suggests that the token subspace is not a fiber bundle and hence also not a manifold. As a consequence of our findings, when an LLM is presented with two semantically equivalent prompts, if one prompt contains a token implicated by our test, the response to that prompt will likely exhibit less stability than the other.

paragraphs: Understanding a language model's input space requires checking whether token embeddings have the geometric structure an analysis assumes. This paper develops a statistical test for local smoothness and relative flatness around individual tokens. Its null hypothesis uses a smooth fiber bundle, a structure that generalizes a manifold with boundary.

The test has an important asymmetry: rejecting the null at a token indicates an irregularity in that token's neighborhood, while failing to reject it is uninformative. Applied to several open-source language models with different embeddings, the test frequently rejects the null. The authors interpret this as evidence that the token subspace is neither a fiber bundle nor a manifold.

The paper connects these geometric findings to response stability. For two semantically equivalent prompts, it states that the one containing a token implicated by the test will likely produce less stable responses. This is a qualified prediction about stability, not a claim that every flagged token inevitably causes failure. The contribution is both a local diagnostic and evidence challenging smooth geometric assumptions about token embeddings.
summary.tldr: A statistical test finds frequent local irregularities in token embeddings, challenging manifold assumptions and suggesting reduced stability for prompts containing implicated tokens.

title: Token Embeddings Violate the Manifold Hypothesis

abstract: We consider the problem of time series prediction in the presence of missing data. We cast the problem as an online learning problem in which the goal of the learner is to minimize prediction error. We then devise an efficient algorithm for the problem, which is based on autoregressive model, and does not assume any structure on the missing data nor on the mechanism that generates the time series. We show that our algorithm’s performance asymptotically approaches the performance of the best AR predictor in hindsight, and corroborate the theoretic results with an empirical study on synthetic and real-world data.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of time series prediction in the presence of missing data. We cast the problem as an online learning problem in which the goal of the learner is to minimize prediction error. We then devise an efficient algorithm for the problem, which is based on autoregressive model, and does not assume any structure on the missing data nor on the mechanism that generates the time series. We show that our algorithm’s performance asymptotically approaches the performance of the best AR predictor in hindsight, and corroborate the theoretic results with an empirical study on synthetic and real-world data.

paragraphs: Predicting a time series becomes harder when some past observations are missing. This paper treats the task as online learning: the learner makes predictions as the sequence unfolds and seeks to minimize prediction error. It develops an efficient method based on an autoregressive model, which uses earlier values to predict later ones.

A central feature is that the method does not assume a particular structure in the missing data or a particular mechanism generating the time series. This avoids making the learning approach depend on a specified pattern of missing observations. The theoretical comparison is instead made against the best autoregressive predictor chosen after seeing the sequence.

The authors show that their algorithm's performance asymptotically approaches that hindsight benchmark. This is a long-run comparison with a particular predictor class, rather than a claim of perfect predictions or superiority to every forecasting method. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data corroborate the theory, supporting an online approach to autoregressive prediction when observations are incomplete.
summary.tldr: An efficient online predictor handles missing observations and asymptotically approaches the best autoregressive predictor in hindsight.

title: Online Time Series Prediction with Missing Data

abstract: Nonparametric extension of tensor regression is proposed. Nonlinearity in a high-dimensional tensor space is broken into simple local functions by incorporating low-rank tensor decomposition. Compared to naive nonparametric approaches, our formulation considerably improves the convergence rate of estimation while maintaining consistency with the same function class under specific conditions. To estimate local functions, we develop a Bayesian estimator with the Gaussian process prior. Experimental results show its theoretical properties and high performance in terms of predicting a summary statistic of a real complex network.
originalAbstract: Nonparametric extension of tensor regression is proposed. Nonlinearity in a high-dimensional tensor space is broken into simple local functions by incorporating low-rank tensor decomposition. Compared to naive nonparametric approaches, our formulation considerably improves the convergence rate of estimation while maintaining consistency with the same function class under specific conditions. To estimate local functions, we develop a Bayesian estimator with the Gaussian process prior. Experimental results show its theoretical properties and high performance in terms of predicting a summary statistic of a real complex network.

paragraphs: The paper develops a nonparametric extension of tensor regression, allowing nonlinear relationships in a high-dimensional tensor space. Its organizing idea is to break a complicated relationship into simpler local functions. Low-rank tensor decomposition supplies the structure for that breakdown, connecting the representation of the tensor with the representation of the nonlinear function.

The authors show that their formulation can substantially improve the convergence rate of estimation relative to naive nonparametric approaches. Under specific conditions, it also retains consistency for the same function class. These claims concern both how quickly estimation improves and whether it approaches the intended function, with the stated conditions governing the comparison.

To estimate the local functions, the paper develops a Bayesian estimator using a Gaussian process prior. Experiments support the theoretical properties and show strong performance when predicting a summary statistic of a real complex network. The approach matters because it connects flexible nonlinear estimation with a structured decomposition, using simpler component functions to address an otherwise high-dimensional regression problem.
summary.tldr: Low-rank decomposition breaks nonlinear tensor regression into local functions, improving estimation rates under specified conditions.

title: Doubly Decomposing Nonparametric Tensor Regression

abstract: We create a new online reduction of multiclass classification to binary classification for which training and prediction time scale logarithmically with the number of classes. We show that several simple techniques give rise to an algorithm which is superior to previous logarithmic time classification approaches while competing with one-against-all in space. The core construction is based on using a tree to select a small subset of labels with high recall, which are then scored using a one-against-some structure with high precision.
originalAbstract: We create a new online reduction of multiclass classification to binary classification for which training and prediction time scale logarithmically with the number of classes. We show that several simple techniques give rise to an algorithm which is superior to previous logarithmic time classification approaches while competing with one-against-all in space. The core construction is based on using a tree to select a small subset of labels with high recall, which are then scored using a one-against-some structure with high precision.

paragraphs: The paper addresses multiclass classification when the number of possible labels makes training and prediction expensive. It introduces an online reduction that solves the multiclass problem using binary classification components. Both training time and prediction time grow logarithmically with the number of classes, making the growth in computation much slower than the growth in the label set.

The construction divides the decision into two stages. A tree first selects a small subset of candidate labels with high recall, aiming to retain the relevant label among those candidates. A one-against-some structure then scores the subset with high precision. Candidate selection and final discrimination therefore play complementary roles in the algorithm.

The authors report that combining several simple techniques yields an algorithm superior to earlier logarithmic-time classification approaches while remaining competitive with one-against-all in space. The contribution links computational scaling to a concrete selection-and-scoring design. Its stated benefits cover both the cost of learning and the cost of making predictions.
summary.tldr: A tree selects candidate labels and a one-against-some classifier scores them, enabling logarithmic training and prediction time in the number of classes.

title: Logarithmic Time One-Against-Some

abstract: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) exploits Hamiltonian dynamics to construct efficient proposals for Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). In this paper, we present a generalization of HMC which exploits non-canonical Hamiltonian dynamics. We refer to this algorithm as magnetic HMC, since in 3 dimensions a subset of the dynamics map onto the mechanics of a charged particle coupled to a magnetic field. We establish a theoretical basis for the use of non-canonical Hamiltonian dynamics in MCMC, and construct a symplectic, leapfrog-like integrator allowing for the implementation of magnetic HMC. Finally, we exhibit several examples where these non-canonical dynamics can lead to improved mixing of magnetic HMC relative to ordinary HMC.

We establish a theoretical basis for the use of non-canonical Hamiltonian dynamics in MCMC, and construct a symplectic, leapfrog-like integrator allowing for the implementation of magnetic HMC. Finally, we exhibit several examples where these non-canonical dynamics can lead to improved mixing of magnetic HMC relative to ordinary HMC.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo uses Hamiltonian dynamics to construct proposals for a Markov chain sampling procedure. This paper broadens that approach by allowing non-canonical Hamiltonian dynamics. The resulting algorithm, magnetic HMC, explores a larger family of dynamics for proposing moves within Markov chain Monte Carlo.

The name comes from a physical connection: in three dimensions, a subset of the proposed dynamics corresponds to a charged particle interacting with a magnetic field. The authors establish a theoretical basis for using the broader dynamics in MCMC. They also construct a symplectic integrator resembling leapfrog, providing a numerical procedure that makes magnetic HMC implementable.

The paper presents several examples in which the modified dynamics improve mixing relative to ordinary HMC. Better mixing means the sampling process moves more effectively through the distribution being explored. These examples demonstrate that non-canonical dynamics can provide a practical benefit, while the theoretical and numerical developments explain how to incorporate them into a sampling algorithm. The reported advantage is possible and example-dependent, rather than universal.
summary.tldr: Magnetic HMC extends Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with non-canonical dynamics and demonstrates improved mixing in several examples.

title: Magnetic Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

abstract: Many machine learning problems require the prediction of multi-dimensional labels. Such structured prediction models can benefit from modeling dependencies between labels. Recently, several deep learning approaches to structured prediction have been proposed. Here we focus on capturing cardinality constraints in such models. Namely, constraining the number of non-zero labels that the model outputs. Such constraints have proven very useful in previous structured prediction methods, but it is a challenge to introduce them into a deep learning approach. Here we show how to do this via a novel deep architecture. Our approach outperforms strong baselines, achieving state-of-the-art results on multi-label classification benchmarks.

Namely, constraining the number of non-zero labels that the model outputs. Such constraints have proven very useful in previous structured prediction methods, but it is a challenge to introduce them into a deep learning approach. Here we show how to do this via a novel deep architecture. Our approach outperforms strong baselines, achieving state-of-the-art results on multi-label classification benchmarks.

paragraphs: Structured prediction produces several related labels for an input. The paper focuses on one particular relationship among these outputs: their cardinality, meaning the number of labels that are nonzero. A cardinality constraint concerns the prediction as a whole, so it captures information that cannot be expressed merely by considering each label independently.

Such constraints had proved useful in earlier structured prediction methods, but incorporating them into deep learning presents a challenge. The authors introduce a deep architecture that brings cardinality constraints into the prediction process. The central contribution is a way for a neural model to account for how many labels it outputs alongside the individual label predictions.

The proposed approach outperforms strong baselines and achieves state-of-the-art results on the evaluated multi-label classification benchmarks. These findings support modeling output counts as a useful source of structure for these tasks. They show that a relatively direct dependency—the total number of active labels—can contribute meaningfully to the quality of deep structured predictions.
summary.tldr: A deep structured-prediction architecture models the number of active labels and achieves strong multi-label classification results.

title: Predict and Constrain: Modeling Cardinality in Deep Structured Prediction

abstract: In this work we aim to solve a large collection of tasks using a single reinforcement learning agent with a single set of parameters. A key challenge is to handle the increased amount of data and extended training time. We have developed a new distributed agent IMPALA (Importance Weighted Actor-Learner Architecture) that not only uses resources more efficiently in single-machine training but also scales to thousands of machines without sacrificing data efficiency or resource utilisation. We achieve stable learning at high throughput by combining decoupled acting and learning with a novel off-policy correction method called V-trace. We demonstrate the effectiveness of IMPALA for multi-task reinforcement learning on DMLab-30 (a set of 30 tasks from the DeepMind Lab environment (Beattie et al., 2016)) and Atari57 (all available Atari games in Arcade Learning Environment (Bellemare et al., 2013a)). Our results show that IMPALA is able to achieve better performance than previous agents with less data, and crucially exhibits positive transfer between tasks as a result of its multi-task approach.

We have developed a new distributed agent IMPALA (Importance Weighted Actor-Learner Architecture) that not only uses resources more efficiently in single-machine training but also scales to thousands of machines without sacrificing data efficiency or resource utilisation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of IMPALA for multi-task reinforcement learning on DMLab-30 (a set of 30 tasks from the DeepMind Lab environment (Beattie et al., 2016)) and Atari57 (all available Atari games in Arcade Learning Environment (Bellemare et al., 2013a)). Our results show that IMPALA is able to achieve better performance than previous agents with less data, and crucially exhibits positive transfer between tasks as a result of its multi-task approach.

paragraphs: IMPALA addresses learning many tasks with one reinforcement learning agent and one shared set of parameters. This ambition increases both the amount of experience to process and the training time required. The paper focuses on an architecture that can handle that workload while using computational resources and collected data efficiently.

The architecture separates acting from learning and combines that separation with an off-policy correction called V-trace. The correction is part of how IMPALA maintains stable learning at high throughput. The authors report improved resource use on a single machine and scaling to thousands of machines without sacrificing data efficiency or resource utilization.

The evaluation covers DMLab-30 and Atari57, testing the architecture in multi-task reinforcement learning. Reported results show better performance than previous agents with less data, together with positive transfer between tasks. Positive transfer means that shared multi-task learning helps performance across tasks. These findings connect the systems design to the learning objective: scaling experience processing supports a single agent whose tasks can benefit from being learned together.
summary.tldr: IMPALA combines separate acting and learning with V-trace correction to scale multi-task reinforcement learning and achieve positive transfer.

title: IMPALA: Scalable Distributed Deep-RL with Importance Weighted Actor-Learner Architectures

abstract: We provide the first provably joint differentially private algorithm with formal utility guarantees for the problem of user-level privacy-preserving collaborative filtering. Our algorithm is based on the Frank-Wolfe method, and it consistently estimates the underlying preference matrix as long as the number of users $m$ is $\omega(n^{5/4})$, where $n$ is the number of items, and each user provides her preference for at least $\sqrt{n}$ randomly selected items. Along the way, we provide an optimal differentially private algorithm for singular vector computation, based on the celebrated Oja’s method, that provides significant savings in terms of space and time while operating on sparse matrices. We also empirically evaluate our algorithm on a suite of datasets, and show that it consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art private algorithms.
originalAbstract: We provide the first provably joint differentially private algorithm with formal utility guarantees for the problem of user-level privacy-preserving collaborative filtering. Our algorithm is based on the Frank-Wolfe method, and it consistently estimates the underlying preference matrix as long as the number of users $m$ is $\omega(n^{5/4})$, where $n$ is the number of items, and each user provides her preference for at least $\sqrt{n}$ randomly selected items. Along the way, we provide an optimal differentially private algorithm for singular vector computation, based on the celebrated Oja’s method, that provides significant savings in terms of space and time while operating on sparse matrices. We also empirically evaluate our algorithm on a suite of datasets, and show that it consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art private algorithms.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering estimates users' preferences from an incomplete collection of ratings or other preference observations. This paper studies that task with user-level privacy protection. It presents what the authors identify as the first algorithm with both a proof of joint differential privacy and formal guarantees about the usefulness of its estimated preference matrix.

The algorithm builds on the Frank-Wolfe optimization method. Its consistency guarantee requires the number of users m to grow faster than n to the power 5/4, where n is the number of items. It also requires every user to provide preferences for at least the square root of n randomly selected items. Under those conditions, the algorithm consistently estimates the underlying matrix.

A supporting contribution is an optimal differentially private singular-vector algorithm based on Oja's method, with substantial space and time savings for sparse matrices. The authors also evaluate the matrix-completion algorithm across several datasets and report that it consistently outperforms existing leading private algorithms. The work therefore combines conditional estimation guarantees, privacy guarantees, and empirical evidence of practical utility.
summary.tldr: A private collaborative-filtering algorithm combines formal utility guarantees under stated sampling conditions with improved empirical performance over existing private methods.

title: Differentially Private Matrix Completion Revisited

abstract: We study the complexity of the entire regularization path for least squares regression with 1-norm penalty, known as the Lasso. Every regression parameter in the Lasso changes linearly as a function of the regularization value. The number of changes is regarded as the Lasso’s complexity. Experimental results using exact path following exhibit polynomial complexity of the Lasso in the problem size. Alas, the path complexity of the Lasso on artificially designed regression problems is exponential We use smoothed analysis as a mechanism for bridging the gap between worst case settings and the de facto low complexity. Our analysis assumes that the observed data has a tiny amount of intrinsic noise. We then prove that the Lasso’s complexity is polynomial in the problem size.
originalAbstract: We study the complexity of the entire regularization path for least squares regression with 1-norm penalty, known as the Lasso. Every regression parameter in the Lasso changes linearly as a function of the regularization value. The number of changes is regarded as the Lasso’s complexity. Experimental results using exact path following exhibit polynomial complexity of the Lasso in the problem size. Alas, the path complexity of the Lasso on artificially designed regression problems is exponential We use smoothed analysis as a mechanism for bridging the gap between worst case settings and the de facto low complexity. Our analysis assumes that the observed data has a tiny amount of intrinsic noise. We then prove that the Lasso’s complexity is polynomial in the problem size.

paragraphs: The Lasso fits a least-squares regression model with a penalty on the sum of absolute coefficient values. This paper studies the complexity of its entire regularization path as the penalty strength varies. Coefficients follow linear pieces along that path, and complexity is measured by the number of changes between those pieces.

There is a gap between observed and worst-case behavior. Exact path-following experiments exhibit polynomial complexity in problem size, while specially constructed regression problems can have exponentially complex paths. The authors use smoothed analysis to investigate how those two observations can coexist without dismissing either one.

Their analysis assumes that the observed data contains a tiny amount of intrinsic noise. Under that assumption, they prove polynomial path complexity. The result explains how small perturbations can change the relevant complexity picture, even though exponential constructions exist. It is a statement about the whole path under the analyzed noise setting, rather than a claim that every possible Lasso instance has a short path.
summary.tldr: Smoothed analysis shows polynomial Lasso regularization-path complexity under a small intrinsic-noise assumption, helping reconcile empirical behavior with exponential worst cases.

title: The Well-Tempered Lasso

abstract: We propose a novel and flexible rank-breaking-then-composite-marginal-likelihood (RBCML) framework for learning random utility models (RUMs), which include the Plackett-Luce model. We characterize conditions for the objective function of RBCML to be strictly log-concave by proving that strict log-concavity is preserved under convolution and marginalization. We characterize necessary and sufficient conditions for RBCML to satisfy consistency and asymptotic normality. Experiments on synthetic data show that RBCML for Gaussian RUMs achieves better statistical efficiency and computation efficiency than the state-of-the-art algorithm and our RBCML for the Plackett-Luce model provides flexible tradeoffs between running time and statistical efficiency.

We characterize conditions for the objective function of RBCML to be strictly log-concave by proving that strict log-concavity is preserved under convolution and marginalization. We characterize necessary and sufficient conditions for RBCML to satisfy consistency and asymptotic normality. Experiments on synthetic data show that RBCML for Gaussian RUMs achieves better statistical efficiency and computation efficiency than the state-of-the-art algorithm and our RBCML for the Plackett-Luce model provides flexible tradeoffs between running time and statistical efficiency.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn random utility models from ranking information. These models include the Plackett-Luce model. The proposed framework, RBCML, first breaks rankings into smaller pieces and then combines marginal likelihood contributions into a learning objective. This gives a flexible framework for using ranking evidence.

The theoretical work establishes conditions under which the objective is strictly log-concave, an important property for optimization. Supporting this analysis, the authors prove that convolution and marginalization preserve strict log-concavity. They also characterize necessary and sufficient conditions for the resulting estimates to be consistent and asymptotically normal, connecting the construction of the objective to its statistical behavior as data accumulate.

Experiments on synthetic data examine both computation and estimation quality. For Gaussian random utility models, RBCML improves statistical and computational efficiency over the compared state-of-the-art algorithm. For Plackett-Luce models, it offers flexible tradeoffs between running time and statistical efficiency. The findings make the framework useful both as a theoretically characterized estimation approach and as a way to choose a practical balance between speed and precision.
summary.tldr: RBCML learns ranking models through composite marginal likelihood, with characterized statistical guarantees and flexible speed–efficiency tradeoffs.

title: Composite Marginal Likelihood Methods for Random Utility Models

abstract: Distribution estimation is a statistical-learning cornerstone. Its classical min-max formulation minimizes the estimation error for the worst distribution, hence under-performs for practical distributions that, like power-law, are often rather simple. Modern research has therefore focused on two frameworks: structural estimation that improves learning accuracy by assuming a simple structure of the underlying distribution; and competitive , or instance-optimal , estimation that achieves the performance of a genie aided estimator up to a small excess error that vanishes as the sample size grows, regardless of the distribution. This paper combines and strengthens the two frameworks. It designs a single estimator whose excess error vanishes both at a universal rate as the sample size grows, as well as when the (unknown) distribution gets simpler. We show that the resulting algorithm significantly improves the performance guarantees for numerous competitive- and structural-estimation results. The algorithm runs in near-linear time and is robust to model misspecification and domain-symbol permutations.

paragraphs: Distribution estimation often seeks a method that performs well against the hardest possible distribution. Such worst-case protection can leave accuracy available when the actual distribution is simpler. Two alternatives address this: assuming a useful structure in advance, or competing with an estimator given extra information while allowing a small excess error.

This paper combines those approaches in a single estimator. Its excess error vanishes at a universal rate as more samples arrive, and also vanishes as the unknown distribution becomes simpler. The second guarantee makes simplicity useful without requiring the learner to know the underlying structure beforehand. The method therefore adapts along both sample-size and distribution-complexity dimensions.

The authors show improved performance guarantees for numerous existing results in competitive and structural estimation. They also establish near-linear running time and robustness to model misspecification and permutations of domain symbols. These properties matter because the theoretical adaptation is accompanied by computational efficiency and does not rely on a particular naming of outcomes or an exactly correct structural model.
summary.tldr: A single efficient distribution estimator improves its competitive guarantee both with more samples and with simpler unknown distributions.

title: Doubly-Competitive Distribution Estimation

abstract: In order to solve complex problems an agent must be able to reason over a sufficiently long horizon. Temporal abstraction, commonly modeled through options, offers the ability to reason at many timescales, but the horizon length is still determined by the discount factor of the underlying Markov Decision Process. We propose a modification to the options framework that naturally scales the agent’s horizon with option length. We show that the proposed option-step discount controls a bias-variance trade-off, with larger discounts (counter-intuitively) leading to less estimation variance.

We show that the proposed option-step discount controls a bias-variance trade-off, with larger discounts (counter-intuitively) leading to less estimation variance.

paragraphs: An agent solving a complex task may need to reason about consequences far into the future. Options provide temporal abstraction: they let the agent reason using extended behaviors rather than only individual steps. However, the underlying Markov decision process’s discount factor still determines the effective horizon in the usual options framework.

This paper modifies that framework so the agent’s horizon scales naturally with option length. The proposed option-step discount makes the relationship between temporal abstraction and discounting part of the method itself. Longer options can therefore be accompanied by a correspondingly scaled reasoning horizon, addressing a mismatch between the timescale of decisions and the horizon imposed by the underlying process.

The authors show that this discount controls a bias-variance tradeoff. In particular, larger discounts lead to less estimation variance, a relationship they identify as counterintuitive. The finding means the discount affects both the temporal reach of reasoning and the statistical behavior of estimates. It supplies a way to examine those effects together when choosing how an agent reasons over extended actions.
summary.tldr: Option-step discounting scales an agent’s horizon with option length and controls a bias-variance tradeoff in which larger discounts reduce estimation variance.

title: Per-Decision Option Discounting

abstract: When learning policies for real-world domains, two important questions arise: (i) how to efficiently use pre-collected off-policy, non-optimal behavior data; and (ii) how to mediate among different competing objectives and constraints. We thus study the problem of batch policy learning under multiple constraints, and offer a systematic solution. We first propose a flexible meta-algorithm that admits any batch reinforcement learning and online learning procedure as subroutines. We then present a specific algorithmic instantiation and provide performance guarantees for the main objective and all constraints. As part of off-policy learning, we propose a simple method for off-policy policy evaluation (OPE) and derive PAC-style bounds. Our algorithm achieves strong empirical results in different domains, including in a challenging problem of simulated car driving subject to multiple constraints such as lane keeping and smooth driving. We also show experimentally that our OPE method outperforms other popular OPE techniques on a standalone basis, especially in a high-dimensional setting.

We thus study the problem of batch policy learning under multiple constraints, and offer a systematic solution. We first propose a flexible meta-algorithm that admits any batch reinforcement learning and online learning procedure as subroutines. We then present a specific algorithmic instantiation and provide performance guarantees for the main objective and all constraints. As part of off-policy learning, we propose a simple method for off-policy policy evaluation (OPE) and derive PAC-style bounds. Our algorithm achieves strong empirical results in different domains, including in a challenging problem of simulated car driving subject to multiple constraints such as lane keeping and smooth driving. We also show experimentally that our OPE method outperforms other popular OPE techniques on a standalone basis, especially in a high-dimensional setting.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn a decision policy from previously collected data while respecting several constraints. The data may come from a different, non-optimal behavior policy, so learning must make useful decisions without assuming the recorded actions were ideal. At the same time, success must account for competing objectives rather than a single performance measure.

The authors introduce a flexible framework that can use any batch reinforcement learning method and any online learning procedure as subroutines. They then develop a specific version with performance guarantees for both the main objective and every constraint. They also propose an off-policy evaluation method, which estimates a policy’s performance from data collected under another policy, and derive probabilistic accuracy bounds.

Experiments report strong results across domains, including simulated driving with lane-keeping and smooth-driving constraints. The evaluation method also performs better than popular alternatives in standalone tests, especially in a high-dimensional setting. Together, these findings support integrating policy learning, constraint management, and evaluation within one systematic approach.
summary.tldr: A flexible batch reinforcement learning framework learns from existing behavior data while providing guarantees for an objective and multiple constraints.

title: Batch Policy Learning under Constraints

abstract: Numerous empirical evidence has corroborated that the noise plays a crucial rule in effective and efficient training of deep neural networks. The theory behind, however, is still largely unknown. This paper studies this fundamental problem through training a simple two-layer convolutional neural network model. Although training such a network requires to solve a non-convex optimization problem with a spurious local optimum and a global optimum, we prove that a perturbed gradient descent algorithm in conjunction with noise annealing is guaranteed to converge to a global optimum in polynomial time with arbitrary initialization. This implies that the noise enables the algorithm to efficiently escape from the spurious local optimum. Numerical experiments are provided to support our theory.
originalAbstract: Numerous empirical evidence has corroborated that the noise plays a crucial rule in effective and efficient training of deep neural networks. The theory behind, however, is still largely unknown. This paper studies this fundamental problem through training a simple two-layer convolutional neural network model. Although training such a network requires to solve a non-convex optimization problem with a spurious local optimum and a global optimum, we prove that a perturbed gradient descent algorithm in conjunction with noise annealing is guaranteed to converge to a global optimum in polynomial time with arbitrary initialization. This implies that the noise enables the algorithm to efficiently escape from the spurious local optimum. Numerical experiments are provided to support our theory.

paragraphs: Noise has been empirically associated with effective neural-network training, but explaining its role mathematically is harder. This paper studies that question in a simple two-layer convolutional network. Its optimization problem is nonconvex and contains both a spurious local optimum and a global optimum, providing a setting where becoming trapped is a concrete concern.

The authors analyze perturbed gradient descent combined with noise annealing. For the studied model, they prove convergence to a global optimum in polynomial time from arbitrary initialization. The result shows that the added noise enables the algorithm to escape the spurious local optimum efficiently rather than remaining trapped there.

Numerical experiments support the theoretical analysis. The significance is a rigorous example of noise actively helping optimization navigate a problematic landscape. The guarantee applies to the particular simple network studied and to the combination of perturbations with annealing. Within that setting, it connects the use of noise to both successful escape from a misleading optimum and an efficient route to a global solution.
summary.tldr: For a simple two-layer CNN, perturbed gradient descent with noise annealing provably reaches a global optimum in polynomial time from arbitrary initialization.

title: Toward Understanding the Importance of Noise in Training Neural Networks

abstract: We introduce Negative Sampling in Semi-Supervised Learning (NS^3L), a simple, fast, easy to tune algorithm for semi-supervised learning (SSL). NS^3L is motivated by the success of negative sampling/contrastive estimation. We demonstrate that adding the NS^3L loss to state-of-the-art SSL algorithms, such as the Virtual Adversarial Training (VAT), significantly improves upon vanilla VAT and its variant, VAT with Entropy Minimization. By adding the NS^3L loss to MixMatch, the current state-of-the-art approach on semi-supervised tasks, we observe significant improvements over vanilla MixMatch. We conduct extensive experiments on the CIFAR10, CIFAR100, SVHN and STL10 benchmark datasets. Finally, we perform an ablation study for NS3L regarding its hyperparameter tuning.

NS^3L is motivated by the success of negative sampling/contrastive estimation. We demonstrate that adding the NS^3L loss to state-of-the-art SSL algorithms, such as the Virtual Adversarial Training (VAT), significantly improves upon vanilla VAT and its variant, VAT with Entropy Minimization. By adding the NS^3L loss to MixMatch, the current state-of-the-art approach on semi-supervised tasks, we observe significant improvements over vanilla MixMatch. paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses labeled and unlabeled data together. This paper introduces NS3L, a method motivated by negative sampling and contrastive estimation. The authors describe it as simple, fast, and easy to tune, and investigate its usefulness as an additional loss within existing semi-supervised learning algorithms.

Adding the NS3L loss to Virtual Adversarial Training produces significant improvements over both ordinary VAT and its variant with entropy minimization. The authors also add the loss to MixMatch and observe significant gains over the original method. These comparisons test whether NS3L contributes useful learning information when combined with already strong approaches.

The experimental study covers CIFAR10, CIFAR100, SVHN, and STL10, and includes an ablation study of hyperparameter tuning. The stated findings support NS3L as a useful addition across the evaluated semi-supervised methods and benchmarks. Its practical contribution is a loss that can improve established learning procedures, with experiments examining both the resulting performance and the role of its tuning choices.
summary.tldr: NS3L adds a negative-sampling-inspired loss that significantly improves VAT and MixMatch in the reported semi-supervised learning experiments.

title: Negative Sampling in Semi-Supervised learning

abstract: We study generalised linear regression and classification for a synthetically generated dataset encompassing different problems of interest, such as learning with random features, neural networks in the lazy training regime, and the hidden manifold model. We consider the high-dimensional regime and using the replica method from statistical physics, we provide a closed-form expression for the asymptotic generalisation performance in these problems, valid in both the under- and over-parametrised regimes and for a broad choice of generalised linear model loss functions. In particular, we show how to obtain analytically the so-called double descent behaviour for logistic regression with a peak at the interpolation threshold, we illustrate the superiority of orthogonal against random Gaussian projections in learning with random features, and discuss the role played by correlations in the data generated by the hidden manifold model. Beyond the interest in these particular problems, the theoretical formalism introduced in this manuscript provides a path to further extensions to more complex tasks.

We consider the high-dimensional regime and using the replica method from statistical physics, we provide a closed-form expression for the asymptotic generalisation performance in these problems, valid in both the under- and over-parametrised regimes and for a broad choice of generalised linear model loss functions. paragraphs: This paper analyzes generalization in a synthetic data setting that encompasses several learning problems. These include random-feature learning, neural networks in the lazy-training regime, and the hidden manifold model. Studying them within one framework allows the authors to examine how model size, feature construction, and data correlations relate to prediction performance.

Using the replica method from statistical physics, the authors derive a closed-form expression for asymptotic generalization performance in a high-dimensional regime. The expression covers both under-parameterized and over-parameterized models and a broad choice of generalized linear-model losses. Its scope is therefore an asymptotic analysis of the specified synthetic setting, including both regression and classification.

The framework analytically produces double descent for logistic regression, with a performance peak in error at the interpolation threshold. It also illustrates an advantage of orthogonal projections over random Gaussian projections in random-feature learning and examines correlations in hidden-manifold data. Together, these applications show how a shared theoretical treatment can explain distinct generalization phenomena and provide a basis for extensions to more complex tasks.
summary.tldr: A high-dimensional replica analysis characterizes generalization across random-feature and hidden-manifold models, including logistic-regression double descent.

title: Generalisation error in learning with random features and the hidden manifold model

abstract: Off-policy evaluation in reinforcement learning offers the chance of using observational data to improve future outcomes in domains such as healthcare and education, but safe deployment in high stakes settings requires ways of assessing its validity. Traditional measures such as confidence intervals may be insufficient due to noise, limited data and confounding. In this paper we develop a method that could serve as a hybrid human-AI system, to enable human experts to analyze the validity of policy evaluation estimates. This is accomplished by highlighting observations in the data whose removal will have a large effect on the OPE estimate, and formulating a set of rules for choosing which ones to present to domain experts for validation. We develop methods to compute exactly the influence functions for fitted Q-evaluation with two different function classes: kernel-based and linear least squares, as well as importance sampling methods. Experiments on medical simulations and real-world intensive care unit data demonstrate that our method can be used to identify limitations in the evaluation process and make evaluation more robust.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a policy would perform using observations collected under other behavior. In settings such as healthcare, an estimate needs scrutiny before it can inform deployment. Confidence intervals alone may be insufficient when data are noisy, limited, or confounded. This paper makes the observations driving an estimate easier for experts to inspect.

The method identifies transitions whose removal would substantially change the evaluation result. It then applies rules to select which influential observations should be presented to domain experts. This creates a possible human-AI review process: the algorithm directs attention toward consequential evidence, and experts assess whether that evidence supports the evaluation.

The authors derive exact influence functions for fitted Q-evaluation using kernel-based and linear least-squares function classes, as well as for importance-sampling methods. Experiments involving medical simulations and intensive care data show that the approach can expose limitations in evaluation and improve robustness. Its contribution is an interpretable route to checking estimates, rather than a guarantee that an evaluated policy is safe.
summary.tldr: Highlighting transitions that strongly affect off-policy estimates helps experts identify weaknesses and improve evaluation robustness.

title: Interpretable Off-Policy Evaluation in Reinforcement Learning by Highlighting Influential Transitions

abstract: We report a series of robust empirical observations, demonstrating that deep Neural Networks learn the examples in both the training and test sets in a similar order. This phenomenon is observed in all the commonly used benchmarks we evaluated, including many image classification benchmarks, and one text classification benchmark. While this phenomenon is strongest for models of the same architecture, it also crosses architectural boundaries – models of different architectures start by learning the same examples, after which the more powerful model may continue to learn additional examples. We further show that this pattern of results reflects the interplay between the way neural networks learn benchmark datasets. Specifically, when fixing the architecture, we describe synthetic datasets for which this pattern is no longer observed. When fixing the dataset, we show that other learning paradigms may learn the data in a different order. We hypothesize that our results reflect how neural networks discover structure in natural datasets.

paragraphs: This paper examines which examples neural networks learn earlier or later during training. Across all evaluated common benchmarks, including several image classification datasets and one text classification dataset, different networks show similar ordering. The pattern appears for examples in both training and test sets, making it a shared feature of their observed learning behavior.

Agreement is strongest among networks with the same architecture, but it also appears across architectures. Different models initially learn many of the same examples, after which a more powerful model may learn additional ones. The authors investigate the boundaries of this finding by holding either the architecture or dataset fixed while changing the other part of the learning setup.

Synthetic datasets can break the pattern for a fixed architecture, and other learning paradigms can learn a fixed dataset in a different order. The observation therefore reflects an interaction between neural networks and the evaluated datasets. The authors hypothesize that it reveals how neural networks discover structure in natural data.
summary.tldr: Neural networks tend to learn benchmark examples in similar orders, with evidence that the pattern depends on both the learning method and the data.

title: Let’s Agree to Agree: Neural Networks Share Classification Order on Real Datasets

abstract: We take a more rigorous look at Relativistic Generative Adversarial Networks (RGANs) and prove that the objective function of the discriminator is a statistical divergence for any concave function f with minimal properties. We devise additional variants of relativistic f-divergences. We show that the Wasserstein distance is weaker than f-divergences which are weaker than relativistic f-divergences. Given the good performance of RGANs, this suggests that Wasserstein GAN does not performs well primarily because of the weak metric, but rather because of regularization and the use of a relativistic discriminator. We introduce the minimum-variance unbiased estimator (MVUE) for Relativistic paired GANs (RpGANs; originally called RGANs which could bring confusion) and show that it does not perform better. We show that the estimator of Relativistic average GANs (RaGANs) is asymptotically unbiased and that the finite-sample bias is small; removing this bias does not improve performance.

paragraphs: This paper investigates the mathematical foundations of relativistic generative adversarial networks. It proves that their discriminator objective defines a statistical divergence when the concave function used satisfies minimal specified properties. The authors also develop additional variants of relativistic f-divergences, extending the family of distribution comparisons under study.

They establish a strength ordering: Wasserstein distance is weaker than f-divergences, which are weaker than relativistic f-divergences. In light of the reported success of relativistic GANs, this suggests that Wasserstein GAN performance may owe more to regularization and relativistic discrimination than to the weakness of its metric. This is an interpretation of the results, not an established exclusive explanation.

The paper also examines estimation quality. A minimum-variance unbiased estimator for relativistic paired GANs does not improve performance. For relativistic average GANs, the estimator becomes unbiased asymptotically and has small finite-sample bias; removing that bias likewise does not improve performance. These findings distinguish desirable estimator properties from observed gains in GAN training.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes divergence properties of relativistic GAN objectives and finds that improved unbiased estimation does not improve reported performance.

title: On Relativistic f-Divergences

abstract: Inter-domain Gaussian processes (GPs) allow for high flexibility and low computational cost when performing approximate inference in GP models. They are particularly suitable for modeling data exhibiting global structure but are limited to stationary covariance functions and thus fail to model non-stationary data effectively. We propose Inter-domain Deep Gaussian Processes, an extension of inter-domain shallow GPs that combines the advantages of inter-domain and deep Gaussian processes (DGPs), and demonstrate how to leverage existing approximate inference methods to perform simple and scalable approximate inference using inter-domain features in DGPs. We assess the performance of our method on a range of regression tasks and demonstrate that it outperforms inter-domain shallow GPs and conventional DGPs on challenging large-scale real-world datasets exhibiting both global structure as well as a high-degree of non-stationarity.

They are particularly suitable for modeling data exhibiting global structure but are limited to stationary covariance functions and thus fail to model non-stationary data effectively. We propose Inter-domain Deep Gaussian Processes, an extension of inter-domain shallow GPs that combines the advantages of inter-domain and deep Gaussian processes (DGPs), and demonstrate how to leverage existing approximate inference methods to perform simple and scalable approximate inference using inter-domain features in DGPs. We assess the performance of our method on a range of regression tasks and demonstrate that it outperforms inter-domain shallow GPs and conventional DGPs on challenging large-scale real-world datasets exhibiting both global structure as well as a high-degree of non-stationarity.

paragraphs: Inter-domain Gaussian processes offer flexible, relatively inexpensive approximate inference and are useful for modeling global structure. The authors identify a limitation in the shallow formulation they consider: stationary covariance functions make it difficult to capture non-stationary data, where statistical patterns change across the input space.

The proposed Inter-domain Deep Gaussian Processes combine inter-domain modeling with deep Gaussian processes. This brings the benefits of inter-domain features into a deeper model intended to handle the challenging data structure. The authors also show how existing approximate-inference methods can be used with these features, providing a simple and scalable inference approach for the combined model.

The method is evaluated on regression tasks, including challenging large-scale real-world datasets containing both global structure and substantial non-stationarity. In these evaluations, it outperforms both shallow inter-domain Gaussian processes and conventional deep Gaussian processes. The results support combining the two approaches when both kinds of structure matter, rather than relying on either component alone. The reported advantage is empirical on the evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: Inter-domain deep Gaussian processes combine scalable inference with improved modeling of datasets containing global structure and non-stationarity.

title: Inter-domain Deep Gaussian Processes

abstract: Standard reinforcement learning (RL) aims to find an optimal policy that identifies the best action for each state. However, in healthcare settings, many actions may be near-equivalent with respect to the reward (e.g., survival). We consider an alternative objective – learning set-valued policies to capture near-equivalent actions that lead to similar cumulative rewards. We propose a model-free algorithm based on temporal difference learning and a near-greedy heuristic for action selection. We analyze the theoretical properties of the proposed algorithm, providing optimality guarantees and demonstrate our approach on simulated environments and a real clinical task. Empirically, the proposed algorithm exhibits good convergence properties and discovers meaningful near-equivalent actions. Our work provides theoretical, as well as practical, foundations for clinician/human-in-the-loop decision making, in which humans (e.g., clinicians, patients) can incorporate additional knowledge (e.g., side effects, patient preference) when selecting among near-equivalent actions.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy usually recommends one action for each situation. In healthcare, however, several actions may offer nearly the same cumulative reward, such as a similar survival outcome. Selecting only one can hide alternatives that matter to a clinician or patient for reasons beyond that reward.

The paper instead learns policies that return a set of near-equivalent actions. Its model-free algorithm uses temporal difference learning together with a near-greedy action-selection heuristic. The central change is the objective: identify meaningful choices with similar long-term rewards, leaving room for a human to decide among them.

The authors analyze the algorithm's theoretical properties and provide optimality guarantees. Experiments in simulated environments and a real clinical task show good convergence and the discovery of meaningful alternatives. These findings support a decision-making arrangement in which the learned policy supplies a set of options and humans incorporate additional knowledge, including side effects or patient preferences, when choosing an action.
summary.tldr: Set-valued reinforcement learning policies identify near-equivalent actions so clinicians and patients can incorporate additional knowledge when choosing among them.

title: Clinician-in-the-Loop Decision Making: Reinforcement Learning with Near-Optimal Set-Valued Policies

abstract: This paper considers batch Reinforcement Learning (RL) with general value function approximation. Our study investigates the minimal assumptions to reliably estimate/minimize Bellman error, and characterizes the generalization performance by (local) Rademacher complexities of general function classes, which makes initial steps in bridging the gap between statistical learning theory and batch RL. Concretely, we view the Bellman error as a surrogate loss for the optimality gap, and prove the followings: (1) In double sampling regime, the excess risk of Empirical Risk Minimizer (ERM) is bounded by the Rademacher complexity of the function class. (2) In the single sampling regime, sample-efficient risk minimization is not possible without further assumptions, regardless of algorithms. However, with completeness assumptions, the excess risk of FQI and a minimax style algorithm can be again bounded by the Rademacher complexity of the corresponding function classes. (3) Fast statistical rates can be achieved by using tools of local Rademacher complexity. Our analysis covers a wide range of function classes, including finite classes, linear spaces, kernel spaces, sparse linear features, etc.

paragraphs: This paper studies generalization in batch reinforcement learning with general value-function approximators. It treats Bellman error as a surrogate objective for the gap from optimal performance and asks when that error can be reliably estimated or minimized. Rademacher complexity supplies the measure of function-class richness used to express statistical guarantees.

The analysis separates two sampling regimes. With double sampling, the excess risk of empirical risk minimization is bounded by the function class’s Rademacher complexity. With single sampling, sample-efficient risk minimization is impossible without additional assumptions, regardless of the algorithm. Under completeness assumptions, however, analogous complexity bounds become available for fitted Q-iteration and a minimax-style algorithm.

The authors further use local Rademacher complexity to obtain fast statistical rates. Their results cover finite classes, linear spaces, kernel spaces, and sparse linear features. The contribution links familiar statistical learning tools to batch reinforcement learning while showing that the sampling regime and completeness assumptions materially affect what can be learned. Function-class complexity alone is therefore only part of the required statistical picture.
summary.tldr: Rademacher complexity yields batch reinforcement learning risk bounds, with guarantees depending critically on sampling and completeness assumptions.

title: Risk Bounds and Rademacher Complexity in Batch Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Randomized smoothing is a general technique for computing sample-dependent robustness guarantees against adversarial attacks for deep classifiers. Prior works on randomized smoothing against L_1 adversarial attacks use additive smoothing noise and provide probabilistic robustness guarantees. In this work, we propose a non-additive and deterministic smoothing method, Deterministic Smoothing with Splitting Noise (DSSN). To develop DSSN, we first develop SSN, a randomized method which involves generating each noisy smoothing sample by first randomly splitting the input space and then returning a representation of the center of the subdivision occupied by the input sample. In contrast to uniform additive smoothing, the SSN certification does not require the random noise components used to be independent. Thus, smoothing can be done effectively in just one dimension and can therefore be efficiently derandomized for quantized data (e.g., images). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to provide deterministic "randomized smoothing" for a norm-based adversarial threat model while allowing for an arbitrary classifier (i.e., a deep model) to be used as a base classifier and without requiring an exponential number of smoothing samples. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets, we provide substantially larger L_1 robustness certificates compared to prior works, establishing a new state-of-the-art. The determinism of our method also leads to significantly faster certificate computation. Code is available at: https://github.com/alevine0/smoothingSplittingNoise.

paragraphs: Smoothing can turn a classifier into a predictor with guarantees against adversarial input changes. Earlier approaches for L1 attacks used additive noise and produced probabilistic certificates. This paper develops Deterministic Smoothing with Splitting Noise, or DSSN, to obtain deterministic certification through a different way of constructing smoothed inputs.

The starting point is a randomized method that splits the input space into subdivisions. Each smoothing sample represents the center of the subdivision containing the input. Its certification does not require independent random noise components. That property lets the randomness effectively operate in one dimension, enabling efficient removal of randomness when the data are quantized, as images are.

The resulting method allows an arbitrary base classifier without requiring an exponential number of smoothing samples. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, the authors report substantially larger L1 robustness certificates than earlier work and significantly faster certificate computation. The key connection is between the geometry of the splitting procedure and its computational consequences: relaxing the independence requirement makes deterministic smoothing practical for the stated data setting.
summary.tldr: DSSN uses input-space splitting to deliver efficient deterministic L1 robustness certificates for quantized data, with improved reported certificate sizes.

title: Improved, Deterministic Smoothing for L_1 Certified Robustness

abstract: Detecting anomalous inputs, such as adversarial and out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs, is critical for classifiers (including deep neural networks or DNNs) deployed in real-world applications. While prior works have proposed various methods to detect such anomalous samples using information from the internal layer representations of a DNN, there is a lack of consensus on a principled approach for the different components of such a detection method. As a result, often heuristic and one-off methods are applied for different aspects of this problem. We propose an unsupervised anomaly detection framework based on the internal DNN layer representations in the form of a meta-algorithm with configurable components. We proceed to propose specific instantiations for each component of the meta-algorithm based on ideas grounded in statistical testing and anomaly detection. We evaluate the proposed methods on well-known image classification datasets with strong adversarial attacks and OOD inputs, including an adaptive attack that uses the internal layer representations of the DNN (often not considered in prior work). Comparisons with five recently-proposed competing detection methods demonstrates the effectiveness of our method in detecting adversarial and OOD inputs.

paragraphs: A classifier's internal representations can provide clues that an input is unusual, even when its final prediction looks ordinary. This paper studies how to use those representations to detect adversarial inputs and inputs outside the expected data distribution. Its starting point is that existing detectors often assemble their components through separate, heuristic choices.

The authors propose an unsupervised framework organized as a configurable meta-algorithm. This means the contribution is a structure for constructing detectors, with interchangeable components, rather than only one fixed detection rule. They also supply concrete component choices grounded in statistical testing and anomaly detection, giving the framework specific implementations that can be evaluated.

The evaluation uses image classification datasets, strong adversarial attacks, and out-of-distribution inputs. It includes an adaptive attack that itself uses internal network representations, directly challenging the information on which the detectors rely. Comparisons with five competing methods support the proposed approach's effectiveness in these evaluations. The findings support a more systematic construction of representation-based detectors without establishing universal protection against anomalous inputs.
summary.tldr: A configurable, statistically grounded framework uses internal neural-network representations to detect adversarial and out-of-distribution inputs.

title: A General Framework For Detecting Anomalous Inputs to DNN Classifiers

abstract: Causal inference from observational data can be biased by unobserved confounders. Confounders{—}the variables that affect both the treatments and the outcome{—}induce spurious non-causal correlations between the two. Without additional conditions, unobserved confounders generally make causal quantities hard to identify. In this paper, we focus on the setting where there are many treatments with shared confounding, and we study under what conditions is causal identification possible. The key observation is that we can view subsets of treatments as proxies of the unobserved confounder and identify the intervention distributions of the rest. Moreover, while existing identification formulas for proxy variables involve solving integral equations, we show that one can circumvent the need for such solutions by directly modeling the data. Finally, we extend these results to an expanded class of causal graphs, those with other confounders and selection variables.
