paragraphs: Observational data can make a treatment appear to cause an outcome when an unseen variable actually influences both. This paper studies that problem when many treatments share hidden confounding. Its central question is when those shared patterns contain enough information to identify the effects of interventions, despite the confounder remaining unobserved.

The key idea is to use some treatments as proxies for the hidden confounder when studying interventions on the remaining treatments. Those proxy treatments provide indirect information about the common source of bias. The paper develops conditions under which this perspective permits causal identification; the presence of many treatments alone is not presented as sufficient.

The authors also show how directly modeling the observed data can avoid solving the integral equations used in existing proxy-variable identification formulas. They extend their results to a broader class of causal graphs containing additional confounders and selection variables. Together, these contributions connect shared confounding to proxy-based identification and offer a different route for obtaining intervention distributions.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditions for identifying causal effects by using some treatments as proxies for confounders shared with other treatments.

title: A Proxy Variable View of Shared Confounding

abstract: We study image inverse problems with a normalizing flow prior. Our formulation views the solution as the maximum a posteriori estimate of the image conditioned on the measurements. This formulation allows us to use noise models with arbitrary dependencies as well as non-linear forward operators. We empirically validate the efficacy of our method on various inverse problems, including compressed sensing with quantized measurements and denoising with highly structured noise patterns. We also present initial theoretical recovery guarantees for solving inverse problems with a flow prior.

This formulation allows us to use noise models with arbitrary dependencies as well as non-linear forward operators. We empirically validate the efficacy of our method on various inverse problems, including compressed sensing with quantized measurements and denoising with highly structured noise patterns. We also present initial theoretical recovery guarantees for solving inverse problems with a flow prior.

paragraphs: Image inverse problems reconstruct an image from measurements that may be incomplete, transformed, or noisy. This paper uses a normalizing flow prior to describe plausible images and formulates reconstruction as maximum a posteriori estimation. The chosen image is the one favored by the resulting probability model after conditioning on the measurements.

The formulation accommodates noise models with arbitrary dependencies and forward operators that can be nonlinear. These capabilities matter when measurement errors have structure or when the measurement process does more than apply a linear transformation. They allow the reconstruction objective to account for a broader range of observation processes within the same probabilistic framework.

The authors empirically validate the method on several inverse problems, including compressed sensing with quantized measurements and denoising with highly structured noise. These examples exercise the framework's ability to handle complicated measurement and noise behavior. The paper also provides initial theoretical recovery guarantees for inverse problems using a flow prior, complementing the experimental evidence with an early theoretical analysis.
summary.tldr: A flow-prior reconstruction framework handles dependent noise and nonlinear measurements, with empirical validation and initial recovery guarantees.

title: Solving Inverse Problems with a Flow-based Noise Model

abstract: Despite their success, policy gradient methods suffer from high variance of the gradient estimator, which can result in unsatisfactory sample complexity. Recently, numerous variance-reduced extensions of policy gradient methods with provably better sample complexity and competitive numerical performance have been proposed. After a compact survey on some of the main variance-reduced REINFORCE-type methods, we propose ProbAbilistic Gradient Estimation for Policy Gradient (PAGE-PG), a novel loopless variance-reduced policy gradient method based on a probabilistic switch between two types of update. Our method is inspired by the PAGE estimator for supervised learning and leverages importance sampling to obtain an unbiased gradient estimator. We show that PAGE-PG enjoys a $\mathcal{O}\left( \epsilon^{-3} \right)$ average sample complexity to reach an $\epsilon$-stationary solution, which matches the sample complexity of its most competitive counterparts under the same setting. A numerical evaluation confirms the competitive performance of our method on classical control tasks.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods improve a policy using estimated gradients, but noisy estimates can increase the amount of experience needed for learning. This paper addresses that variance problem. After surveying several variance-reduced REINFORCE-type methods, it introduces PAGE-PG, a policy gradient algorithm built around probabilistic gradient estimation.

PAGE-PG switches probabilistically between two kinds of update, producing a loopless method. Its design draws on the PAGE estimator from supervised learning and uses importance sampling to obtain an unbiased gradient estimate. The combination aims to retain the sample-efficiency benefits of variance reduction within a simple update structure.

The authors prove an average sample complexity of O(epsilon^-3) for reaching an epsilon-stationary solution. This matches the most competitive comparison methods under the same setting; the stated target concerns approximate stationarity of the optimization problem. Numerical evaluation on classical control tasks finds competitive performance as well. The contribution is therefore a simpler probabilistic update design that preserves strong theoretical sample complexity and performs competitively in the reported control experiments.
summary.tldr: PAGE-PG uses probabilistic updates and importance sampling to match leading variance-reduced policy-gradient sample complexity with a loopless design.

title: PAGE-PG: A Simple and Loopless Variance-Reduced Policy Gradient Method with Probabilistic Gradient Estimation

abstract: We present You Only Cut Once (YOCO) for performing data augmentations. YOCO cuts one image into two pieces and performs data augmentations individually within each piece. Applying YOCO improves the diversity of the augmentation per sample and encourages neural networks to recognize objects from partial information. YOCO enjoys the properties of parameter-free, easy usage, and boosting almost all augmentations for free. Thorough experiments are conducted to evaluate its effectiveness. We first demonstrate that YOCO can be seamlessly applied to varying data augmentations, neural network architectures, and brings performance gains on CIFAR and ImageNet classification tasks, sometimes surpassing conventional image-level augmentation by large margins. Moreover, we show YOCO benefits contrastive pre-training toward a more powerful representation that can be better transferred to multiple downstream tasks. Finally, we study a number of variants of YOCO and empirically analyze the performance for respective settings.

paragraphs: You Only Cut Once, or YOCO, changes how an image augmentation is applied. It splits an image into two pieces and augments each piece individually. This gives each training sample more varied transformations and encourages a network to recognize objects when only part of their visual information is available.

The method is parameter-free and designed to work easily with existing augmentations. Its main contribution is a simple change in the level at which those operations act: separate image regions can receive their own augmentation. The authors evaluate this idea across different augmentation methods and neural network architectures, reporting classification improvements on CIFAR and ImageNet, sometimes by large margins.

YOCO also benefits contrastive pre-training, producing representations that transfer more effectively to multiple downstream tasks in the experiments. The paper studies several variants and analyzes their performance under different settings. Together, these findings show that the way an augmentation is distributed within an image can matter, and that a single cut can improve both direct classification training and representation learning.
summary.tldr: YOCO improves image augmentation by cutting each image in two and independently augmenting its pieces.

title: You Only Cut Once: Boosting Data Augmentation with a Single Cut

abstract: We implement training of neural networks in secure multi-party computation (MPC) using quantization commonly used in said setting. We are the first to present an MNIST classifier purely trained in MPC that comes within 0.2 percent of the accuracy of the same convolutional neural network trained via plaintext computation. More concretely, we have trained a network with two convolutional and two dense layers to 99.2% accuracy in 3.5 hours (under one hour for 99% accuracy). We have also implemented AlexNet for CIFAR-10, which converges in a few hours. We develop novel protocols for exponentiation and inverse square root. Finally, we present experiments in a range of MPC security models for up to ten parties, both with honest and dishonest majority as well as semi-honest and malicious security.

paragraphs: This paper implements neural-network training within secure multi-party computation, using quantization suited to that setting. The work addresses whether training performed entirely through secure computation can achieve accuracy close to ordinary plaintext training. It combines complete network implementations with new protocols for mathematical operations needed by the training process.

For MNIST, the authors train a network with two convolutional and two dense layers to 99.2% accuracy in 3.5 hours, reaching 99% in under an hour. They report an accuracy gap within 0.2 percent of the same network trained in plaintext and claim the first entirely MPC-trained MNIST classifier to reach that proximity. They also implement AlexNet for CIFAR-10, which converges within a few hours.

The protocol contributions cover exponentiation and inverse square root. Experiments include up to ten parties across honest-majority and dishonest-majority settings, with both semi-honest and malicious security. This range connects the training demonstration to multiple MPC security models, while the reported timings and accuracies establish concrete feasibility for the evaluated networks.
summary.tldr: Quantized secure multi-party training achieves near-plaintext MNIST accuracy and supports neural-network training across several MPC security models.

title: Secure Quantized Training for Deep Learning

abstract: Recently, the standard ResNet-20 network was successfully implemented on the fully homomorphic encryption scheme, residue number system variant Cheon-Kim-Kim-Song (RNS-CKKS) scheme using bootstrapping, but the implementation lacks practicality due to high latency and low security level. To improve the performance, we first minimize total bootstrapping runtime using multiplexed parallel convolution that collects sparse output data for multiple channels compactly. We also propose the imaginary-removing bootstrapping to prevent the deep neural networks from catastrophic divergence during approximate ReLU operations. In addition, we optimize level consumptions and use lighter and tighter parameters. Simulation results show that we have 4.67x lower inference latency and 134x less amortized runtime (runtime per image) for ResNet-20 compared to the state-of-the-art previous work, and we achieve standard 128-bit security. Furthermore, we successfully implement ResNet-110 with high accuracy on the RNS-CKKS scheme for the first time.

paragraphs: This paper improves deep convolutional network inference under fully homomorphic encryption using the RNS-CKKS scheme. A previous implementation had demonstrated ResNet-20 with bootstrapping, but high latency and a low security level limited its practicality. The authors target computational cost and numerical stability while achieving standard 128-bit security.

Their multiplexed parallel convolution packs sparse outputs from multiple channels compactly to reduce total bootstrapping time. They also introduce imaginary-removing bootstrapping to prevent catastrophic divergence during approximate ReLU operations. Additional changes optimize level consumption and use lighter, tighter parameters, addressing several interacting costs of running deep networks in the encrypted setting.

Simulation results report 4.67-fold lower inference latency and 134-fold lower runtime per image for ResNet-20 relative to the previous state of the art. These measure different aspects of efficiency: latency and amortized processing cost. The authors also report the first successful high-accuracy ResNet-110 implementation on RNS-CKKS. The findings demonstrate progress in both the efficiency and supported depth of encrypted neural inference.
summary.tldr: Compact parallel convolutions and improved bootstrapping reduce encrypted ResNet inference costs while achieving 128-bit security.

title: Low-Complexity Deep Convolutional Neural Networks on Fully Homomorphic Encryption Using Multiplexed Parallel Convolutions

abstract: The success of deep learning ignited interest in whether the brain learns hierarchical representations using gradient-based learning. However, current biologically plausible methods for gradient-based credit assignment in deep neural networks need infinitesimally small feedback signals, which is problematic in biologically realistic noisy environments and at odds with experimental evidence in neuroscience showing that top-down feedback can significantly influence neural activity. Building upon deep feedback control (DFC), a recently proposed credit assignment method, we combine strong feedback influences on neural activity with gradient-based learning and show that this naturally leads to a novel view on neural network optimization. Instead of gradually changing the network weights towards configurations with low output loss, weight updates gradually minimize the amount of feedback required from a controller that drives the network to the supervised output label. Moreover, we show that the use of strong feedback in DFC allows learning forward and feedback connections simultaneously, using learning rules fully local in space and time. We complement our theoretical results with experiments on standard computer-vision benchmarks, showing competitive performance to backpropagation as well as robustness to noise. Overall, our work presents a fundamentally novel view of learning as control minimization, while sidestepping biologically unrealistic assumptions.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how deep networks might learn through mechanisms compatible with strong feedback between neural layers. Existing biologically motivated credit-assignment methods often require extremely weak feedback signals. The authors argue that this requirement is problematic in noisy settings and conflicts with evidence that top-down feedback can substantially change neural activity.

Building on deep feedback control, they let a controller drive network activity toward the supervised target. Learning then changes the weights to reduce how much feedback the controller must supply. This reframes optimization as minimizing the control needed to produce the desired output. The authors also show that strong feedback permits simultaneous learning of forward and feedback connections using rules local in both space and time.

Experiments on standard computer-vision benchmarks show performance competitive with backpropagation and robustness to noise. Alongside the theoretical analysis, these results support control minimization as an alternative account of credit assignment. The contribution concerns a learning mechanism that accommodates substantial feedback while retaining gradient-based learning and local updates.
summary.tldr: Strong-feedback learning can train networks by reducing the control needed to reach target outputs, using local learning rules.

title: Minimizing Control for Credit Assignment with Strong Feedback

abstract: The success of deep neural networks greatly relies on the availability of large amounts of high-quality annotated data, which however are difficult or expensive to obtain. The resulting labels may be class imbalanced, noisy or human biased. It is challenging to learn unbiased classification models from imperfectly annotated datasets, on which we usually suffer from overfitting or underfitting. In this work, we thoroughly investigate the popular softmax loss and margin-based loss, and offer a feasible approach to tighten the generalization error bound by maximizing the minimal sample margin. We further derive the optimality condition for this purpose, which indicates how the class prototypes should be anchored. Motivated by theoretical analysis, we propose a simple yet effective method, namely prototype-anchored learning (PAL), which can be easily incorporated into various learning-based classification schemes to handle imperfect annotation. We verify the effectiveness of PAL on class-imbalanced learning and noise-tolerant learning by extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Training labels can be imbalanced, incorrect, or influenced by human bias, making it difficult to learn a classifier that generalizes well. This paper investigates how the geometry encouraged by common classification losses can help with imperfect annotations. Its analysis examines both softmax loss and losses based on classification margins.

The authors identify maximizing the smallest sample margin as a feasible way to tighten a generalization-error bound. They then derive an optimality condition that specifies how class prototypes should be anchored. This connects the placement of class representatives to the margin of the least-separated sample, providing a theoretical motivation for controlling prototype geometry during learning.

The resulting method, prototype-anchored learning or PAL, can be incorporated into various classification schemes. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets verify its effectiveness for class-imbalanced and noise-tolerant learning. Although the motivation includes several forms of annotation imperfection, those two settings are the explicit experimental focus. The contribution links an analysis of generalization bounds to a practical method for shaping class prototypes under difficult labeling conditions.
summary.tldr: Prototype-anchored learning uses margin-based theory to position class prototypes and improve classification with imbalanced or noisy labels.

title: Prototype-Anchored Learning for Learning with Imperfect Annotations

abstract: Outlier-robust principal component analysis (ORPCA) has been broadly applied in scientific discovery in the last decades. In this paper, we study online ORPCA, an important variant that addresses the practical challenge that the data points arrive in a sequential manner and the goal is to recover the underlying subspace of the clean data with one pass of the data. Our main contribution is the first provable algorithm that enjoys comparable recovery guarantee to the best known batch algorithm, while significantly improving upon the state-of-the-art online ORPCA algorithms. The core technique is a robust version of the residual norm which, informally speaking, leverages not only the importance of a data point, but also how likely it behaves as an outlier.
originalAbstract: Outlier-robust principal component analysis (ORPCA) has been broadly applied in scientific discovery in the last decades. In this paper, we study online ORPCA, an important variant that addresses the practical challenge that the data points arrive in a sequential manner and the goal is to recover the underlying subspace of the clean data with one pass of the data. Our main contribution is the first provable algorithm that enjoys comparable recovery guarantee to the best known batch algorithm, while significantly improving upon the state-of-the-art online ORPCA algorithms. The core technique is a robust version of the residual norm which, informally speaking, leverages not only the importance of a data point, but also how likely it behaves as an outlier.

paragraphs: Outlier-robust principal component analysis seeks to recover the underlying subspace of clean data despite the presence of outliers. The online setting adds a practical constraint: examples arrive sequentially, and the algorithm must recover that subspace with only one pass through the data. This changes what information is available while making processing decisions.

The paper's central technique is a robust version of the residual norm. Informally, it considers both how important a data point is and how likely it is to behave as an outlier. This combination is useful because a point's relevance to subspace recovery must be considered alongside the possibility that it represents contamination.

The authors provide a provable online algorithm with a recovery guarantee comparable to the best known batch algorithm, while substantially improving on previous online methods. The comparison concerns recovery guarantees, bringing the stated reliability of one-pass processing closer to that of methods operating on a batch. The contribution centers on this theoretical result and the robust residual-based sampling technique enabling it.
summary.tldr: Robust residual-based sampling gives a one-pass outlier-robust PCA algorithm with recovery guarantees comparable to the best known batch method.

title: Residual-Based Sampling for Online Outlier-Robust PCA

abstract: Deep neural networks have been shown vulnerable to adversarial examples. Even though many defense methods have been proposed to enhance the robustness, it is still a long way toward providing an attack-free method to build a trustworthy machine learning system. In this paper, instead of enhancing the robustness, we take the investigator’s perspective and propose a new framework to trace the first compromised model copy in a forensic investigation manner. Specifically, we focus on the following setting: the machine learning service provider provides model copies for a set of customers. However, one of the customers conducted adversarial attacks to fool the system. Therefore, the investigator’s objective is to identify the first compromised copy by collecting and analyzing evidence from only available adversarial examples. To make the tracing viable, we design a random mask watermarking mechanism to differentiate adversarial examples from different copies. First, we propose a tracing approach in the data-limited case where the original example is also available. Then, we design a data-free approach to identify the adversary without accessing the original example. Finally, the effectiveness of our proposed framework is evaluated by extensive experiments with different model architectures, adversarial attacks, and datasets.

To make copies distinguishable through that evidence, the authors introduce random-mask watermarking. The mechanism is designed to differentiate adversarial examples associated with different model copies. Its role is to establish a traceable connection between an attack artifact and the distributed copy involved, supporting investigation after an attack has occurred.

The paper develops two tracing approaches for different evidence conditions. One uses the original, unmodified example alongside the adversarial example; the other works without access to that original input. Experiments spanning model architectures, attack methods, and datasets evaluate the framework's effectiveness. The contribution is an attribution capability within the model-distribution setting: it helps identify a compromised copy without requiring the tracing mechanism itself to prevent adversarial attacks.
summary.tldr: Random-mask watermarks enable forensic tracing of a compromised model copy from adversarial-example evidence.

title: Identification of the Adversary from a Single Adversarial Example

abstract: In collaborative learning with streaming data, nodes (e.g., organizations) jointly and continuously learn a machine learning (ML) model by sharing the latest model updates computed from their latest streaming data. For the more resourceful nodes to be willing to share their model updates, they need to be fairly incentivized. This paper explores an incentive design that guarantees fairness so that nodes receive rewards commensurate to their contributions. Our approach leverages an explore-then-exploit formulation to estimate the nodes’ contributions (i.e., exploration) for realizing our theoretically guaranteed fair incentives (i.e., exploitation). However, we observe a "rich get richer" phenomenon arising from the existing approaches to guarantee fairness and it discourages the participation of the less resourceful nodes. To remedy this, we additionally preserve asymptotic equality, i.e., less resourceful nodes achieve equal performance eventually to the more resourceful/“rich” nodes. We empirically demonstrate in two settings with real-world streaming data: federated online incremental learning and federated reinforcement learning, that our proposed approach outperforms existing baselines in fairness and learning performance while remaining competitive in preserving equality.

Fairness concerns how rewards reflect contributions, while asymptotic equality concerns the learning performance participants ultimately reach.

The authors evaluate the approach using real-world streaming data in federated online incremental learning and federated reinforcement learning. It outperforms the compared baselines in fairness and learning performance while remaining competitive in preserving equality. These results support designing contribution-sensitive incentives together with a mechanism that keeps resource differences from determining permanent performance differences.
summary.tldr: The method rewards collaborative-learning contributions fairly while preserving eventual performance equality for less resourceful participants.

title: Fair yet Asymptotically Equal Collaborative Learning

abstract: We study the robust interpolation problem of arbitrary data distributions supported on a bounded space and propose a two-fold law of robustness. Robust interpolation refers to the problem of interpolating $n$ noisy training data points in $R^d$ by a Lipschitz function. Although this problem has been well understood when the samples are drawn from an isoperimetry distribution, much remains unknown concerning its performance under generic or even the worst-case distributions. We prove a Lipschitzness lower bound $\Omega(\sqrt{n/p})$ of the interpolating neural network with $p$ parameters on arbitrary data distributions. With this result, we validate the law of robustness conjecture in prior work by Bubeck, Li and Nagaraj on two-layer neural networks with polynomial weights. We then extend our result to arbitrary interpolating approximators and prove a Lipschitzness lower bound $\Omega(n^{1/d})$ for robust interpolation. Our results demonstrate a two-fold law of robustness: a) we show the potential benefit of overparametrization for smooth data interpolation when $n=poly(d)$, and b) we disprove the potential existence of an $O(1)$-Lipschitz robust interpolating function when $n=\exp(\omega(d))$.

paragraphs: This paper asks how smoothly a model can fit noisy training examples exactly. Smoothness is measured through a Lipschitz constant: larger values permit greater changes in predictions between nearby inputs. Earlier understanding relied on a particular distributional property called isoperimetry. The authors instead study arbitrary data distributions supported on a bounded space.

For a neural network with p parameters fitting n examples, they prove a Lipschitz lower bound of order square root of n/p. This establishes a constraint on how smooth an interpolating network can be and validates a prior conjecture for two-layer networks with polynomial weights. Increasing parameter count can relax this particular constraint.

They also establish a lower bound of order n raised to 1/d for arbitrary interpolating approximators in dimension d. Together, the results identify two regimes: overparameterization may help smooth interpolation when sample size is polynomial in dimension, while a constant Lipschitz bound becomes impossible when sample size grows as exp(ω(d)). The benefit of extra parameters therefore coexists with a broader distribution-independent obstruction.
summary.tldr: Two lower bounds reveal when extra parameters may help smooth interpolation and when sample growth rules out constant-Lipschitz interpolation.

title: A Law of Robustness beyond Isoperimetry

abstract: Combinatorial optimization (CO) on the graph is a crucial but challenging research topic. Recent quantum algorithms provide a new perspective for solving CO problems and have the potential to demonstrate quantum advantage. Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a well-known quantum heuristic for CO constructed by a parametric quantum circuit. However, QAOA is originally designed for unconstrained problems and the circuit parameters and solutions are jointly solved with time-consuming iterations. In this paper, we propose a novel quantum neural network (QNN) for learning CO problems in a supervised manner to achieve better and faster results. We focus on the Quadratic Assignment Problem (QAP) with matching constraints and the node permutation invariance property. To this end, a quantum neural network called QAP-QNN is devised to translate the QAP into a constrained vertex classification task. Moreover, we study two QAP tasks: Graph Matching and Traveling Salesman Problem on TorchQauntum simulators, and empirically show the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: Quantum approaches offer a possible route to solving difficult combinatorial optimization problems. However, the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm was originally designed for unconstrained problems and jointly searches for circuit parameters and solutions through time-consuming iterations. This paper explores supervised quantum learning as an alternative for problems with explicit constraints.

The proposed QAP-QNN targets the quadratic assignment problem, accounting for matching constraints and the requirement that relabeling graph nodes should not change the underlying problem. It translates the optimization problem into constrained vertex classification. This reformulation lets a quantum neural network learn the task in a supervised manner while incorporating the structure that valid assignments must respect.

The authors evaluate graph matching and the Traveling Salesman Problem using TorchQuantum simulators and report empirical evidence of effectiveness. The contribution is a quantum-learning formulation for constrained optimization and a demonstration on two tasks. The evidence is simulation-based; the abstract presents quantum advantage as a potential motivation rather than an achieved experimental result.
summary.tldr: QAP-QNN reframes constrained quadratic assignment as supervised quantum vertex classification and demonstrates effectiveness in simulation.

title: Towards Quantum Machine Learning for Constrained Combinatorial Optimization: a Quantum QAP Solver

abstract: Federated Semi-supervised Learning (FedSSL) has emerged as a new paradigm for allowing distributed clients to collaboratively train a machine learning model over scarce labeled data and abundant unlabeled data. However, existing works for FedSSL rely on a closed-world assumption that all local training data and global testing data are from seen classes observed in the labeled dataset. It is crucial to go one step further: adapting FL models to an open-world setting, where unseen classes exist in the unlabeled data. In this paper, we propose a novel Fed erated o pen-world S emi- S upervised L earning ( FedoSSL ) framework, which can solve the key challenge in distributed and open-world settings, i.e., the biased training process for heterogeneously distributed unseen classes. Specifically, since the advent of a certain unseen class depends on a client basis, the locally unseen classes (exist in multiple clients) are likely to receive differentiated superior aggregation effects than the globally unseen classes (exist only in one client). We adopt an uncertainty-aware suppressed loss to alleviate the biased training between locally unseen and globally unseen classes. Besides, we enable a calibration module supplementary to the global aggregation to avoid potential conflicting knowledge transfer caused by inconsistent data distribution among different clients. The proposed FedoSSL can be easily adapted to state-of-the-art FL methods, which is also validated via extensive experiments on benchmarks and real-world datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and CINIC-10).

paragraphs: Federated semi-supervised learning combines limited labeled data with abundant unlabeled data across clients. Existing approaches often assume that every class appears in the labeled set. FedoSSL addresses an open-world setting, where unlabeled examples can belong to previously unseen classes and their distribution differs across clients.

The paper identifies a resulting training imbalance. An unseen class present on several clients can receive stronger aggregation benefits than one present on only a single client. The authors call these locally unseen and globally unseen classes, respectively. Their uncertainty-aware suppressed loss is designed to reduce the unequal training effects between these groups.

The contribution is to make the distribution of unseen classes across clients an explicit training concern, addressing both unequal aggregation benefits and conflicts in transferred knowledge.
summary.tldr: FedoSSL addresses uneven learning of unseen classes across federated clients through uncertainty-aware loss suppression and aggregation calibration.

title: Towards Unbiased Training in Federated Open-world Semi-supervised Learning

abstract: While graph neural networks (GNNs) dominate the state-of-the-art for exploring graphs in real-world applications, they have been shown to be vulnerable to a growing number of privacy attacks. For instance, link stealing is a well-known membership inference attack (MIA) on edges that infers the presence of an edge in a GNN’s training graph. Recent studies on independent and identically distributed data (e.g., images) have empirically demonstrated that individuals from different groups suffer from different levels of privacy risks to MIAs, i.e., uneven vulnerability. However, theoretical evidence of such uneven vulnerability is missing. In this paper, we first present theoretical evidence of the uneven vulnerability of GNNs to link stealing attacks, which lays the foundation for demystifying such uneven risks among different groups of edges. We further demonstrate a group-based attack paradigm to expose the practical privacy harm to GNN users derived from the uneven vulnerability of edges. Finally, we empirically validate the existence of obvious uneven vulnerability on nine real-world datasets (e.g., about 25% AUC difference between different groups in the Credit graph). Compared with existing methods, the outperformance of our group-based attack paradigm confirms that customising different strategies for different groups results in more effective privacy attacks.

paragraphs: A link-stealing attack tries to determine whether an edge was present in the graph used to train a graph neural network. This paper investigates whether different groups of edges face different levels of exposure. That question matters because an overall attack score can leave substantial differences in privacy risk between groups unexamined.

The authors provide theoretical evidence that vulnerability to link stealing is uneven across edge groups. They also develop an attack approach that customizes its strategy for different groups. This connects the theoretical observation to a practical consequence: an attacker can exploit those differences instead of applying the same strategy to every edge.

The group-based approach also outperforms existing attack methods in the evaluation. Together, these findings show that unequal exposure is both measurable and useful to attackers, making group differences relevant to assessing graph privacy.
summary.tldr: The paper shows that edge groups face unequal link-stealing risks and that attackers can exploit those differences.

title: Demystifying Uneven Vulnerability of Link Stealing Attacks against Graph Neural Networks

abstract: On a variety of tasks, the performance of neural networks predictably improves with training time, dataset size and model size across many orders of magnitude. This phenomenon is known as a neural scaling law. Of fundamental importance is the compute-optimal scaling law, which reports the performance as a function of units of compute when choosing model sizes optimally. We analyze a random feature model trained with gradient descent as a solvable model of network training and generalization. This reproduces many observations about neural scaling laws. First, our model makes a prediction about why the scaling of performance with training time and with model size have different power law exponents. Consequently, the theory predicts an asymmetric compute-optimal scaling rule where the number of training steps are increased faster than model parameters, consistent with recent empirical observations. Second, it has been observed that early in training, networks converge to their infinite-width dynamics at a rate $1/\text{width}$ but at late time exhibit a rate $\text{width}^{-c}$, where $c$ depends on the structure of the architecture and task. We show that our model exhibits this behavior. Lastly, our theory shows how the gap between training and test loss can gradually build up over time due to repeated reuse of data.

paragraphs: Neural scaling laws describe how prediction performance changes as training time, data, and model size increase. This paper studies these relationships through a random feature model trained with gradient descent. Because the model can be analyzed mathematically, it provides a way to connect observed scaling patterns to the dynamics of learning.

The analysis predicts why performance can improve with different power law exponents for training time and model size. This difference leads to an asymmetric prescription for allocating computation: increase training steps faster than the number of model parameters. The prediction is consistent with recent empirical observations, rather than establishing a universal allocation rule for every neural network.

The model also reproduces a change in how finite networks approach infinite-width behavior between early and late training. Finally, it explains how repeatedly using the same data can gradually widen the gap between training and test loss. Together, these results link resource allocation and generalization within one tractable account of training.
summary.tldr: A solvable training model explains several neural scaling patterns and predicts increasing training steps faster than model size when allocating compute.

title: A Dynamical Model of Neural Scaling Laws

abstract: Recently, a noticeable trend has emerged in developing pre-trained foundation models in the domains of CV and NLP. However, for molecular pre-training, there lacks a universal model capable of effectively applying to various categories of molecular tasks, since existing prevalent pre-training methods exhibit effectiveness for specific types of downstream tasks. Furthermore, the lack of profound understanding of existing pre-training methods, including 2D graph masking, 2D-3D contrastive learning, and 3D denoising, hampers the advancement of molecular foundation models. In this work, we provide a unified comprehension of existing pre-training methods through the lens of contrastive learning. Thus their distinctions lie in clustering different views of molecules, which is shown beneficial to specific downstream tasks. To achieve a complete and general-purpose molecular representation, we propose a novel pre-training framework, named UniCorn, that inherits the merits of the three methods, depicting molecular views in three different levels. SOTA performance across quantum, physicochemical, and biological tasks, along with comprehensive ablation study, validate the universality and effectiveness of UniCorn.

paragraphs: Molecular pretraining methods often work well for particular kinds of downstream tasks without providing a broadly useful representation. This paper examines three established approaches: masking parts of two-dimensional molecular graphs, contrasting two- and three-dimensional views, and denoising three-dimensional structures. It seeks both a shared explanation of these methods and a way to combine their strengths.

The authors interpret the methods through contrastive learning. In their account, the approaches differ in which molecular views they bring together into clusters, helping explain why each benefits particular tasks. UniCorn builds on this interpretation with a pretraining framework that represents molecular views at three levels and incorporates merits of all three approaches.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance across quantum, physicochemical, and biological tasks, supported by an extensive ablation study. Those results provide evidence for a representation useful across the tested task categories. The contribution is therefore both conceptual and practical: a unified perspective on existing pretraining objectives and a combined framework whose broader usefulness is evaluated across distinct molecular prediction settings.
summary.tldr: UniCorn unifies three molecular pretraining approaches through contrastive learning and achieves state-of-the-art results across several molecular task categories.

title: UniCorn: A Unified Contrastive Learning Approach for Multi-view Molecular Representation Learning

abstract: Understanding and controlling biasing effects in neural networks is crucial for ensuring accurate and fair model performance. In the context of classification problems, we provide a theoretical analysis demonstrating that the structure of a deep neural network (DNN) can condition the model to assign all predictions to the same class, even before the beginning of training, and in the absence of explicit biases. We prove that, besides dataset properties, the presence of this phenomenon, which we call Initial Guessing Bias (IGB), is influenced by model choices including dataset preprocessing methods, and architectural decisions, such as activation functions, max-pooling layers, and network depth. Our analysis of IGB provides information for architecture selection and model initialization. We also highlight theoretical consequences, such as the breakdown of node-permutation symmetry, the violation of self-averaging and the non-trivial effects that depth has on the phenomenon.

paragraphs: This paper shows theoretically that a classifier can favor a single class before training begins. A deep network’s structure can cause all its predictions to fall into the same class even without explicit biases. The authors call this phenomenon Initial Guessing Bias, emphasizing that a systematic preference can already exist at initialization.

The analysis identifies several factors that influence whether this behavior occurs. Dataset properties matter, but so do preprocessing choices, activation functions, max-pooling layers, and network depth. These findings connect the initial prediction pattern to concrete modeling decisions and provide information relevant to selecting architectures and initialization procedures.

The theory also identifies consequences involving node-permutation symmetry, self-averaging, and the effects of depth. In particular, the reported violation of self-averaging highlights that averaging behavior need not describe an individual network’s behavior in the expected way. Overall, the paper establishes that untrained classification behavior deserves analysis in its own right, because architecture and preprocessing can shape class preferences before any learning from labels occurs.
summary.tldr: Network architecture and preprocessing can make an untrained classifier assign every input to one class, even without explicit biases.

title: Initial Guessing Bias: How Untrained Networks Favor Some Classes

abstract: The Weisfeiler–Leman algorithm (1-WL) is a well-studied heuristic for the graph isomorphism problem. Recently, the algorithm has played a prominent role in understanding the expressive power of message-passing graph neural networks (MPNNs) and being effective as a graph kernel. Despite its success, the 1-WL faces challenges in distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs, leading to the development of more expressive MPNN and kernel architectures. However, the relationship between enhanced expressivity and improved generalization performance remains unclear. Here, we show that an architecture’s expressivity offers limited insights into its generalization performance when viewed through graph isomorphism. Moreover, we focus on augmenting 1-WL and MPNNs with subgraph information and employ classical margin theory to investigate the conditions under which an architecture’s increased expressivity aligns with improved generalization performance. In addition, we introduce variations of expressive 1-WL-based kernel and MPNN architectures with provable generalization properties. Our empirical study confirms the validity of our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Graph-learning architectures are often compared by their ability to distinguish graphs with different structures. The Weisfeiler–Leman procedure, especially 1-WL, is a standard reference for this kind of expressivity. This paper asks how much such distinctions actually reveal about generalization, finding that expressivity viewed through graph isomorphism gives only limited insight into predictive performance.

The authors examine versions of 1-WL and message-passing graph neural networks augmented with subgraph information. They use classical margin theory to study conditions under which greater expressivity is associated with improved generalization. This shifts attention toward how the resulting representations support separation in a learning problem, alongside which graphs they can distinguish.

The paper also introduces expressive 1-WL-based kernel and neural architectures with provable generalization properties. An empirical study supports the theoretical findings. The overall result is a more conditional account of why additional graph information can help: increased expressive power becomes informative when connected to the generalization conditions studied, rather than serving as a sufficient performance ranking by itself.
summary.tldr: Margin-based analysis identifies conditions linking richer graph representations to better generalization, beyond expressivity measured by graph distinction alone.

title: Weisfeiler-Leman at the margin: When more expressivity matters

abstract: Many settings in machine learning require the selection of a rotation representation. However, choosing a suitable representation from the many available options is challenging. This paper acts as a survey and guide through rotation representations. We walk through their properties that harm or benefit deep learning with gradient-based optimization. By consolidating insights from rotation-based learning, we provide a comprehensive overview of learning functions with rotation representations. We provide guidance on selecting representations based on whether rotations are in the model’s input or output and whether the data primarily comprises small angles.

This paper serves as a survey and practical guide to making that choice for models trained with gradient-based optimization.

The authors consolidate insights from rotation-based learning and organize them around properties that can help or hinder optimization. Their subject is learning functions that involve rotations, so the role of the representation extends beyond simply recording an orientation. The guide connects representation properties to the conditions under which a model must learn from or predict rotations.

Its recommendations distinguish between rotations supplied as model inputs and rotations produced as model outputs. They also account for whether the data primarily contains small angles. These distinctions make the guidance conditional on the task and data. The paper's contribution is a consolidated basis for choosing a suitable representation, with attention to the specific way rotations enter the learning problem.
summary.tldr: This survey guides rotation-representation choices according to their optimization properties, their input or output role, and whether angles are mostly small.

title: Learning with 3D rotations, a hitchhiker’s guide to SO(3)

abstract: Monotonicity constraints are powerful regularizers in statistical modelling. They can support fairness in computer-aided decision making and increase plausibility in data-driven scientific models. The seminal min-max (MM) neural network architecture ensures monotonicity, but often gets stuck in undesired local optima during training because of partial derivatives being zero when computing extrema. We propose a simple modification of the MM network using strictly-increasing smooth minimum and maximum functions that alleviates this problem. The resulting smooth min-max (SMM) network module inherits the asymptotic approximation properties from the MM architecture. It can be used within larger deep learning systems trained end-to-end. The SMM module is conceptually simple and computationally less demanding than state-of-the-art neural networks for monotonic modelling. Our experiments show that this does not come with a loss in generalization performance compared to alternative neural and non-neural approaches.

They can help make scientific models more plausible and support fairness in automated decisions. Min-max neural networks guarantee monotonicity, but their minimum and maximum operations can produce zero derivatives that leave training stuck in undesirable local optima.

The paper replaces those extrema operations with smooth minimum and maximum functions that are strictly increasing. The resulting smooth min-max module alleviates the training problem while retaining the original architecture's asymptotic approximation properties. It can also be included in larger deep-learning systems and trained together with their other components.

The authors describe the module as conceptually simple and computationally cheaper than state-of-the-art neural approaches to monotonic modeling. Their experiments find that this reduced computational burden does not sacrifice generalization compared with the evaluated neural and non-neural alternatives. The contribution is therefore both architectural and practical: smoothing the operations improves trainability while preserving the useful function-approximation properties of the monotonic construction.
summary.tldr: Smooth min-max networks improve the trainability of monotonic models while retaining approximation properties and competitive generalization.

title: Smooth Min-Max Monotonic Networks

abstract: The alignment of language models with human preferences is vital for their application in real-world tasks. The problem is formulated as optimizing the model’s policy to maximize the expected reward that reflects human preferences with minimal deviation from the initial policy. While considered as a straightforward solution, reinforcement learning (RL) suffers from high variance in policy updates, which impedes efficient policy improvement. Recently, direct preference optimization (DPO) was proposed to directly optimize the policy from preference data. However, we show that DPO derived based on the optimal solution of the problem leads to a compromised mean-seeking approximation of the optimal solution in practice. In this paper, we propose efficient exact optimization (EXO) of the alignment objective. EXO is guaranteed to optimize in the same direction as RL algorithms asymptotically for arbitrary policy parametrization. This leads to the same mode-seeking solution, while enables efficient optimization by circumventing the complexities of RL. We also compare our method to DPO with both theoretical and empirical analyses, and further demonstrate the advantages of our method over existing approaches on realistic human preference data. Code is available at https://github.com/haozheji/exact-optimization.

paragraphs: Language-model alignment is formulated here as increasing expected preference-based reward while limiting departure from the initial policy. Reinforcement learning directly addresses that objective but can suffer from high-variance updates. The paper examines whether a more direct optimization procedure can preserve the objective's intended solution while avoiding the complexities that make reinforcement learning inefficient.

The authors argue that practical direct preference optimization leads to a mean-seeking approximation of the optimal solution. They propose efficient exact optimization, or EXO, to obtain the mode-seeking behavior associated with reinforcement learning. For arbitrary policy parameterizations, EXO is guaranteed asymptotically to optimize in the same direction as reinforcement learning algorithms.

That asymptotic qualification matters: the directional guarantee describes the stated limiting behavior rather than an unconditional claim about every finite update. The paper compares EXO with DPO theoretically and empirically, and reports advantages over existing methods on realistic human-preference data. Its contribution is to connect efficient preference optimization more closely to the original alignment objective, rather than relying only on the fact that a procedure can be derived from an optimal-policy expression.
summary.tldr: EXO efficiently optimizes language-model alignment with an asymptotic guarantee of matching reinforcement learning's optimization direction and mode-seeking solution.

title: Towards Efficient Exact Optimization of Language Model Alignment

abstract: Given any algorithm for convex optimization that uses exact first-order information (i.e., function values and subgradients), we show how to use such an algorithm to solve the problem with access to inexact first-order information. This is done in a “black-box” manner without knowledge of the internal workings of the algorithm. This complements previous work that considers the performance of specific algorithms like (accelerated) gradient descent with inexact information. In particular, our results apply to a wider range of algorithms beyond variants of gradient descent, e.g., projection-free methods, cutting-plane methods, or any other first-order methods formulated in the future. Further, they also apply to algorithms that handle structured nonconvexities like mixed-integer decision variables.

paragraphs: Optimization algorithms often assume that each query returns an exact function value and an exact subgradient, which supplies directional information for improving a solution. This paper asks how an algorithm built around those exact answers can still solve an optimization problem when the available answers are inexact. Its contribution is a general transfer theorem connecting these two settings.

The proposed conversion treats the original algorithm as a black box: it does not require access to, or knowledge of, the algorithm’s internal workings. This changes the scope of the analysis. Instead of separately studying how errors affect individual methods such as gradient descent, the result provides a way to reuse a much broader class of algorithms.

The stated coverage includes projection-free methods, cutting-plane methods, and future methods using first-order information. The results also extend to algorithms handling certain structured nonconvexities, including mixed-integer decision variables. The significance is therefore methodological: a general mechanism makes algorithms designed for exact information applicable when information is inexact, across the problem classes covered by the theorem.
summary.tldr: A black-box transfer theorem adapts algorithms using exact first-order information to optimization with inexact information.

title: A Universal Transfer Theorem for Convex Optimization Algorithms Using Inexact First-order Oracles

abstract: Most reinforcement learning practitioners evaluate their policies with online Monte Carlo estimators for either hyperparameter tuning or testing different algorithmic design choices, where the policy is repeatedly executed in the environment to get the average outcome. Such massive interactions with the environment are prohibitive in many scenarios. In this paper, we propose novel methods that improve the data efficiency of online Monte Carlo estimators while maintaining their unbiasedness. We first propose a tailored closed-form behavior policy that provably reduces the variance of an online Monte Carlo estimator. We then design efficient algorithms to learn this closed-form behavior policy from previously collected offline data. Theoretical analysis is provided to characterize how the behavior policy learning error affects the amount of reduced variance. Compared with previous works, our method achieves better empirical performance in a broader set of environments, with fewer requirements for offline data.

paragraphs: Evaluating a reinforcement learning policy often means running it repeatedly and averaging the outcomes. These online Monte Carlo estimates are useful for comparing design choices, but acquiring enough environment interactions can be costly. This paper seeks more data-efficient evaluation while preserving unbiasedness, so the estimator still targets the policy’s actual expected performance.

The authors derive a tailored behavior policy, which controls how evaluation data is collected, in closed form. They prove that this policy reduces estimator variance, then develop algorithms to learn it from previously collected offline data. The offline information therefore helps shape new interactions, connecting existing experience to the efficiency of subsequent online evaluation.

The theory also characterizes how errors in learning the behavior policy affect the amount of variance reduction. That connection matters because practical use relies on a learned version of the ideal policy. Experiments show better performance than previous methods across a broader set of environments, with fewer offline-data requirements. Together, these results support designing data collection specifically for accurate, efficient policy evaluation.
summary.tldr: Offline data helps learn a behavior policy that reduces the variance of unbiased online policy evaluation.

title: Efficient Policy Evaluation with Offline Data Informed Behavior Policy Design

abstract: Humans are able to segment images effortlessly without supervision using perceptual grouping. Here, we propose a counter-intuitive computational approach to solving unsupervised perceptual grouping and segmentation: that they arise because of neural noise, rather than in spite of it. We (1) mathematically demonstrate that under realistic assumptions, neural noise can be used to separate objects from each other; (2) that adding noise in a DNN enables the network to segment images even though it was never trained on any segmentation labels; and (3) that segmenting objects using noise results in segmentation performance that aligns with the perceptual grouping phenomena observed in humans, and is sample-efficient. We introduce the Good Gestalt (GG) datasets — six datasets designed to specifically test perceptual grouping, and show that our DNN models reproduce many important phenomena in human perception, such as illusory contours, closure, continuity, proximity, and occlusion. Finally, we (4) show that our model improves performance on our GG datasets compared to other tested unsupervised models by $24.9$%. Together, our results suggest a novel unsupervised segmentation method requiring few assumptions, a new explanation for the formation of perceptual grouping, and a novel potential benefit of neural noise.

paragraphs: This paper proposes that neural noise can help create perceptual grouping and image segmentation. Instead of treating noise solely as interference, the authors investigate whether it can supply information for separating objects. They mathematically show that this is possible under assumptions they describe as realistic, making the claim conditional on the setting of their analysis.

They also demonstrate that adding noise to a deep neural network enables image segmentation without training on segmentation labels. To examine how closely this behavior resembles human grouping, they introduce six Good Gestalt datasets. On the Good Gestalt datasets, the model improves segmentation performance by a reported 24.9% compared with the other unsupervised models tested. These results support noise as a useful ingredient in unsupervised segmentation and suggest a possible explanation for perceptual grouping. The proposed connection to human perception is an interpretation supported by the observed grouping behaviors, rather than a definitive account of how human vision works.
summary.tldr: Neural noise can enable segmentation without segmentation labels and reproduce several human perceptual grouping phenomena.

title: Latent Noise Segmentation: How Neural Noise Leads to the Emergence of Segmentation and Grouping

abstract: Despite the successes of large language models (LLMs), they exhibit significant drawbacks, particularly when processing long contexts. Their inference cost scales quadratically with respect to sequence length, making it expensive for deployment in some real-world text processing applications, such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Additionally, LLMs also exhibit the "distraction phenomenon", where irrelevant context in the prompt degrades output quality. To address these drawbacks, we propose a novel RAG prompting methodology, superposition prompting, which can be directly applied to pre-trained transformer-based LLMs without the need for fine-tuning. At a high level, superposition prompting allows the LLM to process input documents in parallel prompt paths, discarding paths once they are deemed irrelevant. We demonstrate the capability of our method to simultaneously enhance time efficiency across a variety of question-answering benchmarks using multiple pre-trained LLMs. Furthermore, our technique significantly improves accuracy when the retrieved context is large relative the context the model was trained on. For example, our approach facilitates a $93\times$ reduction in compute time while improving accuracy by $43%$ on the NaturalQuestions-Open dataset with the MPT-7B instruction-tuned model over naive RAG.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation supplies a language model with documents relevant to a question. Large retrieved contexts can increase computational cost and introduce irrelevant material that degrades answers. Superposition prompting addresses both issues through a prompting method that works with pretrained transformer language models without requiring fine-tuning.

The method organizes documents into parallel prompt paths. The model processes those paths and discards ones judged irrelevant, limiting continued processing of unhelpful context. This organization connects efficiency with relevance: reducing unnecessary document processing also addresses the distraction caused by material that does not help answer the question.

Across multiple language models and question-answering benchmarks, the authors demonstrate improved time efficiency. Accuracy improves substantially when retrieved context is large relative to the context used in training. In one reported example, MPT-7B on NaturalQuestions-Open uses 93 times less compute time while improving accuracy by 43% relative to naive retrieval-augmented generation. That example illustrates the potential size of the gains in a particular setting, alongside the broader evidence for efficiency improvements.
summary.tldr: Superposition prompting processes retrieved documents in parallel paths and drops irrelevant ones, improving RAG efficiency and accuracy without fine-tuning.

title: Superposition Prompting: Improving and Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation

abstract: Differentially private (DP) machine learning is considered the gold-standard solution for training a model from sensitive data while still preserving privacy. However, a major barrier to achieving this ideal is its sub-optimal privacy-accuracy trade-off, which is particularly visible in DP representation learning. Specifically, it has been shown that under modest privacy budgets, most models learn representations that are not significantly better than hand-crafted features. In this work, we show that effective DP representation learning can be done via image captioning and scaling up to internet-scale multimodal datasets. Through a series of engineering tricks, we successfully train a DP image captioner (DP-Cap) on a 233M subset of LAION-2B from scratch using a reasonable amount of computation, and obtaining unprecedented high-quality image features that can be used in a variety of downstream vision and vision-language tasks. For example, under a privacy budget of $\varepsilon=8$ for the LAION dataset, a linear classifier trained on top of learned DP-Cap features attains $65.8%$ accuracy on ImageNet-1K, considerably improving the previous SOTA of $56.5%$. Our work challenges the prevailing sentiment that high-utility DP representation learning cannot be achieved by training from scratch.

paragraphs: Differentially private training aims to learn from sensitive data while preserving privacy, but useful representations can be difficult to obtain under privacy constraints. The paper addresses this privacy–accuracy trade-off through image captioning. Its central idea is to learn visual features by training a private model to describe images at a very large scale.

The reported success combines the captioning objective with internet-scale multimodal training data.
summary.tldr: Training a differentially private image captioner from scratch at large scale produces substantially improved reusable visual features.

title: Differentially Private Representation Learning via Image Captioning

abstract: Learning dynamics from dissipative chaotic systems is notoriously difficult due to their inherent instability, as formalized by their positive Lyapunov exponents, which exponentially amplify errors in the learned dynamics. However, many of these systems exhibit ergodicity and an attractor: a compact and highly complex manifold, to which trajectories converge in finite-time, that supports an invariant measure, i.e., a probability distribution that is invariant under the action of the dynamics, which dictates the long-term statistical behavior of the system. In this work, we leverage this structure to propose a new framework that targets learning the invariant measure as well as the dynamics, in contrast with typical methods that only target the misfit between trajectories, which often leads to divergence as the trajectories’ length increases. We use our framework to propose a tractable and sample efficient objective that can be used with any existing learning objectives. Our Dynamics Stable Learning by Invariant Measure (DySLIM) objective enables model training that achieves better point-wise tracking and long-term statistical accuracy relative to other learning objectives. By targeting the distribution with a scalable regularization term, we hope that this approach can be extended to more complex systems exhibiting slowly-variant distributions, such as weather and climate models. Code to reproduce our experiments is available here: https://github.com/google-research/swirl-dynamics/tree/main/swirl_dynamics/projects/ergodic.

paragraphs: Chaotic systems amplify small errors exponentially, making learned trajectories increasingly difficult to keep accurate over time. Many dissipative chaotic systems nevertheless have stable long-term statistical structure: an attractor supports a probability distribution that remains unchanged under the dynamics. This invariant measure describes how the system behaves statistically even when individual trajectories are sensitive.

DySLIM trains a model to capture both the dynamics and this invariant distribution. The authors introduce a tractable, sample-efficient objective that can accompany existing training objectives. Its distributional regularization adds a target beyond matching trajectories, which can diverge as prediction sequences grow longer.

The authors report improvements in both point-by-point tracking and long-term statistical accuracy relative to other learning objectives. These findings suggest that matching persistent statistical structure can also help learned dynamics behave better over time. They further propose extending the approach to systems with slowly changing distributions, including weather and climate models; that extension is presented as a future possibility.
summary.tldr: DySLIM improves learned chaotic dynamics by training models to match both trajectories and the system's invariant probability distribution.

title: DySLIM: Dynamics Stable Learning by Invariant Measure for Chaotic Systems

abstract: Recently, it has been shown that transformers pre-trained on diverse datasets with multi-episode contexts can generalize to new reinforcement learning tasks in-context. A key limitation of previously proposed models is their reliance on a predefined action space size and structure. The introduction of a new action space often requires data re-collection and model re-training, which can be costly for some applications. In our work, we show that it is possible to mitigate this issue by proposing the Headless-AD model that, despite being trained only once, is capable of generalizing to discrete action spaces of variable size, semantic content and order. By experimenting with Bernoulli and contextual bandits, as well as a gridworld environment, we show that Headless-AD exhibits significant capability to generalize to action spaces it has never encountered, even outperforming specialized models trained for a specific set of actions on several environment configurations.

paragraphs: Transformers trained on contexts containing multiple episodes can adapt to new reinforcement-learning tasks through their context. However, earlier models often assume a fixed number of actions with a predefined structure. Changing the available actions can therefore require collecting new data and training the model again.

This paper introduces Headless-AD to reduce that dependence on a fixed action space. After one training process, the model can generalize to discrete action sets that differ in size, meaning, and order. These are separate forms of variation: the available choices can become more numerous, represent different behaviors, or appear in a different arrangement.

The authors evaluate Headless-AD on Bernoulli bandits, contextual bandits, and a gridworld. They report substantial ability to handle action spaces absent from training. In several environment configurations, it even outperforms specialized models trained for a particular action set. The findings support greater flexibility within the tested discrete-action settings, showing that changing the action set need not always require a separately trained model.
summary.tldr: Headless-AD generalizes after a single training process to unseen discrete action spaces with different sizes, meanings, and orderings.

title: In-Context Reinforcement Learning for Variable Action Spaces

abstract: In adversarial machine learning, neural networks suffer from a significant issue known as robust overfitting, where the robust test accuracy decreases over epochs (Rice et al., 2020). Recent research conducted by Xing et al., 2021;Xiao et al., 2022 has focused on studying the uniform stability of adversarial training. Their investigations revealed that SGD-based adversarial training fails to exhibit uniform stability, and the derived stability bounds align with the observed phenomenon of robust overfitting in experiments. This finding motivates us to develop uniformly stable algorithms specifically tailored for adversarial training. To this aim, we introduce Moreau envelope-$\mathcal{A}$ (ME-$\mathcal{A}$), a variant of the Moreau Envelope-type algorithm. We employ a Moreau envelope function to reframe the original problem as a min-min problem, separating the non-strong convexity and non-smoothness of the adversarial loss. Then, this approach alternates between solving the inner and outer minimization problems to achieve uniform stability without incurring additional computational overhead. In practical scenarios, we demonstrate the efficacy of ME-$\mathcal{A}$ in mitigating the issue of robust overfitting. Beyond its application in adversarial training, this represents a fundamental result in uniform stability analysis, as ME-$\mathcal{A}$ is the first algorithm to exhibit uniform stability for weakly-convex, non-smooth problems.

paragraphs: Adversarial training can suffer from robust overfitting: performance on adversarial test examples deteriorates as training continues. Earlier stability analyses connect this behavior to the lack of uniform stability in SGD-based adversarial training. This paper develops an algorithm designed to obtain that stability, addressing the optimization process behind the observed problem.

ME-A uses a Moreau envelope function to reformulate the objective as a problem with two nested minimizations. The reformulation separates the adversarial loss's non-smoothness from its lack of strong convexity. The algorithm alternates between the inner and outer minimization problems and achieves uniform stability without additional computational overhead, according to the paper.

Practical experiments demonstrate mitigation of robust overfitting. The theoretical contribution also extends beyond adversarial training: the authors identify ME-A as the first uniformly stable algorithm for weakly convex, non-smooth problems. The experimental finding concerns reducing robust overfitting, while the broader result concerns stability for this specified mathematical class of objectives; these are related but distinct contributions.
summary.tldr: ME-A uses a Moreau-envelope reformulation to achieve uniform stability for weakly convex, non-smooth optimization and mitigate robust overfitting.

title: Uniformly Stable Algorithms for Adversarial Training and Beyond

abstract: The diagonal of a model’s Fisher Information Matrix (the "Fisher") has frequently been used as a way to measure parameter sensitivity. Typically, the Fisher is estimated by computing the squared gradient of the model’s outputs with respect to its parameters, averaged over a few hundred or thousand examples — a process which incurs nontrivial computational costs. At the same time, adaptive gradient methods like the ubiquitous Adam optimizer compute a moving average of the squared gradient over the course of training. This paper therefore explores whether an approximation of the Fisher can be obtained "for free" by recycling the squared gradient accumulator that has already been computed over the course of training. Through a comprehensive set of experiments covering five applications of the Fisher, we demonstrate that the "Squisher" (Squared gradient accumulator as an approximation of the Fisher) consistently performs similarly to the Fisher while outperforming baseline methods. Additionally, we clarify the exact differences between the Squisher and the Fisher and provide empirical quantification of their respective impact.

Computing it typically requires averaging squared gradients over hundreds or thousands of examples. That additional calculation can be costly, even when the model has already undergone extensive training.

This paper asks whether training has already produced a useful substitute. Adaptive optimizers such as Adam maintain a moving average of squared gradients. The authors reuse that accumulator as an approximation called Squisher, potentially avoiding a separate pass to estimate the Fisher. The proposal turns an existing optimization statistic into a resource for other model-processing tasks.

The authors also clarify the exact differences between the two quantities and empirically measure the effects of those differences. The findings support reuse as a practical approximation in the tested applications, while retaining the distinction between an optimizer’s accumulated gradients and the Fisher itself.
summary.tldr: Squisher reuses an optimizer’s squared-gradient accumulator as a low-cost Fisher approximation with similar performance across five tested applications.

title: Fishers for Free? Approximating the Fisher Information Matrix by Recycling the Squared Gradient Accumulator

abstract: Time-series Generation (TSG) is a prominent research area with broad applications in simulations, data augmentation, and counterfactual analysis. While existing methods have shown promise in unconditional single-domain TSG, real-world applications demand for cross-domain approaches capable of controlled generation tailored to domain-specific constraints and instance-level requirements. In this paper, we argue that text can provide semantic insights, domain information and instance-specific temporal patterns, to guide and improve TSG. We introduce “Text-Controlled TSG”, a task focused on generating realistic time series by incorporating textual descriptions. To address data scarcity in this setting, we propose a novel LLM-based Multi-Agent framework that synthesizes diverse, realistic text-to-TS datasets. Furthermore, we introduce Bridge, a hybrid text-controlled TSG framework that integrates semantic prototypes with text description for supporting domain-level guidance. This approach achieves state-of-the-art generation fidelity on 11 of 12 datasets, and improves controllability by up to 12% on MSE and 6% MAE compared to no text input generation, highlighting its potential for generating tailored time-series data.
