These findings support text as a useful control channel in the evaluated settings, with gains in both realism and adherence to requested characteristics.
summary.tldr: Bridge combines synthetic text–time-series training data with textual and prototype guidance to improve time-series realism and controllability.

title: BRIDGE: Bootstrapping Text to Control Time-Series Generation via Multi-Agent Iterative Optimization and Diffusion Modeling

abstract: Conversational Tabular Data Analysis, a collaboration between humans and machines, enables real-time data exploration for informed decision-making. The challenges and costs of collecting realistic conversational logs for tabular data analysis hinder comprehensive quantitative evaluation of Large Language Models (LLMs) in this task. To mitigate this issue, we introduce CoTA, a new benchmark to evaluate LLMs on conversational tabular data analysis. CoTA contains 1013 conversations, covering 4 practical scenarios: Normal, Action, Private, and Private Action. Notably, CoTA is constructed by an economical multi-agent environment, Decision Company, with few human efforts. This environment ensures efficiency and scalability of generating new conversational data. Our comprehensive study, conducted by data analysis experts, demonstrates that Decision Company is capable of producing diverse and high-quality data, laying the groundwork for efficient data annotation. We evaluate popular and advanced LLMs in CoTA, which highlights the challenges of conversational tabular data analysis. Furthermore, we propose Adaptive Conversation Reflection (ACR), a self-generated reflection strategy that guides LLMs to learn from successful histories. Experiments demonstrate that ACR can evolve LLMs into effective conversational data analysis agents, achieving a relative performance improvement of up to 35.14%.

The authors also introduce Adaptive Conversation Reflection, which generates reflections from successful conversation histories to guide subsequent behavior. Experiments report relative performance improvements of up to 35.14%. The findings suggest that learning from successful interactions can improve conversational analysis, while CoTA provides a way to measure those improvements.
summary.tldr: CoTA benchmarks conversational table analysis, and a reflection strategy improves evaluated language models by up to 35.14% relatively.

title: Are Large Language Models Ready for Multi-Turn Tabular Data Analysis?

abstract: This work presents a systematic investigation into the trustworthiness of explanations generated by self-interpretable graph neural networks (GNNs), revealing why models trained with different random seeds yield inconsistent explanations. We identify redundancy—resulting from weak conciseness constraints—as the root cause of both explanation inconsistency and its associated inaccuracy, ultimately hindering user trust and limiting GNN deployment in high-stakes applications. Our analysis demonstrates that redundancy is difficult to eliminate; however, a simple ensemble strategy can mitigate its detrimental effects. We validate our findings through extensive experiments across diverse datasets, model architectures, and self-interpretable GNN frameworks, providing a benchmark to guide future research on addressing redundancy and advancing GNN deployment in critical domains. Our code is available at https://github.com/ICDM-UESTC/TrustworthyExplanation.

paragraphs: Self-interpretable graph neural networks generate explanations as part of their modeling approach, but those explanations can change when training uses a different random seed. This paper systematically investigates that instability. The concern is consequential: an explanation is difficult to trust when repeated training produces inconsistent accounts of the model's decisions.

The authors identify redundancy arising from weak conciseness constraints as the root cause of both explanation inconsistency and associated inaccuracy. In this account, requiring an explanation to be concise is central to its reliability. Their analysis also finds that redundancy is difficult to remove, making a straightforward elimination strategy challenging.

A simple ensemble strategy nevertheless mitigates redundancy's harmful effects. Experiments span multiple datasets, architectures, and self-interpretable GNN frameworks, and the work provides a benchmark for further investigation. The contribution combines a diagnosis with a practical mitigation: built-in interpretability alone does not settle explanation quality, and evaluating redundancy and consistency can help assess whether the explanations support trustworthy use.
summary.tldr: Redundant explanations undermine self-interpretable GNNs, while a simple ensemble strategy can mitigate their inconsistency and inaccuracy.

title: Redundancy Undermines the Trustworthiness of Self-Interpretable GNNs

abstract: Model merging offers an effective way to integrate the capabilities of multiple fine-tuned models. However, the performance degradation of the merged model remains a challenge, particularly when none or few data are available. This paper first highlights the necessity of domain-specific data for model merging by proving that data-agnostic algorithms can have arbitrarily bad worst-case performances. Building on this theoretical insight, we explore the relationship between model merging and distillation, introducing a novel few-shot merging algorithm, ProDistill (Progressive Layer-wise Distillation). Unlike common belief that layer-wise training hurts performance, we show that layer-wise teacher-student distillation not only enhances the scalability but also improves model merging performance. We conduct extensive experiments to show that compared to existing few-shot merging methods,ProDistill achieves state-of-the-art performance, with up to 6.14% and 6.61% improvements in vision and NLU tasks. Furthermore, we extend the experiments to models with over 10B parameters, showcasing the exceptional scalability of ProDistill.

paragraphs: Model merging combines capabilities from multiple fine-tuned models, but the combined model can lose performance when little task data is available. This paper first establishes a worst-case result: merging algorithms that ignore data can perform arbitrarily badly. The result motivates using domain-specific examples to guide the merging process.

summary.tldr: ProDistill uses progressive layer-wise distillation and a few domain examples to improve model merging and scale beyond ten billion parameters.

title: Scalable Model Merging with Progressive Layer-wise Distillation

abstract: Safe offline reinforcement learning (RL), which aims to learn the safety-guaranteed policy without risky online interaction with environments, has attracted growing recent attention for safety-critical scenarios. However, existing approaches encounter out-of-distribution problems during the testing phase, which can result in potentially unsafe outcomes. This issue arises due to the infinite possible combinations of reward-related and cost-related states. In this work, we propose State Decoupling with Q-supervised Contrastive representation (SDQC), a novel framework that decouples the global observations into reward- and cost-related representations for decision-making, thereby improving the generalization capability for unfamiliar global observations. Compared with the classical representation learning methods, which typically require model-based estimation (e.g., bisimulation), we theoretically prove that our Q-supervised method generates a coarser representation while preserving the optimal policy, resulting in improved generalization performance. Experiments on DSRL benchmark problems provide compelling evidence that SDQC surpasses other baseline algorithms, especially for its exceptional ability to achieve almost zero violations in more than half of the tasks, while the state-of-the-art algorithm can only achieve the same level of success in a quarter of the tasks. Further, we demonstrate that SDQC possesses superior generalization ability when confronted with unseen environments.

paragraphs: Safe offline reinforcement learning aims to learn useful policies from existing data without risky online interaction. A challenge appears when testing presents unfamiliar combinations of reward-related and cost-related state information. SDQC addresses this by separating global observations into representations associated with reward and cost.

The framework uses Q-supervised contrastive representation learning to perform this separation. The authors theoretically show that their method produces a coarser representation while preserving the optimal policy, compared with classical representation approaches that typically require model-based estimation. This supports generalization by allowing a less detailed state representation to retain the distinctions needed for optimal decisions.

These results support state decoupling as a useful approach to unfamiliar observations, while the reported near-zero violations remain empirical outcomes rather than a claim of universal safety.
summary.tldr: SDQC separates reward and cost representations to improve safe offline RL generalization, achieving almost zero violations on more than half the evaluated DSRL tasks.

title: Q-Supervised Contrastive Representation: A State Decoupling Framework for Safe Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their impressive capabilities, often fail to accurately repeat a single word when prompted to, and instead output unrelated text. This unexplained failure mode represents a vulnerability, allowing even end users to diverge models away from their intended behavior. We aim to explain the causes for this phenomenon and link it to the concept of "attention sinks", an emergent LLM behavior crucial for fluency, in which the initial token receives disproportionately high attention scores. Our investigation identifies the neural circuit responsible for attention sinks and shows how long repetitions disrupt this circuit. We extend this finding to other nonrepeating sequences that exhibit similar circuit disruptions. To address this, we propose a targeted patch that effectively resolves the issue without negatively impacting the overall performance of the model. This study provides a mechanistic explanation for an LLM vulnerability, demonstrating how interpretability can diagnose and address issues, and offering insights that pave the way for more secure and reliable models.

The study links an observable behavioral problem, a disrupted internal circuit, and a focused intervention. It demonstrates how mechanistic interpretability can contribute to repairing a specific reliability vulnerability in language models.
summary.tldr: The paper traces repetition-induced language-model failures to disrupted attention-sink circuitry and reports a targeted patch that resolves the issue.

title: Interpreting the Repeated Token Phenomenon in Large Language Models

abstract: We study sequential decision-making in partially observable environments against strategic, adaptive opponents, modeled as partially observable Markov games (POMGs). The central challenge is to learn latent dynamics from partial observations while facing an adversary whose behavior depends on the learner’s strategy, making standard regret notions inadequate. We prove that an epoch-based optimistic maximum-likelihood algorithm achieves $\tilde O(\sqrt{T})$ policy regret for fixed problem parameters, with explicit dependence on the horizon, adversary memory, confidence radius, and the aggregate Eluder dimension of the observable-operator class. The algorithm selects one policy per geometrically growing epoch using confidence sets built cumulatively from past data, which keeps the cost of comparing adversary responses across policies logarithmic in $T$. We also prove a lower bound matching the $\sqrt{T}$ and aggregate-Eluder-dimension dependence, up to problem-dependent and logarithmic factors. Finally, we extend the framework to horizon-adaptive guarantees and adversaries with geometric fading memory.

The learner must infer hidden dynamics while recognizing that an opponent may respond differently to different strategies. This paper studies partially observable Markov games using policy regret, a comparison that accounts for such strategy-dependent opponent behavior.

The results characterize achievable performance while retaining explicit dependence on properties of the game and opponent.
summary.tldr: An epoch-based optimistic algorithm achieves near-matching upper and lower policy-regret rates in partially observable games with adaptive opponents.

title: Minimax-Optimal Policy Regret in Partially Observable Markov Games

abstract: Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) is a powerful acceleration paradigm, yet its stability is often compromised in Forbidden Zones—regions where the real teacher provides unreliable guidance while the fake teacher exerts insufficient repulsive force. In this work, we propose a unified optimization framework that reinterprets prior art as implicit strategies to avoid these corrupted regions. Based on this insight, we introduce Adaptive Matching Distillation (AMD), a self-correcting mechanism that utilizes reward proxies to explicitly detect and escape Forbidden Zones. AMD dynamically prioritizes corrective gradients via structural signal decomposition and introduces Repulsive Landscape Sharpening to enforce steep energy barriers against failure mode collapse. Extensive experiments across image and video generation tasks (e.g., SDXL, Wan2.1) and rigorous benchmarks (e.g., VBench, GenEval) demonstrate that AMD significantly enhances sample fidelity and training robustness. For instance, AMD improves the HPSv2 score on SDXL from 30.64 to 31.25, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. These findings validate that explicitly rectifying optimization trajectories within Forbidden Zones is essential for pushing the performance ceiling of few-step generative models.

title: Optimizing Few-Step Generation with Adaptive Matching Distillation

abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as CLIP have revolutionized zero-shot classification and safety-critical tasks, including Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection. However, their high computational cost hinders efficient real-world deployment. While quantization is a standard solution for efficiency, its broader impact on reliability metrics beyond simple Top-1 accuracy remains critically under-explored. In this study, we conduct a large-scale evaluation of VLM quantization across a comprehensive experimental suite of over 700k evaluation runs with varying configurations. We find that, contrary to the assumption that quantization’s noise degrades performance, it can simultaneously improve accuracy, calibration, OOD detection, and robustness to noise, though not to covariate shift or spurious correlations. We leverage these counterintuitive findings to characterize the mechanics of quantization beyond simple regularization: we show that quantization dampens high-rank spectral components, compelling the model to rely more heavily on robust, low-rank features. Ultimately, this spectral filtering effect drives the observed improvements in generalization and noise tolerance, establishing a pathway to deploy faster, more reliable VLMs by utilizing quantization beyond its conventional role.

paragraphs: Quantization reduces numerical precision to make models cheaper to run. Its evaluation often centers on classification accuracy, but vision-language models also need reliable confidence estimates and the ability to recognize unfamiliar inputs. This paper examines those broader effects through more than 700,000 evaluation runs with varying configurations.

The authors find that quantization can improve accuracy, calibration, out-of-distribution detection, and resistance to noise at the same time. Those benefits do not extend to covariate shift or spurious correlations in their findings. This distinction matters because better performance against one kind of disruption does not imply improved reliability under every distribution change.

The proposed explanation is spectral filtering. Quantization dampens high-rank spectral components and makes the model rely more on robust, low-rank features. The authors connect this change to the observed gains in generalization and noise tolerance, going beyond an explanation based only on regularization. The study shows that reduced precision can sometimes contribute to reliability as well as efficiency, while keeping the claim tied to the kinds of reliability that actually improved.
summary.tldr: Quantization can improve several vision-language reliability measures through spectral filtering, although the reported benefits exclude covariate shift and spurious correlations.

title: Less Precise Can Be More Reliable: A Systematic Evaluation of Quantization’s Impact on VLMs Beyond Accuracy

abstract: Prompt optimization is a key way to steer large language models when fine-tuning is impractical. However, instruction optimization (IO) and in-context learning (ICL) demonstration selection are often optimized separately and combined post hoc, implicitly assuming that a "best” instruction and a "best" demonstration set compose well. In practice, their interactions are strong, making such decoupled pipelines brittle. We propose SMILE, an efficient method that jointly selects instructions and demonstrations. Our key observation is that the ICL performance exhibits consistent diminishing returns across diverse instructions. Leveraging this structure, SMILE learns an instruction-conditioned surrogate aligned with LLM feedback and instantiates it as an Extended Deep Submodular Function that captures sample–sample coverage, sample–query relevance, and sample–instruction compatibility. SMILE then performs greedy, query-adaptive selection of the instruction–demonstration pair. Experiments on six datasets and multiple LLM backbones show that SMILE consistently outperforms IO-only, ICL-only, and existing joint baselines, supporting a context engineering view of prompting: jointly optimizing interacting components rather than tuning them in isolation.

SMILE then performs greedy, query-adaptive selection of the instruction–demonstration pair. paragraphs: SMILE addresses a weakness in prompt optimization: an instruction and a set of examples that work well separately may not work well together. Existing pipelines often optimize these components independently and combine them afterward. The paper instead treats their interaction as part of the selection problem.

The authors observe diminishing returns in in-context-learning performance across diverse instructions. They use this structure to learn an instruction-conditioned surrogate from language-model feedback. Implemented as an Extended Deep Submodular Function, it represents coverage among examples, relevance to the current query, and compatibility with the instruction. A greedy procedure then selects the instruction and demonstrations jointly for each query.

Experiments on six datasets and multiple language-model backbones report consistent improvements over instruction-only, demonstration-only, and existing joint-selection baselines. The findings support optimizing the prompt as an interacting whole. The practical significance is that selection considers which examples suit a particular instruction and question, rather than treating example quality as independent of context.
summary.tldr: SMILE jointly selects instructions and demonstrations using a learned model of relevance, coverage, and compatibility.

title: SMILE: Extended Deep Submodular Function-Based Instruction and In-context Learning Demonstration Selection

abstract: We consider max-min and min-max problems with objective functions that are possibly non-smooth, submodular with respect to the minimiser and concave with respect to the maximiser. We investigate the performance of a zeroth-order method applied to this problem. The method is based on the subgradient of the Lovász extension of the objective function with respect to the minimiser and based on Gaussian smoothing to estimate the smoothed function gradient with respect to the maximiser. In expectation sense, we prove the convergence of the algorithm to an $\epsilon$-saddle point in the offline case. Moreover, we show that, in the expectation sense, in the online setting, the algorithm achieves $O(\sqrt{N(1+\bar{P}_N)})$ online duality gap, where $N$ is the number of iterations and $\bar{P}_N$ is the path length of the sequence of optimal decisions. The complexity analysis and hyperparameter selection are presented for all the cases. The theoretical results are illustrated via numerical examples.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization problems in which one decision maker minimizes an objective while another maximizes it. The objective may be nonsmooth, with submodular structure on the minimizing side and concavity on the maximizing side. The authors consider both offline problems and online settings where the sequence of optimal decisions can change.

Their zeroth-order method combines two techniques suited to these different structures. For the minimizer, it uses a subgradient of the objective’s Lovász extension. For the maximizer, it applies Gaussian smoothing to estimate the gradient of a smoothed objective. This provides an algorithmic route for handling the two sides without requiring a smooth original objective.

Online, they establish an expected duality-gap bound of order sqrt(N(1 + P̄_N)), where N counts iterations and P̄_N measures the movement of optimal decisions. The bound explicitly reflects how much that target sequence changes. The paper also supplies complexity analyses and hyperparameter choices, with numerical examples illustrating the theoretical results.
summary.tldr: A zeroth-order method obtains expected offline convergence and an online duality-gap bound for nonsmooth submodular–concave optimization.

title: Solving the Offline and Online Min-Max Problem of Non-smooth Submodular-Concave Functions: A Zeroth-Order Approach

abstract: Polytrees are a subclass of Bayesian networks that seek to capture the conditional dependencies between a set of $n$ variables as a directed forest and are motivated by their more efficient inference and improved interpretability. Since the problem of learning the best polytree is NP-hard, we study which restrictions make it more tractable by considering for example in-degree bounds, properties of score functions measuring the quality of a polytree, and approximation algorithms. We devise an algorithm that finds the optimal polytree in time $\mathcal{O}((2+\epsilon)^n)$ for arbitrarily small $\epsilon > 0 $ and any constant in-degree bound $k$, improving over the fastest previously known algorithm of time complexity $\mathcal{O}(3^n)$. We further give polynomial-time algorithms for finding a polytree whose score is within a factor of $k$ from the optimal one for arbitrary scores and a factor of $2$ for additive ones. Many of the results are complemented by (nearly) tight lower bounds for either the time complexity or the approximation factors.

paragraphs: Polytrees describe conditional relationships among variables using a restricted form of Bayesian network whose underlying structure is a forest. Their appeal is more efficient inference and improved interpretability, but finding the highest-scoring polytree is NP-hard. This paper investigates how restrictions on parent counts and scoring functions change the computational difficulty, and what can be achieved through approximation.

For any constant maximum in-degree k, the authors give an exact algorithm with running time O((2+ε)^n), for arbitrarily small positive ε. This improves the previous O(3^n) bound. The algorithm remains exponential in the number of variables, but lowers the exponential base while still finding an optimal structure under the stated in-degree restriction.

The paper also gives polynomial-time approximation algorithms. Their scores are within a factor of k of optimal for arbitrary scoring functions and within a factor of two for additive scores. Many results come with tight or nearly tight lower bounds on runtime or approximation quality. Together, these findings distinguish settings where exact search can be accelerated from those where bounded-quality approximations offer a tractable alternative.
summary.tldr: The paper improves exact polytree learning under constant in-degree bounds and provides polynomial-time approximations with provable quality guarantees.

title: Exact and Approximate Algorithms for Polytree Learning

abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have driven substantial progress in image and video generation but suffer from prohibitive computational costs. Feature caching accelerates inference by reusing intermediate representations. Existing methods rely on historical features for implementation simplicity, yet suffer from severe error accumulation at high acceleration ratios. To address this limitation, we investigate the nature of the requisite feature correction. We demonstrate that the optimal calibration update is characterized by a shared low-rank subspace across diverse prompts. Guided by this structural insight, we propose LearniBridge, a learnable calibration mechanism for feature caching that bridges multiple timesteps through lightweight LoRA updates. This mechanism enables effective calibration requiring only $3-5$ training samples. Extensive experiments on image and video generation show that LearniBridge achieves up to $5.87\times$, $5.75\times$, and $4.10\times$ acceleration on FLUX, HunyuanVideo, and WAN 2.1, respectively. On WAN 2.1, it improves VBench by 1.28% over the previous SOTA at $4.10\times$ acceleration.

Feature caching speeds this up by reusing intermediate representations, but old features become increasingly inaccurate as reuse grows. At high acceleration ratios, those errors can accumulate severely and undermine the usefulness of the shortcut.

LearniBridge investigates the correction needed to make cached features useful across timesteps. The authors find that the optimal calibration update lies in a shared low-rank subspace across diverse prompts. They use that structure to build lightweight LoRA updates that bridge multiple timesteps. The reported calibration requires only three to five training samples, making the correction mechanism inexpensive to fit.

These results indicate that learning a compact correction can improve the quality-speed tradeoff of feature reuse in both image and video generation.
summary.tldr: LearniBridge learns compact corrections to cached diffusion features from three to five samples, enabling substantial image and video generation acceleration.

title: LearniBridge: Learnable Calibration of Feature Caching for Diffusion Models Acceleration

abstract: We consider the task of end-to-end spreadsheet generation, where language models are prompted to produce spreadsheet artifacts to satisfy users’ explicit and implicit constraints, specified in natural language. We introduce SpreadsheetArena, a platform for evaluating models’ performance on the task via blind pairwise evaluations of LLM-generated spreadsheet workbooks. As with other complex, open-ended tasks, relevant evaluation criteria can vary greatly across use cases and prompts, often in ways that are difficult to formalize. Compared to general dialogue or text generation settings, spreadsheet generation presents unique challenges and opportunities: the task output structure is well-defined and multi-dimensional, and there are often complex interactivity and layout considerations. We observe that stylistic, structural, and functional features of preferred spreadsheets vary meaningfully across prompts. Expert evaluations of spreadsheets for finance prompts suggest that even highly ranked models do not reliably produce spreadsheets aligned with domain-specific best practices. We host a live arena and release a dataset of prompts, generated spreadsheets, and preference votes, which we hope will facilitate further study of tasks operating over spreadsheets as a challenging and interesting class of complex, open-ended tasks for LLMs.

SpreadsheetArena evaluates this end-to-end task through blind comparisons between pairs of generated workbooks. The approach allows evaluators to judge complete artifacts even when the criteria for a good spreadsheet are difficult to formalize in advance.

Spreadsheets offer a defined output structure but also involve interacting dimensions, including layout and interactivity. The study finds that the stylistic, structural, and functional properties associated with preferred workbooks vary meaningfully across prompts. This makes preference dependent on the particular use case rather than a single fixed idea of workbook quality.

Expert assessments of finance-oriented workbooks reveal that even highly ranked models do not reliably follow domain-specific best practices. The authors release prompts, generated workbooks, and preference votes alongside a live arena. These resources support research into how overall preferences relate to particular artifact features and help distinguish strong comparative rankings from dependable performance in a specialized domain.
summary.tldr: SpreadsheetArena evaluates generated workbooks through blind preferences and finds that high rankings do not ensure alignment with finance best practices.

title: SpreadsheetArena: Decomposing Preference in LLM Generation of Spreadsheet Workbooks

abstract: Traditional neural topic models are typically optimized by reconstructing the document’s Bag-of-Words (BoW) representations, overlooking contextual information and struggling with data sparsity. In this work, we introduce a novel topic model training framework by Distilling Soft Labels (DSL) from Language Models (LMs). To construct the contextually enriched reconstruction signals, we project the next token probabilities, conditioned on a specialized prompt, onto a pre-defined vocabulary, and train the topic models to reconstruct the soft labels using the LM hidden states. This produces higher-quality topics that are more closely aligned with the underlying thematic structure of the corpus. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DSL achieves substantial improvements in topic coherence and assignment accuracy over existing baselines. Additionally, we also introduce a retrieval-based metric, which shows that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in identifying semantically similar documents, highlighting its effectiveness for retrieval-oriented applications.

paragraphs: Neural topic models often learn by reconstructing which words appear in each document. That bag-of-words target discards context and provides sparse evidence when documents contain few words. This paper replaces the reconstruction signal with soft labels derived from a language model, aiming to give topic learning a richer account of document meaning.

The framework, DSL, obtains next-token probabilities under a specialized prompt and projects them onto a predefined vocabulary. These probabilities form context-sensitive targets rather than simple observed word counts. The topic model uses language-model hidden states and learns to reconstruct those soft targets, transferring contextual information into the topic-training process.

Experiments report substantial improvements in topic coherence and topic-assignment accuracy over existing baselines. The authors also introduce a retrieval-based metric and find stronger performance at identifying documents with similar meanings. These results connect the training change to two practical outcomes: topics better aligned with the corpus’s themes and representations more useful for finding related documents.
summary.tldr: DSL improves topic learning by replacing sparse word-count reconstruction targets with contextual soft labels from a language model.

title: Improving Topic Modeling by Distilling Soft Labels from Language Models

abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate impressive general capabilities, they struggle with fine-grained perception in ultra-high-resolution (UHR) images, particularly for tiny objects in cluttered scenes. Existing methods face a dilemma: they either rely on inefficient prior-free scanning, or depend on static prior-driven heuristics that lack posterior correction to rectify initial model biases. To address this, we propose BVS (Bayesian Visual Search), a framework that formulates perception as a global optimization problem over a continuous spatial-scale manifold. Specifically, BVS bridges prior guidance with posterior correction: it utilizes an early-stop attention rollout of MLLM to construct reasoning-aware priors, while employing a scale-aware non-stationary kernel and GP-UCB to dynamically rectify noise and recover missing information in the prior through iterative local observations. We provide theoretical guarantees via sub-linear regret bounds, and extensive experiments demonstrate that BVS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with a superior trade-off between accuracy and efficiency.

paragraphs: Tiny objects in crowded, extremely high-resolution images remain difficult for multimodal language models to perceive. Searching without guidance can waste computation, while following a fixed initial guess can preserve the model’s early mistakes. BVS treats visual inspection as an optimization problem over both image location and viewing scale.

The framework first derives a reasoning-aware prior from an early-stopped attention rollout. It then gathers local observations and updates its search using a Gaussian-process upper-confidence-bound method. A scale-aware, non-stationary kernel supports this process, allowing the search to account for changing relationships across locations and scales. Initial attention therefore guides exploration without permanently determining where the system looks.

The authors provide sublinear regret bounds and report substantial improvements over leading baselines in the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency. The central idea is to connect model-generated guidance with evidence-based correction: later observations can repair noisy initial beliefs and recover information those beliefs missed. The stated theory and experiments support this adaptive search approach for fine-grained perception.
summary.tldr: BVS searches high-resolution images using model-guided priors that are continually corrected by local visual observations.

title: BVS: Bayesian Visual Search with Multimodal Large Language Model for Fine-grained Perception

abstract: Recent advances in foundation models have transformed LLMs from passive conversational systems into autonomous agents capable of reasoning and tool execution. While these capabilities unlock substantial practical value, they also introduce new security risks, as adversaries can manipulate agents into performing harmful actions in real-world environments. Existing defense strategies mitigate such threats but frequently struggle to balance safety and utility, resulting in over-refusal of benign user requests. To mitigate this trade-off, we propose SafeHarbor, a novel framework designed to establish precise decision boundaries for LLM agents. Unlike static guidelines, SafeHarbor extracts context-aware defense rules through enhanced adversarial generation. We design a local hierarchical memory system for dynamic rule injection, offering a training-free, efficient, and plug-and-play solution. Furthermore, we introduce an information entropy-based self-evolution mechanism that continuously optimizes the memory structure through dynamic node splitting and merging. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SafeHarbor achieves state-of-the-art performance on both ambiguous benign tasks and explicit malicious attacks, notably attaining a peak benign utility of 63.6% on GPT-4o while maintaining a robust refusal rate exceeding 93% against harmful requests. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ljj-cyber/SafeHarbor.

paragraphs: Agents that reason and execute tools can be manipulated into harmful actions, but aggressive defenses can also block legitimate requests. SafeHarbor aims to sharpen the boundary between these cases. Its central idea is to supply context-sensitive defense rules through a changing memory system, helping the guardrail distinguish benign ambiguity from malicious intent.

The framework extracts rules through enhanced adversarial generation and stores them in a local hierarchical memory. Relevant rules can then be injected dynamically without retraining the agent. An information-entropy-based mechanism updates the memory structure by splitting and merging nodes, allowing the organization of defensive knowledge to evolve over time.

These figures describe the evaluated safety–utility balance. The results support a training-free, plug-and-play guardrail that uses adaptive rule organization to improve decisions about when an agent should comply or refuse.
summary.tldr: SafeHarbor dynamically supplies context-aware safety rules from hierarchical memory to balance harmful-request refusal with benign usefulness.

title: SafeHarbor: Defining Precise Decision Boundaries via Hierarchical Memory-Augmented Guardrail for LLM Agent Safety

abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) gain agentic abilities, they will have to navigate complex multi-agent scenarios, interacting with human users and other agents in cooperative and competitive settings. This will require new reasoning skills, a crucial one being theory of mind (ToM), or the ability to reason about the “mental” states of other agents. However, ToM and other multi-agent abilities in LLMs are poorly understood, since existing benchmarks suffer from narrow scope, data leakage, saturation, and lack of interactivity. We thus propose Decrypto, a game-based benchmark for multi-agent reasoning and ToM drawing inspiration from cognitive science, computational pragmatics and multi-agent reinforcement learning. It is designed to be as easy as possible in all other dimensions, eliminating confounding factors common in other benchmarks. To our knowledge, it is also the first platform that isolates ToM evaluation in an interactive setting. We validate the benchmark design through comprehensive empirical evaluations of frontier LLMs, robustness studies, and human-AI cross-play experiments. We find that LLMs lag behind humans and simple word-embedding baselines on key game metrics. We then create variants of two classic cognitive science experiments within Decrypto to evaluate three distinct ToM abilities. Surprisingly, our results show that state-of-the-art reasoning models are significantly worse at those tasks than their older counterparts. This demonstrates that Decrypto addresses a crucial gap in current reasoning and ToM evaluations, and paves the path towards better artificial agents. Code at https://github.com/facebookresearch/decrypto.

summary.tldr: Decrypto tests interactive multi-agent reasoning and finds that leading language models struggle with key game and theory-of-mind tasks.

title: The Decrypto Benchmark for Multi-Agent Reasoning and Theory of Mind

abstract: Iterative generative policies, such as diffusion models and flow matching, offer superior expressivity for continuous control but complicate Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning because their action log-densities are not directly accessible. To address this, we propose Field Least-Energy Actor-Critic (FLAC), a likelihood-free framework that regulates policy stochasticity by penalizing the kinetic energy of the velocity field. Our key insight is to formulate policy optimization as a Generalized Schrödinger Bridge (GSB) problem relative to a high-entropy reference process (e.g., uniform). Under this view, the maximum-entropy principle emerges naturally as staying close to a high-entropy reference while optimizing return, without requiring explicit action densities. In this framework, kinetic energy serves as a physically grounded proxy for divergence from the reference: minimizing path-space energy bounds the deviation of the induced terminal action distribution. Building on this view, we derive an energy-regularized policy iteration scheme and a practical off-policy algorithm that automatically tunes the kinetic energy via a Lagrangian dual mechanism. Empirically, FLAC achieves superior or comparable performance on high-dimensional benchmarks relative to strong baselines, while avoiding explicit density estimation.

paragraphs: Diffusion and flow-based policies can express complex continuous actions, but their action probabilities are not directly available. That complicates maximum-entropy reinforcement learning, which seeks strong returns while retaining policy randomness. FLAC addresses this difficulty by controlling the energy of the generative process instead of explicitly estimating action densities.

The method formulates policy optimization as a Generalized Schrödinger Bridge problem relative to a high-entropy reference process. Staying close to that reference encourages stochastic behavior while the policy improves its return. The kinetic energy of the velocity field provides a proxy for departure from the reference: reducing energy along the generative paths bounds the deviation of the resulting action distribution.

From this formulation, the authors derive energy-regularized policy iteration and a practical off-policy algorithm. A Lagrangian dual mechanism automatically adjusts the energy regulation. On high-dimensional benchmarks, FLAC performs better than or comparably to strong baselines while avoiding explicit density estimation. The contribution is therefore both a theoretical route to entropy-oriented policy learning and an implementable algorithm for expressive generative policies.
summary.tldr: FLAC regulates generative policies through kinetic energy, enabling maximum-entropy reinforcement learning without explicit action-density estimation.

title: FLAC: Maximum Entropy RL via Kinetic Energy Regularized Bridge Matching

abstract: Neural operators learn mappings between function spaces, enabling fast surrogate solutions to partial differential equations. Despite remarkable architectural diversity, these methods often share a common input representation: raw coordinate-value pairs $(x, u(x))$. We ask whether inputs aligned with PDE differential structure can improve learning. Through Picard iteration on mild solutions, we show that derivatives of the input appear explicitly in the solution operator, suggesting that providing derivative features should reduce the network’s implicit differentiation burden. We prove this intuition: providing derivative features improves approximation bounds from $O(W^{-(s-m)/d})$ to $O(W^{-s/d})$, where $W$ is parameter count, $s$ is input regularity, $m$ is the PDE order, and $d$ is spatial dimension. Our central finding, however, is a surprise: the optimal derivative order $\beta^*$ is strictly less than the PDE order $m$. This gap arises from a bias-variance tradeoff in spectral space that we characterize in closed form. Learning $\beta$ from data achieves automatic spectral regularization. We introduce $\partial$-NO (del-NO), for derivative-augmented neural operators, an architecture-agnostic augmentation that provides learnable fractional derivative features to any neural operator backbone. Across benchmark problems and architectures, $\partial$-NO consistently improves prediction accuracy, with learned orders that reflect a representation of known physics modulated by noise and finite-sample constraints.

Across benchmark problems and architectures, $\partial$-NO consistently improves prediction accuracy, with learned orders that reflect a representation of known physics modulated by noise and finite-sample constraints.

paragraphs: Neural operators learn mappings between functions, making them useful as fast approximations to partial differential equation solvers. They commonly receive coordinates and function values as input. This paper asks whether supplying derivative information can reduce the work a network must do to learn the equation’s underlying differential structure.

Using Picard iteration on mild solutions, the authors show that input derivatives appear explicitly in the solution operator. They prove an improvement in approximation bounds from O(W^{-(s-m)/d}) to O(W^{-s/d}) when derivative features are supplied. Here, W is parameter count, s is input regularity, m is equation order, and d is spatial dimension.

Their analysis also finds that the optimal derivative order is strictly below the PDE’s order, reflecting a spectral bias–variance tradeoff. The proposed del-NO augmentation learns fractional derivative orders from data, providing automatic spectral regularization. Across the tested problems and architectures, it consistently improves prediction accuracy. The learned orders reflect physical structure while adjusting for noise and finite samples, explaining why directly matching the equation’s order need not be optimal.
summary.tldr: Learnable fractional derivative features improve neural operator approximation and prediction while balancing physical structure against noise and finite-sample effects.

title: Fractional is Better: Learnable Derivative Orders in Neural Operator Learning

abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) excel on dense continuous data, but are not designed for sparse continuous data. They do not model exact zeros that represent the deliberate absence of a signal. As a result, they erase sparsity patterns and perform unnecessary computation on mostly zero entries. With Sparsity-Exploiting Diffusion (SED), we model only non-zero values, preserving sparsity. SED delivers computational savings while maintaining or improving generation quality by skipping zeros during training and inference. Across physics and biology benchmarks, SED matches or surpasses conventional DMs and domain-specific baselines, while vision experiments provide intuitive insights into the limitations of dense DMs and the benefits of SED.

paragraphs: Sparse continuous data contains many exact zeros that indicate a signal is absent. Conventional diffusion models are designed for dense continuous data and do not naturally represent this kind of exact absence. Applying them to sparse data can therefore destroy meaningful sparsity patterns while spending computation on entries that should remain zero.

Sparsity-Exploiting Diffusion, or SED, focuses modeling on nonzero values and skips zeros during both training and inference. This makes preserving sparsity part of the generative approach itself. The same design also avoids unnecessary processing, connecting the statistical structure of sparse data to a direct opportunity for computational savings.

Across physics and biology benchmarks, SED matches or exceeds conventional diffusion models and domain-specific baselines while reducing computation. Vision experiments illustrate the difficulties dense diffusion models face and the benefits of the sparse approach. The reported findings show that exploiting exact zeros can support generation quality and efficiency together, particularly when those zeros carry information about deliberate signal absence.
summary.tldr: SED preserves sparse data by modeling nonzero values and skipping zeros, saving computation while maintaining or improving generation quality.

title: Skipping the Zeros in Diffusion Models for Sparse Data Generation

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly perform multi-step reasoning, where intermediate claims form implicit directed acyclic graphs whose node correctness is structurally conditioned on their ancestors. This makes factuality uncertainty structural, rather than a trivial accumulation of node-wise errors, and necessitates inference-time uncertainty quantification over the reasoning structure. While conformal prediction (CP) offers flexible user-specified factuality control, existing work remains post-hoc and cannot intervene during generation. To fill the gap between CP’s flexibility and its post-hoc limitation, we propose an Inference-Time Conformal Reasoning (ITCR) framework that integrates CP directly into reasoning graph generation. ITCR learns a structure-level factuality uncertainty function that aggregates claim-level factuality signals over reasoning graphs without complex modeling assumptions. We then design the non-conformity score based on graph-level factuality uncertainty and calibrate the conformal threshold to decide when to stop generation. We theoretically show such generation is nested, yielding valid coverage guarantees for factuality control. Experiments over multiple datasets and coverage objectives demonstrate empirically valid coverage. In downstream reasoning tasks, inference-time calibrated graphs yield more accurate generation than post-hoc pruned graphs.

paragraphs: Multi-step reasoning contains dependencies: later claims can rely on earlier ones. The paper represents these relationships as directed acyclic graphs and argues that factual uncertainty must account for their structure. Treating claim errors as an uncomplicated accumulation misses how the correctness of a claim is conditioned on the claims supporting it.

Inference-Time Conformal Reasoning, or ITCR, brings conformal calibration into graph generation itself. It learns a graph-level uncertainty function that combines factuality signals from individual claims without complex modeling assumptions. On downstream reasoning tasks, graphs calibrated during generation produce more accurate outputs than graphs pruned afterward. The contribution is therefore both calibrated factuality control and evidence that intervening during construction can improve the resulting reasoning.
summary.tldr: ITCR calibrates graph-level factual uncertainty during reasoning generation to determine when to stop, with theoretical and empirical coverage support.

title: Inference-Time Conformal Reasoning with Valid Factuality Control for Large Language Models

abstract: Accurately capturing local variations in long series has always been one of the most challenging problems in time-series forecasting especially in medical signals, where local variations often indicate pathological events. Our study reveals a previously overlooked key bottleneck in this field: traditional global and local branches learn similar representations, leading to strong feature coupling and reduced sensitivity to local variations. To address this challenge, we propose the novel Dual-Stream Enhancement Mechanism, which structurally enlarges the difference between global and local patterns, enabling weak interactions between the two. Based on this idea, we introduce a new baseline model for blood glucose prediction: Dual-Stream Enhancement Network (DSENet), which fundamentally alleviates the problem of excessively strong coupling between global and local features. Experimental results show that our model achieves SOTA performance on multiple public datasets. Moreover, benefiting from extremely low computational cost, our model demonstrates strong application potential and can serve as a baseline model in multiple domains in the future.

paragraphs: Forecasting long time series requires recognizing broad patterns while remaining sensitive to brief local changes. In medical signals, those changes can indicate pathological events. This paper identifies a problem with architectures that use separate global and local branches: the branches can learn similar representations, reducing their ability to distinguish local variations from the larger pattern.

The proposed Dual-Stream Enhancement Mechanism changes the structure of learning to increase the distinction between global and local patterns. It allows weak interactions between the streams while alleviating excessively strong feature coupling. The purpose is to make the two branches provide more complementary information rather than repeatedly describing similar aspects of the signal.

The authors build DSENet around this mechanism for blood glucose prediction. They report state-of-the-art performance on multiple public datasets alongside extremely low computational cost. These findings support separating global and local representations as a useful forecasting design in the evaluated settings. The proposed use of DSENet as a baseline in additional domains remains a future application opportunity.
summary.tldr: DSENet improves blood glucose forecasting by keeping global trends and local variations more distinct within a low-cost dual-stream architecture.

title: DSENet: A Novel Dual-Stream Enhancement Network for Multi-Scale Non-Stationary Time Series Forecasting

abstract: World models are central to building AI agents capable of flexible reasoning and planning. Yet current evaluations (i) test only properties measurable from observed interactions, such as next-frame prediction or task return, and (ii) do not test whether a learned model supports diverse queries about the environment. In contrast, humans build general-purpose models that can answer many different questions about an environment—including questions that require understanding global structure and counterfactual consequences. We propose WorldTest: a protocol for evaluating whether agents learn models that support multiple environment-level queries—questions whose answers depend on properties of the full environment, not just observed trajectories. Individually, these queries can target properties (e.g., reachability or the effects of interventions) that no single rollout distribution determines. Collectively, they assess model generality across query types. We instantiate WorldTest as AutumnBench, a benchmark of 43 interactive grid-world environments and 129 tasks across three query families for both humans and learning agents. Experiments with 517 human participants and five frontier models on AutumnBench show that humans substantially outperform these models, a gap we attribute to differences in exploration and belief updating.

paragraphs: An agent can predict its next observation or perform a task successfully without having a broadly useful understanding of its environment. This paper argues that world-model evaluations should also ask questions about overall structure and hypothetical changes. Such questions test whether knowledge gained through interaction supports reasoning beyond the particular trajectories observed.

The proposed WorldTest protocol evaluates multiple environment-level queries, including whether states are reachable and what interventions would change. Individual queries can depend on properties that no single rollout distribution determines. Testing several query types together assesses whether a learned model supports different uses, rather than measuring success on one narrow prediction problem.

The authors implement the protocol as AutumnBench, containing 43 interactive grid worlds and 129 tasks across three query families. In experiments with 517 human participants and five frontier models, humans substantially outperform the models. The authors attribute this gap to differences in exploration and belief updating, pointing to how agents gather evidence and revise their understanding as important parts of world-model learning.
summary.tldr: WorldTest evaluates broad environmental understanding, and its AutumnBench implementation reveals a substantial human advantage over five frontier models.

title: Benchmarking World-Model Learning with Environment-Level Queries

abstract: As real-world tasks grow increasingly complex, long-context reasoning has become a core capability for Large Language Models (LLMs). However, few studies explore which data types are effective for long-context reasoning and why. We find that structured table data with periodic structures shows strong potential for long-context reasoning. Motivated by this observation, we mathematically analyze tabular dependency structures using mutual information, revealing periodic non-vanishing dependencies in table data. Furthermore, we systematically analyze the capabilities of structured table data, conduct relevant scaling experiments, and validate its underlying mechanisms for enhancing long-context reasoning, yielding several meaningful insights. Leveraging these insights, we propose a simple yet scalable pipeline(TableLong) for synthesizing high-quality, diverse, and verifiable structured table data to boost long-context reasoning via RL. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that table data significantly enhances the long-context reasoning capability of LLMs across multiple long-context benchmarks (+8.24% on average), and even improves performance on out-of-domain benchmarks (+8.06% on average). We hope that our insights provide practical guidance for effective post-training data to enhance long-context reasoning in LLMs.

paragraphs: This paper investigates which training data can strengthen reasoning over long contexts and why it helps. Its focus is structured tables with recurring organization. The authors identify periodic dependencies that remain present across table data, suggesting that these structures can provide useful material for learning to connect information across a long input.

They analyze those dependencies mathematically through mutual information and study the capabilities and scaling behavior of table-based data. Building on the resulting insights, they introduce TableLong, a pipeline for generating diverse, verifiable structured tables at scale. The latter result indicates that the observed gains extend beyond the immediate training domain in the evaluations. The contribution combines an explanation of a useful data property with a practical synthesis pipeline, providing evidence that structured tables can support broader long-context abilities.
summary.tldr: TableLong uses scalable, verifiable table data for reinforcement learning, improving long-context reasoning and out-of-domain benchmark performance.

title: Probing How Scalable Table Data Enhances General Long-Context Reasoning

abstract: Federated causal discovery for time series is becoming increasingly important in many application domains. In practice, intervention policies on each client often change over time, causing the local underlying causal mechanisms to drift rather than remain fixed. Moreover, different sampling frequencies across clients yield incompatible time scales in the observed data, making the resulting local causal graphs naturally heterogeneous and difficult to aggregate consistently. Accordingly, we propose Fed-CAW, a Credibility-Aware Weighting Federated causal discovery framework for time series. Specifically, we define edge-level credibility scores that quantify per-edge reliability by summarizing (i) within-client temporal stability across windows and (ii) cross-client temporal consistency after mapping heterogeneous sampling frequencies onto a unified time scale. We then aggregate privatized edge statistics under differential privacy, treating credibility scores as weights to recover a global causal graph while preserving personalized local structures without sharing raw data. Theoretically, we demonstrate the rationale for the unified time scale mapping and establish rigorous differential privacy guarantees. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

paragraphs: Learning causal relationships jointly across clients becomes difficult when their time-series data describe changing mechanisms at different sampling rates. A relationship may drift within one client as intervention policies change. Meanwhile, two clients may represent timing differently, making their local causal graphs difficult to combine directly.

Fed-CAW addresses these problems by assigning credibility to individual causal edges. Each score summarizes how stable an edge is across time windows within a client and how consistent it is across clients after their sampling frequencies are mapped to a common time scale. Aggregation therefore accounts for the reliability of particular relationships rather than giving every local edge equal influence.

The framework combines privatized edge statistics using these credibility weights, producing a global causal graph while retaining personalized local structures and keeping raw data local. The authors provide theoretical support for the time-scale mapping and rigorous differential privacy guarantees. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the method’s effectiveness under the studied settings.
summary.tldr: Fed-CAW combines local causal graphs using edge reliability, aligned time scales, and differentially private statistics.

title: Credibility-Aware Weighting Federated Causal Discovery for Time Series

abstract: Operating room (OR) scene graph generation (SGG) enables holistic modeling of OR domains by encoding interactions among medical staff, tools, and equipment as triplet-based structured scene graphs. Although existing OR SGG methods demonstrate satisfactory overall performance, they exhibit substantially lower accuracy on long-tail categories compared to head categories in OR data. We introduce SGG-ICL, a novel framework that represents the first attempt to address the long-tail problem in OR SGG by leveraging in-context learning (ICL). SGG-ICL first identifies long-tail samples via an Adaptive Router module and selectively applies ICL only to these samples. This selective routing strategy enhances performance on long-tail categories without degrading head-category accuracy. Subsequently, SGG-ICL constructs a candidate pool through multimodal retrieval and then employs a trained MLLM Reranker to re-rank the candidates, selecting the most similar examples to the test sample for ICL. The reranker is supervised by IoU scores derived from annotated SGG triplets and exploits rich multimodal information to estimate pairwise sample similarity. Experimental results show that SGG-ICL improves accuracy on long-tail categories by 6.9%, while also achieving a 2.6% improvement in overall accuracy.

paragraphs: Operating-room scene graphs describe relationships among staff, instruments, and equipment using structured triplets. Existing methods can perform well overall while remaining much less accurate on uncommon relationships. SGG-ICL targets this imbalance by providing relevant examples through in-context learning, concentrating that assistance on the samples most likely to involve rare categories.

Multimodal retrieval builds a pool of candidate examples, and a trained multimodal language model reranks them to select the most similar ones. The reranker learns from intersection-over-union scores computed from annotated scene-graph triplets, tying its similarity judgments to the structured relationships being predicted.

This selective strategy improves recognition of rare categories without reducing accuracy on common categories. The experiments report a 6.9% improvement in long-tail accuracy and a 2.6% improvement overall. The findings show how routing and task-informed example selection can focus additional contextual support where aggregate performance otherwise hides a substantial weakness.
summary.tldr: SGG-ICL selectively retrieves and reranks contextual examples to improve recognition of rare operating-room relationships without degrading common-category accuracy.

title: Modeling Long-Tail Relations in the Operating Room via In-Context Multimodal Learning

abstract: The Linear Assignment Problem is a fundamental combinatorial optimization task where classical exact solvers ensure optimality but suffer from an $\mathcal{O}(N^{3})$ bottleneck, while recent neural approximations struggle with scalability and exactness. We propose a learning-augmented framework that accelerates exact solvers by predicting dual variables to warm-start the search, backed by a fallback mechanism to preserve worst-case guarantees. Central to our approach is RowDualNet, a lightweight, row-independent architecture that avoids the $\mathcal{O}(N^{2})$ memory bottleneck of graph models, enabling scalable neural warm-starting up to $N=16{,}384$. Feasibility is guaranteed by construction via the Min-Trick mechanism, completely eliminating the need for costly iterative projections. Empirically, our method drastically reduces the search effort of the Jonker-Volgenant (LAPJV) algorithm, yielding robust zero-shot generalization with strict optimality and end-to-end speedups of over 2x on complex synthetic data, 1.25x on real-world tracking, and 1.5x on transportation networks.

paragraphs: The linear assignment problem asks for an optimal matching between two sets. Exact solvers preserve optimality but face a cubic scaling bottleneck, while neural approximations can struggle to remain both scalable and exact. This paper uses learning to provide a better starting point for an exact solver by predicting its dual variables, which guide the optimization search.

Its RowDualNet architecture processes rows independently, avoiding the quadratic memory bottleneck associated with graph-based models and supporting neural warm-starts up to N = 16,384. A mechanism called Min-Trick guarantees feasibility of the predicted starting information by construction, removing the need for iterative projection. A fallback mechanism preserves worst-case guarantees when using the learned initialization.

The method reduces search effort in the Jonker-Volgenant solver while retaining strict optimality. Reported end-to-end speedups exceed 2 times on complex synthetic data, reach 1.25 times on real-world tracking, and reach 1.5 times on transportation networks. The experiments also report robust zero-shot generalization, showing that learned initialization can accelerate exact optimization across the tested settings.
summary.tldr: RowDualNet predicts feasible starting information that speeds up exact assignment solving while preserving optimality and worst-case guarantees.

title: Learning-Augmented Scalable Linear Assignment Problem Optimization via Neural Dual Warm-Starts

abstract: This paper introduces a nonparametric test for conditional mean independence between a manifold-valued $Y$ and Euclidean predictors $X$. The test is built on a new measure called the Manifold Martingale Difference Divergence (MMDD), which characterizes conditional mean dependence by projecting observations onto the tangent space via the logarithmic map. We provide an empirical estimator for the MMDD, establish its asymptotic null distribution, and implement a wild bootstrap procedure for finite-sample inference. Simulations on three representative manifolds demonstrate that the proposed test maintains correct size under the null even when the distribution of $Y$ depends on $X$, in contrast to the severe size distortion exhibited by the distance covariance (dCov) test. At the same time, it achieves competitive power across a range of alternatives. An application to real data illustrates its practical utility.

paragraphs: This paper tests whether the conditional mean of a manifold-valued response changes with ordinary Euclidean predictors. That question is narrower than asking whether the entire response distribution depends on the predictors. A useful test must preserve that distinction, including when other aspects of the distribution change while conditional mean independence still holds.

The authors introduce Manifold Martingale Difference Divergence, or MMDD, to characterize conditional mean dependence. It uses the logarithmic map to project observations into a tangent space. They provide an empirical estimator, derive its asymptotic distribution under the null hypothesis, and use a wild bootstrap procedure for inference with finite samples.

Simulations on three representative manifolds show that the proposed test maintains the correct false-positive rate under the null, even when the response distribution depends on the predictors. The distance covariance test exhibits severe size distortion in these settings. MMDD also achieves competitive power across tested alternatives, and a real-data application illustrates its practical use.
summary.tldr: MMDD tests conditional mean independence for manifold-valued data while distinguishing mean dependence from broader distributional dependence.

title: On Testing Conditional Mean Independence for Manifold-Valued Data

abstract: While explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) empowers large reasoning models (LRMs), it enables the generation of riskier final answers. Current alignment paradigms primarily rely on externally enforced compliance, optimizing models to detect malicious prompts rather than evaluating the safety of their own outputs. We argue that this approach remains largely behavioral: our empirical analysis reveals that ostensibly aligned models lack intrinsic safety understanding, often failing to verify their own response safety and remaining vulnerable to adversarial jailbreaks. To address this fundamental limitation, we propose Safety Internal (SInternal), a framework that internalizes safety specifications by training LRMs exclusively on safety verification tasks to critique their own generated answers using expert reasoning trajectories. We demonstrate that learning to verify induces a strong generalization for response safety, significantly enhancing robustness against out-of-domain jailbreaks. Furthermore, when combined with reinforcement learning, SInternal serves as a superior initialization compared to standard supervised fine-tuning, suggesting that internalizing safety understanding creates a more robust foundation for alignment than merely mimicking safe behaviors. Our codes are available at https://github.com/AlphaLab-USTC/SInternal

paragraphs: Large reasoning models can produce risky final answers despite appearing aligned. The authors’ empirical analysis finds that such models often struggle to verify the safety of their own responses and remain vulnerable to adversarial jailbreaks. They argue that alignment focused on identifying malicious prompts does not sufficiently develop the ability to assess generated answers.

Safety Internal, or SInternal, trains reasoning models exclusively on safety verification tasks. Expert reasoning trajectories teach the models to critique their own generated answers against safety specifications. The central training objective is therefore to practice evaluating response safety, making verification the route through which the model learns those specifications.

The authors demonstrate that this verification training generalizes to response safety and significantly improves robustness against jailbreaks outside the training domain. When followed by reinforcement learning, SInternal also provides a better initialization than standard supervised fine-tuning. summary.tldr: SInternal trains reasoning models to verify their own answers’ safety, improving robustness to unseen jailbreaks and initialization for reinforcement learning.

title: Internalizing Safety Understanding in Large Reasoning Models via Verification

abstract: Transformer-based Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) combine Transformer performance with SNN energy efficiency through an event-driven self-attention mechanism. However, Spiking Transformers still lag behind their Artificial Neural Network (ANN) counterparts. Most existing studies address this issue through new architectural designs, yet few have explored optimization algorithms tailored to Spiking Transformers. We substantiate the excessive noise problem in Spiking Transformer training by quantitatively defining parameter-update noise and, based on this definition, providing theoretical analysis and experimental validation. To address this problem, we propose AdaS, an adaptive gradient descent method for Spiking Transformers. AdaS reduces excessive noise by adaptively incorporating a gradient update component into adaptive optimization. Instead of simply removing noise, AdaS maintains it at an appropriate level to preserve its generalization benefits, thereby improving the performance of Spiking Transformers. We conduct extensive experiments on various Spiking Transformer architectures and datasets from both computer vision and natural language processing. The results demonstrate that the proposed AdaS consistently enhances performance across different Spiking Transformers, validating its effectiveness and generalizability. This work is among the first systematic studies of optimizer design specifically for Spiking Transformers, offering a practical tool to narrow the accuracy gap with ANNs while preserving the energy advantages of spike-based computation. Code is available at https://github.com/CayleyZ/AdaS.

However, Spiking Transformers still lag behind their Artificial Neural Network (ANN) counterparts. Most existing studies address this issue through new architectural designs, yet few have explored optimization algorithms tailored to Spiking Transformers. We substantiate the excessive noise problem in Spiking Transformer training by quantitatively defining parameter-update noise and, based on this definition, providing theoretical analysis and experimental validation. To address this problem, we propose AdaS, an adaptive gradient descent method for Spiking Transformers. AdaS reduces excessive noise by adaptively incorporating a gradient update component into adaptive optimization. Instead of simply removing noise, AdaS maintains it at an appropriate level to preserve its generalization benefits, thereby improving the performance of Spiking Transformers. We conduct extensive experiments on various Spiking Transformer architectures and datasets from both computer vision and natural language processing. The results demonstrate that the proposed AdaS consistently enhances performance across different Spiking Transformers, validating its effectiveness and generalizability. This work is among the first systematic studies of optimizer design specifically for Spiking Transformers, offering a practical tool to narrow the accuracy gap with ANNs while preserving the energy advantages of spike-based computation. Code is available at https://github.com/CayleyZ/AdaS.

paragraphs: Spiking Transformers combine attention mechanisms with event-driven neural computation, aiming to retain the energy advantages of spikes while improving predictive performance. Their accuracy still trails conventional neural networks. This paper examines whether part of that gap comes from how the models are optimized, complementing research focused on changing their architecture.

The researchers define noise in parameter updates and use theoretical analysis and experiments to substantiate an excessive-noise problem during training. Their optimizer, AdaS, adaptively adds a gradient update component to adaptive optimization. Its aim is to regulate noise rather than eliminate it: some noise can help a trained model generalize, while too much can interfere with learning.

Experiments across several Spiking Transformer architectures and datasets in vision and natural language processing report consistent performance improvements. These findings support optimizer design as a practical route toward narrowing the accuracy gap with conventional networks while preserving spike-based computation. The contribution is therefore both a diagnosis of training behavior and an optimization method tailored to that diagnosis.
summary.tldr: AdaS improves Spiking Transformer training by adaptively regulating parameter-update noise while retaining its generalization benefits.

title: AdaS: Adaptive Gradient Descent for Spiking Transformers

abstract: Existing image inpainting frameworks rely on strictly supervised training paradigms, often suffering from an over-reliance on ground-truth reconstruction, which leads to conservative outputs with misaligned creativity and limited diversity. To this end, we propose the first framework to explore Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) for text-guided image inpainting, formulating an efficient online reinforcement learning pipeline that enables flexible, human-aligned aesthetic control via a preference scoring model. Crucially, by decoupling the rigid one-to-one correspondence between text prompts and masked images, our method enables the model to explore diverse, controllable, and high-quality solutions beyond a single target. Furthermore, to balance semantic consistency with physical naturalness at mask boundaries, we introduce a scale-aware dynamic reward mechanism that adaptively emphasizes boundary gradient coherence for small occlusions while prioritizing visual aesthetics in large-scale generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach consistently produces higher-quality results across different backbone architectures such as Stable Diffusion and FLUX, significantly enhancing the generative capacity of base models.
