paragraphs: Image inpainting fills a masked region, but many different completions can be plausible. Training mainly to reproduce a single reference image can favor conservative results and restrict diversity. This paper explores preference-guided learning for text-directed inpainting, allowing the model to pursue aesthetically desirable completions beyond one prescribed target.

The framework investigates GRPO and DPO and introduces an online reinforcement learning pipeline guided by a preference scoring model. It loosens the fixed correspondence between prompts and masked images to support varied, controllable solutions. A scale-aware reward changes emphasis with the size of the missing region, addressing different demands of local repair and larger-scale generation.

For small occlusions, the reward emphasizes gradient coherence at the boundary so the fill connects naturally with surrounding content. For larger regions, visual aesthetics receive greater priority. Experiments across backbones including Stable Diffusion and FLUX report consistently higher-quality outputs and stronger generative capacity. The contribution combines preference-based exploration with rewards that reflect how the inpainting problem changes as the masked area grows.
summary.tldr: Preference-guided inpainting encourages diverse completions while adapting rewards to balance boundary consistency and visual aesthetics.

title: Preference-Enhanced Reinforcement Learning for Pluralistic Image Inpainting

abstract: The integration of foundation models (FMs) into robotics has accelerated real-world deployment, while introducing new safety challenges arising from open-ended semantic reasoning and embodied physical action. These challenges require safety notions beyond physical constraint satisfaction. In this position paper, we characterize FM-enabled robot safety along three dimensions: action safety (physical feasibility and constraint compliance), decision safety (semantic and contextual appropriateness), and human-centered safety (conformance to human intent, norms, and expectations). We argue that existing approaches, including static verification, monolithic controllers, and end-to-end learned policies, are insufficient in settings where tasks, environments, and human expectations are open-ended, long-tailed, and subject to adaptation over time. To address this gap, we propose modular safety guardrails, consisting of monitoring (evaluation) and intervention layers, as an architectural foundation for comprehensive safety across the autonomy stack. Beyond modularity, we highlight possible cross-layer co-design opportunities through representation alignment and conservatism allocation to enable faster, less conservative, and more effective safety enforcement. We call on the community to explore richer guardrail modules and principled co-design strategies to advance safe real-world physical AI deployment.

paragraphs: Foundation models connect open-ended interpretation with robots that act physically. This paper argues that robot safety must therefore extend beyond whether an action is physically feasible or obeys constraints. It distinguishes action safety, the contextual appropriateness of decisions, and alignment with human intentions, norms, and expectations.

The authors argue that static verification, monolithic controllers, and end-to-end learned policies are insufficient when tasks and environments are open-ended and human expectations change. They propose modular guardrails distributed across the autonomy stack. These combine monitoring layers that evaluate behavior with intervention layers that can respond when safety concerns arise.

The paper also identifies opportunities to design layers together. Aligning their representations and coordinating how conservatively they operate could make enforcement faster, less restrictive, and more effective. These are proposed opportunities, rather than established performance guarantees. The research agenda is to develop richer modules and principled coordination between them, with the aim of addressing physical, semantic, and human-centered safety within a common architectural approach.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes modular monitoring and intervention layers to address physical, contextual, and human-centered robot safety.

abstract: To achieve good generalization in supervised learning, the training and testing examples are usually required to be drawn from the same source distribution. In this paper we propose a method to relax this requirement in the context of logistic regression. Assuming Dp and Da are two sets of examples drawn from two mismatched distributions, where Da are fully labeled and Dp partially labeled, our objective is to complete the labels of Dp . We introduce an auxiliary variable μ for each example in Da to reﬂect its mismatch with Dp . Under an appropriate constraint the μ’s are estimated as a byproduct, along with the classiﬁer. We also present an active learning approach for selecting the labeled examples in Dp . The proposed algorithm, called “Migratory-Logit” or M-Logit, is demonstrated successfully on simulated as well as real data sets.

paragraphs: Supervised learning commonly assumes that training and test examples come from the same distribution. This paper relaxes that requirement for logistic regression. It considers a fully labeled auxiliary dataset and a partially labeled primary dataset drawn from a different distribution, with the goal of filling in the primary dataset’s missing labels.

The proposed method, Migratory-Logit or M-Logit, introduces an auxiliary variable for each example in the auxiliary dataset. These variables represent how the auxiliary examples mismatch the primary data. Under an appropriate constraint, the method estimates them along with the classifier. The distribution mismatch is therefore represented within training instead of treating both sources as interchangeable.

The paper also presents an active learning approach for choosing which primary examples to label. This addresses how to obtain supervision from the distribution where predictions are needed, alongside using the already labeled auxiliary source. Demonstrations on simulated and real datasets are reported as successful. The contribution is a logistic-regression method for combining these two sources while explicitly accounting for their mismatch.
summary.tldr: M-Logit learns from a labeled auxiliary source while estimating its mismatch with the partially labeled dataset it aims to complete.

title: Logistic regression with an auxiliary data source

abstract: Temporal-difference (TD) networks have been introduced as a formalism for expressing and learning grounded world knowledge in a predictive form (Sutton & Tanner, 2005). Like conventional TD(0) methods, the learning algorithm for TD networks uses 1-step backups to train prediction units about future events. In conventional TD learning, the TD(λ) algorithm is often used to do more general multi-step backups of future predictions. In our work, we introduce a generalization of the 1-step TD network specification that is based on the TD(λ) learning algorithm, creating TD(λ) networks. We present experimental results that show TD(λ) networks can learn solutions in more complex environments than TD networks. We also show that in problems that can be solved by TD networks, TD(λ) networks generally learn solutions much faster than their 1-step counterparts. Finally, we present an analysis of our algorithm that shows that the computational cost of TD(λ) networks is only slightly more than that of TD networks.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference networks represent world knowledge as predictions about future events. Their original learning procedure trains prediction units using one-step backups, so each update draws on a prediction one step ahead. This paper generalizes that network specification using TD(lambda), bringing more general multi-step backups into the learning of interconnected predictions.

The resulting TD(lambda) networks extend the role that TD(lambda) already plays in conventional temporal-difference learning. The technical aim is to make multi-step prediction updates available within the network formalism. This matters because the network’s learned knowledge is itself predictive, so changing how future predictions inform updates changes how that knowledge can be acquired.

Experiments show that TD(lambda) networks can learn solutions in more complex environments than the original TD networks. On problems the original networks can solve, the new networks generally learn much faster. An analysis also finds that their computational cost is only slightly higher. The reported combination is broader demonstrated learning capability and faster learning with modest additional computation.
summary.tldr: TD(lambda) networks add multi-step updates, showing faster learning and solutions in more complex environments with only slightly greater computational cost.

title: TD(lambda) networks: temporal-difference networks with eligibility traces

abstract: Nonlinear ICA may not result in nonlinear blind source separation, since solutions to nonlinear ICA are highly non-unique. In practice, the nonlinearity in the data generation procedure is usually not strong. Thus it is reasonable to select the solution with the mixing procedure close to linear. In this paper we propose to solve nonlinear ICA with the “minimal nonlinear distortion” principle. This is achieved by incorporating a regularization term to minimize the mean square error between the mixing mapping and the best-ﬁtting linear one. As an application, the proposed method helps to identify linear, non-Gaussian, and acyclic causal models when mild nonlinearity exists in the data generation procedure. Using this method to separate daily returns of a set of stocks, we successfully identify their linear causal relations. The resulting causal relations give some interesting insights into the stock market.

In this paper we propose to solve nonlinear ICA with the “minimal nonlinear distortion” principle. This is achieved by incorporating a regularization term to minimize the mean square error between the mixing mapping and the best-ﬁtting linear one. As an application, the proposed method helps to identify linear, non-Gaussian, and acyclic causal models when mild nonlinearity exists in the data generation procedure. Using this method to separate daily returns of a set of stocks, we successfully identify their linear causal relations. The resulting causal relations give some interesting insights into the stock market.

paragraphs: Nonlinear independent component analysis can produce many different solutions, so finding independent components does not necessarily recover the original sources. This paper addresses that ambiguity using a preference motivated by mildly nonlinear data generation: among possible solutions, favor one whose mixing process stays close to a linear mapping.

The proposed minimal nonlinear distortion principle becomes a regularization term in the learning objective. It measures the mean squared difference between the mixing mapping and its best-fitting linear counterpart. The method therefore permits nonlinearity while discouraging unnecessary departure from linear mixing, giving the otherwise highly nonunique problem an additional selection criterion.

The authors apply the method to identifying linear, non-Gaussian, acyclic causal models when the data-generation process contains mild nonlinearity. In an application to daily stock returns, they report identifying linear causal relationships and obtaining insights into the market. These findings illustrate the proposed principle in the stated modeling setting. The mild-nonlinearity motivation is central to why proximity to a linear solution is considered useful here.
summary.tldr: A regularizer favors nearly linear mixing in nonlinear ICA to address solution ambiguity when data generation is only mildly nonlinear.

title: Nonlinear independent component analysis with minimal nonlinear distortion

abstract: Multi-instance learning and semi-supervised learning are diﬀerent branches of machine learning. The former attempts to learn from a training set consists of labeled bags each containing many unlabeled instances; the latter tries to exploit abundant unlabeled instances when learning with a small number of labeled examples. In this paper, we establish a bridge between these two branches by showing that multi-instance learning can be viewed as a special case of semi-supervised learning. Based on this recognition, we propose the MissSVM algorithm which addresses multi-instance learning using a special semisupervised support vector machine. Experiments show that solving multi-instance problems from the view of semi-supervised learning is feasible, and the MissSVM algorithm is competitive with state-of-the-art multiinstance learning algorithms.
originalAbstract: Multi-instance learning and semi-supervised learning are diﬀerent branches of machine learning. The former attempts to learn from a training set consists of labeled bags each containing many unlabeled instances; the latter tries to exploit abundant unlabeled instances when learning with a small number of labeled examples. In this paper, we establish a bridge between these two branches by showing that multi-instance learning can be viewed as a special case of semi-supervised learning. Based on this recognition, we propose the MissSVM algorithm which addresses multi-instance learning using a special semisupervised support vector machine. Experiments show that solving multi-instance problems from the view of semi-supervised learning is feasible, and the MissSVM algorithm is competitive with state-of-the-art multiinstance learning algorithms.

paragraphs: Multi-instance learning provides labels for bags of examples while leaving the individual examples unlabeled. Semi-supervised learning instead combines a small collection of labeled examples with many unlabeled ones. Both settings involve incomplete information about individual labels, but their training data are organized differently. This paper establishes a formal connection between them.

The central result shows that multi-instance learning can be viewed as a special case of semi-supervised learning. This perspective makes methods from one branch available for addressing problems in the other. Building on the connection, the authors introduce MissSVM, which uses a specially constructed semi-supervised support vector machine to solve multi-instance learning problems.

Experiments show that this approach is feasible and that MissSVM is competitive with state-of-the-art multi-instance algorithms. The evidence supports the usefulness of the connection as an algorithm-design principle, beyond its conceptual interest. The reported finding is competitiveness, rather than a claim that the semi-supervised formulation always improves on methods designed directly for labeled bags.
summary.tldr: The paper casts multi-instance learning as a special case of semi-supervised learning and develops the competitive MissSVM algorithm from that connection.

title: On the relation between multi-instance learning and semi-supervised learning

abstract: Recent developments in programmable, highly parallel Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) have enabled high performance implementations of machine learning algorithms. We describe a solver for Support Vector Machine training, using Platt's Sequential Minimal Optimization algorithm and an adaptive first and second order working set selection heuristic, which achieves speedups of 9-35x over LIBSVM running on a traditional processor. We also present a GPU-based system for SVM classification which achieves speedups of 81-138x over LibSVM (5-24x over our own CPU-based SVM classifier).
originalAbstract: Recent developments in programmable, highly parallel Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) have enabled high performance implementations of machine learning algorithms. We describe a solver for Support Vector Machine training, using Platt's Sequential Minimal Optimization algorithm and an adaptive first and second order working set selection heuristic, which achieves speedups of 9-35x over LIBSVM running on a traditional processor. We also present a GPU-based system for SVM classification which achieves speedups of 81-138x over LibSVM (5-24x over our own CPU-based SVM classifier).

paragraphs: This paper uses programmable graphics processors to accelerate support vector machines. It addresses both training, which constructs the classifier, and classification, which applies it to examples. The motivation is the substantial parallel computing capacity of GPUs, which creates opportunities for faster implementations of machine learning algorithms.

For training, the authors implement a solver based on Platt's Sequential Minimal Optimization algorithm. It uses an adaptive working-set selection heuristic incorporating first- and second-order information. Working-set selection determines which parts of the optimization problem receive attention during an update. The reported training implementation runs 9–35 times faster than LIBSVM on a conventional processor.

The paper also presents a GPU classification system. It achieves reported speedups of 81–138 times over LIBSVM and 5–24 times over the authors' own CPU classifier. Those separate comparisons matter because the observed gain depends on the CPU implementation used as the reference. Together, the results demonstrate substantial acceleration for both stages of SVM use in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: GPU implementations accelerate SVM training by 9–35 times and classification by 81–138 times relative to LIBSVM in the reported comparisons.

title: Fast support vector machine training and classification on graphics processors

abstract: The success of kernel methods including support vector machines (SVMs) strongly depends on the design of appropriate kernels. While initially kernels were designed in order to handle fixed-length data, their extension to unordered, variable-length data became more than necessary for real pattern recognition problems such as object recognition and bioinformatics. We focus in this paper on object recognition using a new type of kernel referred to as "context-dependent". Objects, seen as constellations of local features (interest points,regions, etc.), are matched by minimizing an energy function mixing (1) a fidelity term which measures the quality of feature matching, (2) a neighborhood criteria which captures the object geometry and (3) a regularization term. We will show that the fixed-point of this energy is a "context-dependent" kernel ("CDK") which also satisfies the Mercer condition. Experiments conducted on object recognition show that when plugging our kernel in SVMs, we clearly outperform SVMs with "context-free" kernels.

paragraphs: Object recognition often represents an object through a collection of local features, such as interest points or regions. These collections can vary in size and lack a fixed ordering, complicating kernel design. The paper develops a context-dependent kernel that accounts for both feature matching and the geometric relationships among features.

Matching is expressed through an energy function with three ingredients. A fidelity term measures the quality of feature correspondences, a neighborhood term captures object geometry, and a regularization term completes the objective. This construction allows the surrounding arrangement of features to influence the resulting comparison between objects.

The authors show that the energy’s fixed point defines a context-dependent kernel satisfying the Mercer condition, establishing its suitability for kernel methods. In object-recognition experiments, SVMs using this kernel clearly outperform SVMs using context-free kernels. The results support incorporating geometric context into object comparisons, while the theoretical result connects the matching construction to a valid kernel.
summary.tldr: A valid context-dependent kernel combines local feature similarity with object geometry and improves SVM recognition in the reported experiments.

title: Robust matching and recognition using context-dependent kernels

abstract: We introduce a new algorithm for binary classification in the selective sampling protocol. Our algorithm uses Regularized Least Squares (RLS) as base classifier, and for this reason it can be efficiently run in any RKHS. Unlike previous margin-based semi-supervised algorithms, our sampling condition hinges on a simultaneous upper bound on bias and variance of the RLS estimate under a simple linear label noise model. This fact allows us to prove performance bounds that hold for an arbitrary sequence of instances. In particular, we show that our sampling strategy approximates the margin of the Bayes optimal classifier to any desired accuracy $\ve$ by asking $\widetilde{\scO}\bigl(d/\ve^2\bigr)$ queries (in the RKHS case $d$ is replaced by a suitable spectral quantity). While these are the standard rates in the fully supervised i.i.d.\ case, the best previously known result in our harder setting was $\widetilde{\scO}\bigl(d^3/\ve^4\bigr)$. Preliminary experiments show that some of our algorithms also exhibit a good practical performance.

In particular, we show that our sampling strategy approximates the margin of the Bayes optimal classifier to any desired accuracy $\ve$ by asking $\widetilde{\scO}\bigl(d/\ve^2\bigr)$ queries (in the RKHS case $d$ is replaced by a suitable spectral quantity). paragraphs: Selective sampling lets a classifier decide which incoming examples need labels. This paper proposes a binary classification algorithm using regularized least squares, which also supports efficient operation in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The key question is how to request labels while retaining meaningful performance guarantees.

Its sampling rule uses a simultaneous upper bound on the estimator's bias and variance under a simple linear label-noise model. This supports guarantees for an arbitrary sequence of instances, rather than requiring the instances to be independently sampled. The noise-model assumption remains part of the setting in which the analysis applies.

The strategy approximates the Bayes-optimal classifier's margin to accuracy epsilon using roughly d/epsilon squared label queries, with logarithmic factors suppressed. In kernel spaces, a suitable spectral quantity replaces d. This improves the previous bound of roughly d cubed/epsilon to the fourth in the same harder setting, matching standard rates from fully supervised independent sampling. Preliminary experiments also show good practical performance for some of the proposed algorithms.
summary.tldr: Bias-and-variance-based label selection improves query bounds for arbitrary instance sequences under a linear label-noise model.

title: Robust bounds for classification via selective sampling

abstract: The problem of choosing fast implementations for a class of recursive algorithms such as the fast Fourier transforms can be formulated as an optimization problem over the language generated by a suitably defined grammar. We propose a novel algorithm that solves this problem by reducing it to maximizing an objective function over the sinks of a directed acyclic graph. This algorithm valuates nodes using Monte-Carlo and grows a subgraph in the most promising directions by considering local maximum k-armed bandits. When used inside an adaptive linear transform library, it cuts down the search time by an order of magnitude compared to the existing algorithm. In some cases, the performance of the implementations found is also increased by up to 10% which is of considerable practical importance since it consequently improves the performance of all applications using the library.

We propose a novel algorithm that solves this problem by reducing it to maximizing an objective function over the sinks of a directed acyclic graph. This algorithm valuates nodes using Monte-Carlo and grows a subgraph in the most promising directions by considering local maximum k-armed bandits. When used inside an adaptive linear transform library, it cuts down the search time by an order of magnitude compared to the existing algorithm. In some cases, the performance of the implementations found is also increased by up to 10% which is of considerable practical importance since it consequently improves the performance of all applications using the library.

paragraphs: A recursive algorithm can often be implemented in many different ways, with different execution speeds. This paper studies how to choose fast implementations when the possibilities can be described by a grammar, including algorithms such as fast Fourier transforms. The challenge is to search this structured collection without spending excessive time evaluating alternatives.

The proposed algorithm reformulates the task as maximizing an objective over the terminal nodes, or sinks, of a directed acyclic graph. It estimates node values through Monte Carlo sampling and expands a subgraph toward promising choices. Local multi-armed bandit problems guide this expansion, connecting decisions about where to search with sampled evidence about implementation quality.

Inside an adaptive linear transform library, the method reduces search time by an order of magnitude compared with the existing algorithm. In some cases, the resulting implementations also perform up to 10% better. The two benefits are distinct: faster tuning reduces the effort needed to choose an implementation, while faster implementations can improve applications that use the library.
summary.tldr: A graph search guided by sampling and bandit decisions substantially reduces library tuning time and sometimes finds faster implementations.

title: Bandit-based optimization on graphs with application to library performance tuning
